#2856. Netflix, Amazon, Fox to bid for 2030 men's World Cup rights; Disney out

Netflix, Amazon, YouTube and Fox are all expected to submit offers to win the U.S. media rights for the 2030 men's World Cup before today's deadline, according to people familiar with the matter — but Disney will not be putting in a bid.

Fox and NBCU's Telemundo are the incumbent rights holders. FIFA would prefer to sell both the English and Spanish rights together, to one buyer, for the 2030 World Cup, to be held in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Media companies also have the right to bid on the 2034 World Cup, which will be held in Saudi Arabia.

CNBC previously reported that media executives are planning on the winning bid coming in around $1.5 billion — or maybe even higher — although that amount could vary somewhat depending on whether both 2030 and 2034 are acquired.

FIFA is open to the idea of a potential partnership bid in which rights are split between a traditional broadcaster and a streamer, to maximize reach. Still, unlike in other countries where there are government mandates on airing games for free, FIFA will not mandate that a subscription streamer sublicense games. That decision will be up to the winning bidder.

FIFA is satisfied that enough people in the U.S. already have a Netflix or Amazon Prime Video subscription that reach won't be an issue, according to people familiar with the matter. The 2027 Women's World Cup will be on Netflix in the U.S., and Netflix plans to air all of the games without a partner.

Disney/ESPN will not be bidding, according to people familiar with the matter. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro said he was interested in World Cup rights earlier this year at CNBC Sport x Boardroom's Game Plan Summit.

In recent weeks, ESPN ran the numbers and couldn't get to $1.5 billion or higher while also having to save money for NHL, MLB and European soccer — English Premier League and Champions League — all of which will likely renew their media rights deals in 2027, said the people, who asked not to be named because the discussions were private. ESPN looked into entering a bid with a partner but ultimately decided not to bid, one of the people said.

NBCUniversal still hasn't made a decision on bidding, potentially putting Telemundo in jeopardy of losing the games for 2030, according to a person familiar with the matter. NBCUniversal has already spent billions on NBA and also needs to save money for both MLB and EPL potentially as well as the NFL, which will likely be a 2028 negotiation.

Skydance and Apple will not bid, according to people familiar with the matter.

A FIFA spokesperson declined to comment, citing confidentiality of the tender process.

FIFA executives plan to travel to the U.S. next week to meet personally with bidders to assess their bids and potentially get final offers. FIFA plans to choose a winner before the end of the year.

#2855. NFL Week 11: How to watch every football game this week during the 2026 season

If you buy something through a link in this article, we may earn commission.

Week 11 of the 2026-27 NFL season is here, featuring matchups between the Indianapolis Colts and the Houston Texans, the Cincinnati Bengals vs. Washington Commanders, and the full slate of Sunday games.

Are you ready to watch some football? This season, NFL games will air across 10+ channels and streaming platforms. If you're worried about the challenge of following your favorite team through the upcoming season, from the NFL season opener to the 2027 Super Bowl, Yahoo Sports has you covered. Here's your playbook for how to watch the 2026-27 NFL season.

TV channels: ESPN, NBC, CBS, Fox, ABC and NFL Network

Streaming: Prime Video, Peacock, ESPN+, Paramount+, NFL+, Netflix

Indianapolis Colts vs. Houston Texans: 8:15 p.m. (Prime Video)

Baltimore Ravens vs. Carolina Panthers: 1 p.m. (Fox)

Miami Dolphins vs. Buffalo Bills: 1 p.m. (CBS)

New Orleans Saints vs. Chicago Bears: 1 p.m. (Fox)

Tennessee Titans vs. Dallas Cowboys: 1 p.m. (Fox)

Tampa Bay Buccaneers vs. Detroit Lions: 1 p.m. (Fox)

Arizona Cardinals vs. Kansas City Chiefs: 1 p.m. (CBS)

Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Philadelphia Eagles: 1 p.m. (CBS)

New York Jets vs. Los Angeles Chargers: 4:05 p.m. (Fox)

Jacksonville Jaguars vs. New York Giants: 4:25 p.m. (CBS)

Las Vegas Raiders vs. Denver Broncos: 4:25 p.m. (CBS)

Minnesota Vikings vs. San Francisco 49ers (International Game): 8:20 p.m. (NBC/Peacock)

Cincinnati Bengals vs. Washington Commanders: 8:15 p.m. (ESPN/ABC)

Many NFL games are broadcast on local channels, so if you're looking to catch an in-market game, it may be as simple as turning on your TV (or setting up a digital TV antenna) or finding a live TV streaming service that carries the correct RSN (Regional Sports Network). A $7 monthly subscription to NFL+ will let you watch every local and primetime game live on your phone — but only a select few regular-season games on your TV. You could also spring for the uber-expensive NFL Sunday Ticket package to get every out-of-market Sunday game of the season.

When it comes to nationally broadcast games, the NFL typically airs on ESPN, NBC, CBS, Fox, ABC and NFL Network. Thursday Night Football games stream exclusively on Amazon Prime Video; select football games stream exclusively on Peacock; games on CBS stream live on Paramount+ Premium; and select games stream on ESPN's app this season. For those keeping count, that's six channels and four streaming platforms to keep up with. Plus, Netflix is once again hosting at least two Christmas Day matches, a playoff game and the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve battle, so don't forget to add that subscription into the mix.

Confused? You're not alone. Here's a breakdown of the platforms we recommend checking out so that tuning into your favorite team's games will be as easy as simply turning on the TV.

To recap, here are all the ways you can watch NFL games in 2026.

YouTube TV gets you nearly every channel you need to watch the NFL, including Fox, NBC, ABC, CBS, ESPN and NFL Network. Plus, YouTube TV is the home of NFL Sunday Ticket. The Sunday Ticket package, while pricey on its own, gets you ALL the Sunday out-of-market games (160+ games per season).

Current pricing for new users for the 2026 Sunday Ticket is $27/month for four months. Factor in the cost of YouTube TV's Sports and News plan at $49.99/month for your first five months, then $71.99/month thereafter.

That's $76.99/month for the next four months of YouTube TV + NFL Sunday Ticket. You can also opt, with or without a YouTube TV subscription, to pay for the rest of the season of Sunday Ticket upfront on its own for $108.

Fubo's Sports package gives you access to ESPN, NFL Network, Fox, ABC, CBS, NBC, and 20+ more live channels. Starting at $54.99/month for your first month, the live TV streaming service is definitely pricey (though certainly not the most expensive option on this list), but it offers most channels you'll need to watch both the NFL preseason and regular season.

DirecTV's Choice tier (currently $78.98/month after fees for your first two months) gets you access to nearly every channel you need to watch NFL games throughout the year: NFL Network, ESPN, NBC, CBS, Fox, SEC Network and an abundance of local RSNs. DirecTV Choice (and most other DirecTV plans) also come with free ESPN Unlimited, which gets you access to every ESPN channel, an amazing value and a must for watching tons of college and pro sports all year round.

Amazon Prime Video is home to the NFL's Thursday Night Football. On top of Amazon Prime Video, an Amazon Prime subscription includes free shipping, exclusive deals, access to the Prime Day sales events, Amazon Music, a year of free GrubHub+ and more.

A standard Amazon Prime subscription is $15 monthly or $139 annually, but discounts are available for students and those on qualified government assistance. You can try Amazon Prime free for 30 days.

A basic $6.99 per month (or $49.99 annually) NFL+ subscription will get you live local and primetime regular and preseason NFL games exclusively on your phone or tablet, plus live audio for every game of the season across supported devices and access to NFL Network.

NFL+ Premium, while a little pricier at $14.99 per month (or $99.99 annually), also includes access to NFL RedZone, plus full and condensed replays of every game across supported devices.

#2854. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#2853. As Sanofi's Pompe drug shortage drags on, some patients struggle to access treatments

Two weeks ago, Monique Griffin got a troubling email.

The French drugmaker Sanofi told her that a shipping delay had interrupted supply of the drug that she relies on to manage her rare muscle-wasting disease. Her next infusion was canceled. Griffin, who is 51 and uses a wheelchair due to Pompe disease, fears what will happen if the shortage isn't resolved soon.

"You're basically letting the disease take over again," she said. "It's terrifying."

More than three months after initial reports of supply problems with treatments for Pompe disease, the disruption drags on, with more patients learning their infusions have been canceled. Sanofi said it has made progress restoring the supply to patients in some countries, but added that shipping delays could interrupt infusions for some U.S. patients through the end of November.

For more stories like this, sign up for the CNBC Cures newsletter.

A Sanofi spokesperson said there were no issues with drug quality and the company is "committed to ensuring that the most vulnerable patients receive treatment first during this period." The company added that patients should speak with a health professional before taking another treatment, adding, "these medicines are not interchangeable."

In a statement, the Food and Drug Administration said "patient access to these treatments is a priority for the agency and we have offered our assistance to Sanofi on anything needed to help ensure all patient needs are met."

About one in every 19,000 babies is born with Pompe disease, which is named after the Dutch pathologist who discovered the condition nearly a century ago.

Patients lack an enzyme for breaking down a complex sugar, causing a toxic buildup of glycogen inside their cells. Their muscles weaken and their heart can become enlarged. They have trouble breathing and eating. Left untreated, the disease is often fatal.

Sanofi's Lumizyme and a second-generation version, Nexviazyme, replace the missing enzyme, protecting the patient's muscles. Patients typically receive Sanofi's drugs every two weeks.

"It's a lifeline," said Jenna Yarborough, a rare disease advocate whose two children with Pompe disease have not been affected by the drug shortage.

While Pompe disease patients rely on Sanofi's drugs, several other treatments have entered clinical trials, including separate gene therapies from AskBio and Astellas Pharma.

Sanofi says the drug shortage is the result of issues at its manufacturing facility in Ireland, which public documents show the company has known about for several months. The FDA inspected the plant between January 12 and January 20, 2026 and found violations involving two unrelated drugs. The company began responding to the violations in February, but on June 22, the FDA sent the company a warning letter saying it had still not addressed the "underlying failure" to comply with manufacturing requirements. Addressing the FDA's ongoing concerns has contributed to the supply disruption of the Pompe therapies, according to Sanofi.

There's a sense of frustration within the Pompe community that the company did not do enough to warn patients about the potential for a supply disruption. Ryan Colburn, a person living with Pompe who is active in the advocacy space, says many patients were unaware of the manufacturing issues at Sanofi and were left with no way to prepare for them. "The lack of proactive transparency and apparent lack of buffer are of huge concern for any medicine that people's lives and well-being depend on access to," Colburn said.

A spokesperson for Sanofi responded, "As the situation evolved, and the extent of the disruption became clearer, we engaged global and U.S. patient advocacy organizations, patients and clinicians to inform them, and we have worked to continue to keep these groups and individuals updated through regular communications. We remain committed to continuity of care and to transparent, ongoing communication with the Pompe community as we work to stabilize supply."

Chelsey McGee's 10-year-old son Logan has taken Lumizyme every two weeks since he was diagnosed with Pompe disease as an infant. While his infusions haven't been canceled yet, she's concerned that missing even one appointment will damage his heart. Sanofi's drug has kept him healthy enough to play soccer.

"It's important that we stay on his timeline and keep his heart healthy," she said.

McGee, who lives in Minneapolis, is frustrated by what she says is a lack of transparency from Sanofi. She discovered the FDA cited the pharmaceutical company for manufacturing problems by searching the agency's website, not from the company.

Griffin, who lives in Orlando, has taken Lumizyme since 2010 when she was diagnosed with an adult-onset version of the disease. The diagnosis came after she became so fatigued that she fell while carrying groceries and suffered a concussion.

She knows what it's like to go without her infusions. She missed a few appointments earlier this year due to an insurance mix-up. She likened it to having "a really bad flu." She became extremely fatigued, struggled to breathe and started to feel pain in her legs, arms and back.

Pompe is a progressive disease, meaning it gets worse over time. She worries most about losing the strength to breathe. She sleeps with assisted ventilation.

She works in the theme parks industry and is hoping to attend a conference this week. While her Lumizyme infusions remain on hold, she hopes to get through the week of meetings "on caffeine and goodwill."

#2852. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#2851. Amid recent banking outages, should you start carrying cash again? Top advisors weigh in

For years, Americans have moved away from using physical U.S. currency in favor of credit, debit and digital payments. But amid the recent outages affecting some consumer banking services, experts say it's wise to revisit cash.

JPMorgan Chase on Monday reported a technical issue that disrupted some consumer banking services, with ripple effects extending to several major U.S. banks and the peer-to-peer payments network Zelle. A day later, a separate outage affected Apple, temporarily disrupting Apple Pay and iCloud, the service that keeps data available across various Apple devices.

Those reports came on the heels of separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

As technology outages expose vulnerabilities across parts of the U.S. economy, some top advisors say consumers should reconsider keeping physical money on hand.

"This is about preparedness, not panic," said David La Placa, CEO of Intellectus Partners in San Francisco, which ranked No. 92 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. "I think keeping some cash at home is a reasonable starting point for many households."

La Placa advises consumers to "build redundancy" into their financial lives.

"Maintain access to at least a second financial institution, keep a backup credit card from a different issuer and make sure you have more than one way to access liquidity," he said.

A client's cash management should be diversified, said Seth Fierston, a certified financial planner and co-president of Fierston Financial Group in West Hartford, Connecticut. The firm ranked No. 22 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list.

Having multiple accounts at brokerages or banks and various ways to move money, including Automated Clearing House, or ACH, wire, check, Venmo or Zelle, "can help mitigate technology risk," Fierston said. "One of our guiding principles is flexibility."

When it comes to everyday transactions, Americans are increasingly relying on digital forms of payment.

These days, only about 46% of Americans carry cash with them always or most of the time, according to a survey of nearly 10,000 adults conducted between May and June by the Pew Research Center, a nonpartisan research group.

Roughly 42% of U.S. adults said they don't use cash for any purchases in a typical week, up from 24% in 2015, Pew found.

Young adults are the least likely to carry physical currency. Among adults under 30, 51% said they go completely cashless, according to the survey.

"I recommend to my clients that they always keep three days of average cash spend on hand given the uncertainty of life in general," said Tim Lootens, CFP, managing director at Chilton Capital Management in Houston, which ranked No. 7 on this year's Financial Advisor 100.

Considering the recent technical troubles, Lootens said consumers should keep even more cash at the ready.

"We've had the Microsoft Outlook outage, the FAA ground shutdown and now banking disruption," he said. "This makes me think five to seven days may be a better number."

The right amount is as psychological as it is financial, he added. "The ability to access cash and having comfort knowing it is there when needed is so important," he said.

Brian Vendig, president and chief investment officer at MJP Wealth Advisors, which ranked No. 42 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100, also said he recommends holding a dollar amount that corresponds with a household's discretionary living expenses. He advised having enough for at least one to two weeks, depending on their needs.

While there is little precedent for a banking or payment system outage lasting more than a few business days, Vendig said, a one- to two-week cash reserve provides a "reasonable buffer" for essentials such as groceries, gas and other necessities, if electronic payments become unavailable.

"We apply this range because it is also an emotional concern for most people, and they might want to have a little extra saved at home due to the size of their household and having a little extra 'peace of mind' guarantee," he said.

Vendig said he recommends stashing extra cash in a secure location at home for emergency needs.

Vendig also said consumers should be vigilant in ensuring their electronic devices have the most recent software security patches installed.

Criminals will try to exploit moments of uncertainty, experts say.

"Consumers should assume they will be targeted," said Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial crime group.

"[This week's] reported bank outages are likely to cause widespread confusion and fear among consumers about losing access to their money," he said. "Criminals will try to exploit that anxiety by pushing victims to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access."

As always, "stay alert, never click on links in unexpected bank messages and never share personal information such as passwords or PINs," he advised. "If you need to reach your bank, use a trusted, official channel," Timm said.

Kevin Durant scored 21 points and Reed Sheppard knocked down six triples off the bench on his way to 20 points to lead the Houston Rockets past the Indiana Pacers 119-104 despite Houston losing star center Alperen Sengun to injury. Sengun was poked in the eye and hit in the face and did not return, and Houston head coach Ime Udoka said he's not sure how much time Sengun will miss. And finally, to round out the double-digit scorers, Tari Eason had 11. Sengun had 7 points and 7 boards in just 14 minutes of action.

Pascal Siakam led the way for Indiana with 24 points, and Kelly Oubre Jr. had 17, but the Rockets led for most of the way in this one, despite both teams shooting 49 percent on the night. The difference was Houston won the rebound battle 46-35 and held the Pacers to 10-for-35 from deep. That's not enough to overcome Houston on a night they are shooting well. The Rockets just have too many weapons.

Steven Adams and Oscar Tshiebwe mostly filled in for Sengun, playing 27 minutes between them, but combined for just 8 points and 9 boards. You'll likley see more of the same if Sengun misses time, and if he misses extended time, you could see some Jabari Smith Jr. at a small-ball five on the nights there's no Steve-O.

The Rockets now move to 12-4 on the season and sit squarely in third right now in the Western Conference. They will return to action on Friday with a road contest against the Denver Nuggets. Houston will hopefully have Sengun ready for his match with Nikola Jokic.

#2849. Broncos sign CB Riley Moss to a four-year contract extension worth $67 million

According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero, the Denver Broncos are finalizing a four-year contract extension with cornerback Riley Moss. It is a four-year deal worth up to $67 million dollars as the Broncos lock up one of their key starters in their secondary.

The story heading into the season was: which player would the Broncos re-sign? Cornerback Riley Moss, whom the Broncos spent a 3rd-round pick on, or cornerback Ja'Quan McMillian, a former undrafted free agent this coaching staff inherited? Well, at least for now, it appears Moss is their choice. He signed a four-year extension, which makes him the 23rd highest-paid cornerback in the league right now.

While many wanted the team to re-sign Ja'Quan McMillian, and honestly, they may still, Moss is worthy of this extension. He has one of the hardest jobs in the NFL, which is playing opposite star cornerback Pat Surtain II. Teams avoid going after Surtain II, which means more targets go Moss's way. Yes, he has had some struggles, and the refs, for whatever reason, love to call phantom penalties on him, but he has been a key part of the success of the Broncos' secondary these past few years. Now, both he and Surtain II are locked up and will keep their secondary strong for the foreseeable future.

Now, all eyes go to star slot corner Ja'Quan McMillian. He remains a pending free agent next season, and the narrative always was that the Broncos will likely have to pick between him and Moss. Well, Moss has an extension, so was the decision made? Perhaps, but there is some room for optimism, in my opinion. Slot corners are typically cheaper than outside corners, and the struggles of Jahdae Barron recently could have the Broncos wanting to bring back both. With that said, you do have Jahdae Barron, a former first-round pick who profiles as a slot corner and someone who many assumed would take McMillian's job when he was drafted. #2848. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#2847. Anthropic IPO: Investors who flip the stock may face brokerage penalty

Retail investors with access to Anthropic's initial public offering who sell the stock quickly after buying could get penalized by their brokerage firm.

Anthropic said in an IPO prospectus that it expected to make shares available to retail investors through various brokerages, including Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, E*Trade and some of their respective affiliates.

Follow CNBC's live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut

These broker-dealers have different "anti-flipping" policies meant to discourage investors who purchase IPO shares — including those of Anthropic — from dumping them quickly. Charles Schwab is the only one that doesn't have such a policy in place.

"One purpose is to discourage 'flippers' who are just buying with the hope of making a quick profit," Jay Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida, said in an email. "Their selling could put downward pressure on the price once trading starts."

Investors who run afoul of anti-flipping rules may be prohibited from accessing future IPOs, perhaps for several months or even more than a year for repeat offenders. In the worst case, the brokerage may bar them from all future IPOs.

These policies apply only to retail investors who place an order with their brokerage firm to buy the Anthropic IPO at its offering price — something many investors don't have access to.

For example, Fidelity customers are eligible to participate in the Anthropic IPO if they have at least $25,000 in certain assets, the firm said. Even then, customers are "evaluated and ranked" based on factors like account assets to determine who can access limited shares that may be available, it said.

Importantly, anti-flipping policies don't apply to retail investors who access shares later, once Anthropic stock starts trading on a public exchange, Ritter said.

Of the retail brokerage firms listed in Anthropic's prospectus, Charles Schwab appears to be the only one without an explicit anti-flipping policy.

"At this time, Schwab does not apply a flipping restriction to any IPOs unless required by an issuer," Margaret Farrell, a company spokesperson, wrote in an email. "This is subject to change at Schwab's discretion."

She confirmed that an anti-flipping policy doesn't apply to the Anthropic IPO.

Here's how they could penalize IPO flippers.

E*TRADE said it "prefers investors hold shares for at least 30 calendar days."

However, its policy doesn't lay out an explicit penalty for failing to do so.

Selling or transferring out of an IPO within 30 days "may affect eligibility to participate in other new issues in the future," according to its policy. "E*TRADE reserves the right to exclude customers from future participation," it added.

Investors who are allocated Anthropic shares and sell within the first 15 calendar days from the start of trading in the secondary market won't be able to participate in future stock IPOs through Fidelity for a defined period of time, it said:

"The first day clients can sell without being labeled a 'flipper' is the 16th calendar day after the IPO trades," Fidelity said.

Robinhood's policy stipulates that selling IPO shares within 30 days of the IPO is considered flipping.

Such investors "may be prevented from participating in IPO access for 60 days," it said.

SoFi said that selling an IPO position within the first 30 calendar days after trading starts "may affect your ability to participate in future IPOs on SoFi."

#2845. The Suns avoided the trap and found their offensive rhythm

If defense is your thing, you probably didn't particularly enjoy what you witnessed early on in Wednesday night's matchup between the Phoenix Suns and Sacramento Kings. With much of the country anxiously awaiting the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, nobody was being put in defensive jail on either end of the floor.

Concerning? Maybe. But as many had identified entering this matchup, it had all the makings of a potential trap game for the Phoenix Suns, facing an opponent that had won once in 12 tries. There was no reason to reach for the panic button, as it felt like the Suns were spending those early stretches feeling out their opponent. And quite honestly? Darius Acuff Jr. going nuclear was what kept Sacramento in the basketball game.

In the third quarter, however, the Phoenix Suns locked down and locked in, holding the Kings to 24 points.

When you look back at this matchup holistically, the Suns did exactly what they were supposed to do, and the outcome never truly felt in doubt. Sacramento put together a couple of runs here and there, but Phoenix maintained control throughout.

Perhaps the most impressive aspect of what we witnessed on Wednesday night was how the basketball was popping around the court, regardless of who was in the game. It was selfless basketball, with players passing up good shots in pursuit of great ones. And when those opportunities presented themselves, the Suns did a quality job of knocking them down.

When you play teams like Sacramento, you have an opportunity to work on certain aspects of your game while taking care of business. For Phoenix, a team that has struggled with offensive connectivity throughout the early stages of the season, collective playmaking appeared to be an area of emphasis.

#2843. SMU coach set to face Irish for 1st time: ‘They’ll just wear on you’

SMU four-year head coach Rhett Lashlee knows exactly what the Mustangs are getting when they face US LBM Coaches Poll No. 3 Notre Dame this weekend.

Lashlee had high praise for a Fighting Irish squad that, in the coach's eyes, rarely has flaws. Lashlee, who will take on Notre Dame for the first time in his coaching career, said it all starts with quarterback CJ Carr.

Carr has completed 67.9% of his passes for 2,385 yards, 23 touchdowns and two interceptions so far.

"CJ is a very solid football player," Lashlee said. "He makes everything go and what they want to do on offense. He makes plays even when they're not there at first. He doesn't make mistakes and keeps them on schedule. He's super talented."

Lashlee said that the Irish notably "run the football really well." Notre Dame as a team has carried the ball 359 times for 1,857 yards, 23 TDs and a 5.2 average-per-attempt.

"When they run the football well, they control the game," Lashlee said. "When they run the football well and play defense like they do, they're rarely not in control of the game. They're ahead a lot and play in control. It allows them to play-action and take their shots."

Lashlee also noted that Notre Dame's defense – which ranks near the top in major categories – compliments the offense well, which makes the offense hard to control.

"Their defense is so talented, and it allows the offense to do the things they need to do," Lashlee added. "The way they play allows them to be patient and methodical and they'll just wear on you. Because of their talent, they create explosive plays but they can still go with 10-to-13 play drives."

SMU (7-3) is looking to turn things around after it lost two of its previous three games. The Mustangs were previously in the College Football Playoff conversation, but they've dropped out of contention.

Lashlee noted that in order for SMU to go toe-to-toe with Notre Dame on Saturday, the team will have to keep the Irish off-balanced.

"We've got to stop the run, try to limit the explosive (plays) and make them drive the field, even though they're good at it," Lashlee said. "The goal is to make sure they don't live ahead of the chains all day."

#2841. Kraken parent's acquisition of Tribe Capital flags new chapter in evolution of crypto exchanges

Payward, the owner of crypto exchange Kraken, is pushing into private markets with its latest acquisition, underscoring a broader shift in cryptocurrencies, from trading-led growth to the buildout of financial infrastructure.

Payward said late Wednesday that it's buying venture capital and asset management provider Tribe Capital Management, led by Payward's co-CEO Arjun Sethi. No purchase price was disclosed.

Tribe, where Sethi is co-founder and chairman, invests across early- and late-stage private companies and boasts $2.7 billion in assets under management.

"Joining Payward gives us the opportunity to bring Tribe's investment approach to a global financial platform," Jonathan Hsu, another co-founder of Tribe Capital, said in a statement. "We see a strong fit between our investment approach and Payward's infrastructure, distribution, and product-building capabilities."

Payward didn't respond to a request for comment.

The acquisition is novel among crypto exchanges. Unlike exchange-owned venture arms such as Coinbase Ventures or Binance Labs, Payward is looking to integrate Tribe's investment and fund-management capabilities into an existing custody, trading, collateral and tokenization infrastructure to develop private-market investment products.

Payward is trying to position itself to capture value from a broader crypto-driven transformation of financial services, not use the venture vehicle to draw more capital into the crypto ecosystem.

The acquisition is another step in the evolution in the crypto exchange business model. With cryptocurrency prices continuing to decline this year, crypto exchanges have worked to move past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, focusing instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance.

#2838. Amazon launches in-app push against Mamdani-backed delivery bill in New York City

Amazon is taking its fight against a New York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, to its shopping website and app.

Some users who open the company's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the New York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act.

The bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, which often work solely for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations.

"If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees."

The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin.

Amazon also posted a statement on its company website where it often publishes its policy positions. But rarely has the company used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past.

Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct users to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518."

According to Amazon, 20,000 customers sent emails to city council members in the first six hours that the pop-up appeared.

Menin told CNBC in a statement that Amazon's claim it will need to raise prices due to the proposed legislation "defies logic."

"We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs," Menin said. "If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong."

Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement that the company put up the notices to be "transparent with our customers" about what the bill "would cause them if it passes as written."

"If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill," Nantel said.

The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon's subcontractor model "leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets." He's argued the bill would lead to safer working conditions for drivers, and allow the city to "regulate last-mile operations."

Amazon disputed Mamdani's claims, saying the bill would put Delivery Service Partner jobs "at risk without improving safety." It also argued that other businesses and governments use contractors in their operations, and said the DSP model has allowed it to meet growing customer demand.

"It works because local entrepreneurs — people rooted in their communities — deliver a better experience," Amazon said. "They invest in their teams, their routes, and their neighborhoods. That's not a liability play."

Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill, while logistics and business groups have launched local advertising campaigns, and warned they may sue the city if the bill passes.

#2837. Takeaways coming off a Mile High loss

In an absolute ref show, the Celtics lost 105-101 to the Nuggets in a game marred by poor officiating and a free throw parade.

The only time in Joe Mazzulla's tenure that the Celtics have beat the Nuggets in Denver, Jokic didn't play in the game. Well, Jokic played on Wednesday night.

For the last few days, there's been a bit of a referendum on Boston's center position. Mitchell Robinson started the first five games at center and to his credit, that lineup has a +19.5 net rating. Neemias Queta had a run of nine before sitting out in favor of Luka Garza Sunday night in a loss against the Magic. In that game, Orlando hit 11-of-13 from inside the arc in the fourth quarter en route to outscoring Boston 54-32 in the paint. Losing that interior margin highlighted just how important that center position is, so much so that Mazzulla has said that it's the most important position on both ends of the court.

Queta was incredible in his return. His 17 points didn't come off alley-oops and dunker spot gimmes. Neemy grabbed seven offensive rebounds and on a night when the Celtics shot 11-of-44 from behind the arc, all of Queta's dirty work against the three-time MVP and inarguably the greatest center of his generation was absolutely needed in that slugfest.

The Celtics won the battle in trenches, outscoring the Nuggets in the paint 48-34 and grabbing four more offensive rebounds. Jokic didn't even score a point in the key until midway through the third quarter. Alas, it wasn't enough.

Bench? 45.7% of minutes (1st in the NBA) 43.8 (6th) 29.1 (26th)

In the second quarter, ESPN's broadcast highlighted that the Celtics average the most bench minutes in the league (45.7%). Sure, two blowout wins in the NBA Cup helps this early in the season, but Boston's depth was always going to be their strength.

It helps to have a former Sixth Man of the Year anchoring your second unit. Payton Pritchard extended double-digit scoring streak to eight games with 15. points

There's also the underrated Sam Hauser who hit 3-of-6 from behind the arc. Here's CelticsBlog's Nate Moskowitz on the third longest tenured Celtic and calming force off the bench.

With a very fluid offensive approach for Boston this year, Hauser has played a big part in their on and off-ball screening game. He's been the recipient, flying around stagger screens and knocking shots down on the move. He's also brought his usual ghost screen and pick-and-pop ability, creating advantages for himself or the ballhandler.

And out of nowhere, Chris Cenac Jr. has worked his way into a spark plug role. After showing signs in the blowout win over the Mavericks, he's earned consequential playing time against Orlando and Denver, including being part of the closing lineup last night and finishing with six points and six rebounds.

The Celtics subs are sixth in the league in points (43.8) and conversely, the Nuggets are 26th (29.1). Last night was no different; they outscored the Nuggets' second unit by 14, despite 18 from the elder statesman and Celtics killer DeMar DeRozan.

Unfortunately, that was negated at the free throw line on a night when both teams were miserable from 3. Boston registered 30 fouls — their highest total of the season — including 20 in the second half. That all resulted in a 29-12 edge in free throw attempts in favor of the hosts.

With the game knotted at 97, we saw one of the more inspiring moments of the season:

If you can stomach missing two wide open threes by Tatum and White and a bunny hop floater, you'll be rewarded at the end by Queta's unrelenting hustle around the rim, great hands, and dunk to take the lead.

"He has a level of talent and athleticism and has the ability to make plays on both ends of the floor…he's got the versatility, he's got the toughness, he's got the athleticism, he's got the talent. He just needs the reps to get better and better. I thought that was the bright spot tonight: his development from game 1 to game 2. He's just got to keep it up." — Joe Mazzulla on Chris Cenac Jr.

The first-round pick spent much of the first month of the season with the Maine Celtics with some mixed results, but he's sparkled in his call-up so far. Mazzulla has been cycling through Queta, Robinson, and Garza at the five and mixing in some double big looks, too. With CCJ showing some potential, it's becoming more and more evident that Cenac Jr. should be part of that conversation as well.

The Celtics will continue this four-game road trip with back-to-back games over the weekend in Sacramento and Golden State before returning to the East Coast with an NBA Cup game in the nation's capital.

#2834. Inside the WIAA’s plan to enforce Washington’s new biological sex sports rule

Girls who want to play high school sports in Washington will soon have another box to check during their annual physical exams with their doctors.

Voters approved Initiative 638 earlier this month, a measure limiting participation in girls' interscholastic athletics to biological females. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association (WIAA), which oversees high school sports in Washington, is working to align its rules with state law ahead of its Dec. 3 effective date.

Girls who have already had physicals won't be required to get a new one for the 2026-27 school year but will be required to have their doctor fill out a biological sex attestation form, which will be added to their existing form.

Going forward, physical examination forms will include a section indicating the student-athlete's biological sex, in addition to the other sections already included. The WIAA has updated its "Health & Wellness forms" section on its site.

"Determination of biological sex falls outside the WIAA's purview and is a matter best addressed by medical professionals," the WIAA said in a news release. "Schools will remain responsible for determining eligibility, further addressing the importance of providing member schools with updated guidance. The WIAA continues to monitor all legal developments regarding Initiative 638's implementation."

The winter sports impacted immediately will be girls basketball, girls wrestling, girls flag football, girls bowling, girls gymnastics and competitive cheer. Dance/Drill is not impacted as it is a coed offering and Sideline Cheer is not impacted because there is no competition.

In the spring, girls golf, girls softball (fastpitch), girls tennis and girls track and field will be affected. Next fall, girls cross country, girls golf, girls soccer, girls softball (slowpitch), girls swim and dive, girls tennis and girls volleyball will be affected.

"Initiative 638's language states that these changes only apply to girls sports offerings; however, a school may choose to collect attestations of biological sex for boys and girls," the WIAA's release said. "Once again, that is a school-based decision."

Since transgender athlete participation has become a controversial issue in recent years, the WIAA has remained consistent in its stance that it wishes to follow state law.

"That commitment remains unchanged," the release said. "To clear up any confusion or misunderstanding, the WIAA does not hold a political position on any measure and will not challenge Initiative 638's implementation."

The WIAA's membership has been split on the issue. Made up of administrators and coaches from schools around the state, the organization's representative assembly, which votes on amendments to the WIAA handbook every spring, has floated the issue already over the past two years. During that time, three amendments were proposed to modify the WIAA's gender-identity participation policies.

Those amendments were labeled as "advisory votes" because their language was determined to conflict with Washington state law at the time. Two of the three amendments received more than 50% support but did not meet the 60% threshold required for passage.

#2833. Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX in September as federal deals, White House ties grew

President Donald Trump's investment accounts bought shares of Nvidia, Palantir and Elon Musk's SpaceX in September, around the time the companies secured major federal contracts and their executives met with the president, according to a newly released financial disclosure.

The 25-page filing shows 751 purchases and sales totaling between roughly $40.9 million and $148.1 million, according to a CNBC analysis. Purchases accounted for at least $29.2 million and sales at least $11.7 million. The filing reports transactions in broad dollar ranges, leaving the exact amounts and value of Trump's holdings unclear.

Among the transactions were Palantir purchases before the company received two federal contracts worth $42.5 million combined, according to contracting records, SpaceX investments shortly before and after a $946 million NASA contract expansion, and Nvidia trades as its then-CEO, Jensen Huang, cultivated a close relationship with Trump.

The trades underscore a striking feature of Trump's presidency: His personal fortune remains invested in companies whose fortunes his administration can shape. His accounts reported more than 21,000 trades in 2025, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term. Recent presidents have generally divested individual stocks or used blind trusts to avoid potential conflicts.

The White House has told CNBC previously Trump and his family have no control over the trades, which outside financial managers handle independently. The Trump Organization says the arrangement is designed to avoid even the appearance of a conflict. There is no evidence Trump directed the transactions or that his managers knew government decisions in advance.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said that Trump's portfolio is independently managed and that neither the president nor his family has any input on trades. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers," Ingle told CNBC.

The Trump Organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The timing was particularly notable at Palantir, the artificial intelligence software maker whose technology is used by U.S. military, intelligence and civilian agencies.

Trump's accounts bought between $15,001 and $50,000 in Palantir shares on Sept. 2, followed by another purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 on Sept. 9.

A week later, the Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded Palantir a contract with $10.4 million in initial obligations for AI-powered grant oversight and fraud detection.

On Sept. 29, the Department of Homeland Security awarded Palantir another $32.1 million software contract, bringing the two awards to roughly $42.5 million. That same day, CEO Alex Karp joined Trump, Musk, Huang and other technology executives at the White House for a meeting on artificial intelligence.

Trump's accounts also bought shares and debt in SpaceX in the weeks surrounding a major NASA contract award.

On Sept. 1, the accounts purchased between $100,001 and $250,000 in SpaceX debt carrying a 5.35% interest rate. Eight days later, they bought between $1,001 and $15,000 in shares of the major NASA and Pentagon contractor.

On Sept. 18, NASA announced a $946 million expansion of its SpaceX contract, adding three astronaut missions to the International Space Station and bringing the agreement's total value to $5.92 billion. The agency had signaled plans for additional missions in May.

Six days after the announcement, Trump's accounts bought another $15,001 to $50,000 in SpaceX shares on the same day Musk attended Trump's White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. The filing does not show whether the purchase came before or after the dinner.

The trades followed an even larger SpaceX investment in August, when Trump's accounts bought between $1 million and $5 million in the company's debt just two days before he signed a policy aimed at expanding commercial space transportation.

Trump's accounts also continued buying Nvidia shares as Huang drew closer to the president — a relationship now under congressional scrutiny over Huang's ties to a woman suspected of spying for China.

The September filing shows four Nvidia purchases totaling between $152,004 and $380,000, including two on Sept. 2 worth as much as $350,000 combined.

The accounts also sold between $1,001 and $15,000 in Nvidia shares on Sept. 24, the day Huang also attended the state dinner with Xi.

The trades bring Trump's Nvidia transactions to at least 108 since his return to office in 2025, worth between $27.2 million and $97.9 million, extending a CNBC analysis published Monday.

The relationship between the president and Nvidia's then-CEO has drawn fresh scrutiny after The New York Times reported that intelligence officials warned Trump about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Trump has denied being briefed. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following revelations about his personal relationships.

The September filing also shows substantial trading beyond the three companies. The largest reported transaction was a Sept. 23 purchase of between $5 million and $25 million in Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF shares.

That same day, Trump's accounts sold between $1 million and $5 million each in Comcast, McDonald's, Home Depot and Fidelity National Information Services, along with between $500,001 and $1 million each in Nike and Constellation Brands.

On the buy side, Trump's accounts purchased between $250,001 and $500,000 in TJX shares on each of two consecutive days, Sept. 15 and 16. They also bought between $117,004 and $330,000 in Tesla shares across four transactions, along with smaller investments in CoreWeave, Intel, Microsoft and Apple.

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. "Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. #2831. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."
