#2830. Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access

After a string of outages disrupted airlines, banks and even the National Security Agency, U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen.

The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash, a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person.

Mullin appeared before lawmakers Wednesday morning at the House Homeland Security Committee's annual threat assessment hearing. Patel sent his deputy instead. And as the hearing got underway, a Justice Department jet that's been used by Patel before was still flying back from Florida.

Flight records reviewed by CNBC show the Justice Department aircraft associated with Patel's travel left West Palm Beach, Florida, at 7:51 a.m. ET Wednesday and landed at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington at 10:20 a.m. ET — 20 minutes after the House Homeland Security Committee hearing began.

The FBI confirmed Patel, Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche attended the Mar-a-Lago event.

"The event is approved by Ethics, following all guidelines and regulations," FBI spokesperson Benjamin Williamson told CNBC by email, noting the gala "is an annual event honoring fallen law enforcement officers and their families."

Patel's absence drew bipartisan criticism on Capitol Hill. Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., said lawmakers had spent months trying to secure Patel's testimony, only for the FBI director to make clear he had "no intention" of appearing.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, of Mississippi, the committee's top Democrat, said Patel's absence for a second consecutive year undermined lawmakers' ability to conduct oversight. Before 2024, FBI directors traditionally testified at the annual hearing.

The episode also drew attention to what was being offered at Trump's private club: a chance for donors and corporate sponsors to meet privately with some of the nation's most powerful law enforcement officials.

"Trump's Big Blue Bash is yet another fundraising event that encourages wealthy special interests, particularly those seeking lucrative government contracts, to rub elbows with officials responsible for awarding those contracts," Craig Holman, a government ethics and lobbying expert at the watchdog group Public Citizen, told CNBC.

Billed as a tribute to federal officers and their families, the second annual black-tie gala came with a price list for access.

General admission cost nearly $5,000, a VIP all-access pass $25,000, and a private roundtable with federal agency heads and a night at Trump's resort $50,000, according to the event's ticketing page. A sponsorship prospectus reviewed by CNBC advertised corporate packages reaching $1 million, including private briefings, speaking time, and the chance to name and present an award to a federal agency of the sponsor's choosing.

Alongside Patel and Mullin, the advertised guest list also included White House border czar Tom Homan and leaders of Customs and Border Protection, the Secret Service, Drug Enforcement Administration, and Transportation Security Administration.

It remains unclear which officials attended private meetings or which companies bought the most expensive packages. But several sponsors had substantial business with the agencies represented.

Motorola Solutions, the gala's top named sponsor, had approximately $237.1 million in fiscal 2026 net contract obligations from the Justice and Homeland Security departments, according to CNBC's analysis of federal records. That included a $139.6 million Bureau of Prisons radio contract, a $25.8 million Customs and Border Protection award and a nearly $18 million Secret Service contract option, all in September.

Motorola reported roughly $1.69 million in federal lobbying expenses this year through September, according to its first-quarter, second-quarter and third-quarter disclosures. Its lobbying included homeland security funding, communications technology and other issues.

"Motorola Solutions was proud to support last night's Big Blue Bash, honoring the families of wounded and fallen federal officers, whom we hosted as the night's guests of honor," the company said through a spokesperson. "We did not participate in private briefings."

Two other federal contractors, the Vierra Group and Teya Diversified Services, sponsored a Department of Homeland Security presentation featuring Mullin and Homan, according to the gala's published program.

Federal contracting records show Teya received three Customs and Border Protection contracts in September worth approximately $23.3 million combined for repairs at northern border ports of entry. The awards were $9.1 million for work at 12 ports, $7.9 million for nine ports and $6.4 million for 10 ports.

LEO Technologies, which markets artificial intelligence and surveillance products to law enforcement agencies, was also listed as a sponsor.

Vierra, Teya and LEO Technologies didn't immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

Federal ethics rules require authorization for officials to participate in charitable fundraising in their official capacities and restrict the use of government titles for personal fundraising.

Holman said companies attending such events hope to gain favor with the administration and ultimately benefit through government contracts and policies affecting their businesses.

There is no evidence the sponsorships influenced federal contracts or secured preferential treatment, and some new contract awards added to existing contracts.

The financial questions extend to Trump's own business. Organizers haven't disclosed what Mar-a-Lago was paid or how much reached the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Foundation, the nonprofit that's the event's beneficiary. The gala offered a $1 million sponsorship package — more than the charity's entire 2024 revenue of $725,476, according to its latest available IRS filing — though no purchase has been confirmed. A Republican fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago cost about $318,000 in 2023, according to a New York Times analysis of campaign finance records.

The event also may raise questions about taxpayer-funded travel. Organizers listed Mullin as a speaker, and flight records reviewed by CNBC show a Gulfstream jet registered to DHS arriving in West Palm Beach Tuesday evening, alongside the Justice Department plane associated with Patel's travel. It remains unclear who was aboard either aircraft or whether the flights were connected to the gala.

Days earlier, Mullin used a government plane to attend a Louisiana State University football game shortly after a nationwide FAA ground stop. He defended the trip Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee, saying that government travel was required and that he personally paid for it.

#2829. Eight is enough: Dybantsa, Davis power Wizards to win over depleted Raptors

It wasn't easy or pretty or even all that satisfying, but the Wizards ended their losing streak at eight by beating the Toronto Raptors in Canada last night.

The winning formula was a tight rotation (only seven players got more than 10 minutes) and an opponent missing their three best players. Bonus factor: the opponent lost another member of their top six just four minutes into the game.

There were times last night when it felt like the Wizards were doing good things. Like, in the fourth quarter, Toronto kept running possessions to the very end of the shot clock. It looked like Washington was playing strong defense. And then I'd remember Toronto was relying on Immanuel Quickley, Jamal Shead, and Ja'Kobe Walter for offense.

Which is not to slur any of those three — they're all some degree of solid professional players. But they all fit best as third, fourth, or fifth options. Supplementary, not driving forces.

Or, Anthony Davis would look awesome ripping down an offensive board. And then I'd notice that he'd overpowered the 6-1 Shead or the 6-2 Alijah Martin.

The lack of talent available to Toronto helped the Wizards in at least one other way. Up six with under two minutes to play, the Wizards gave the Raptors a wide open three, which they missed. Thirty seconds later, Walter picked Trae Young, who was trying to bring the ball up court and had an opportunity for a layup. He dribbled the ball off his foot, turning an easy two into a turnover.

The Wizards still turned the final minute into an adventure. First, when they were up five with about 36 seconds to play and for some reason Anthony Davis took a fadeaway 20-footer (which he missed). And then when AJ Dybantsa brought the ball up court and lost it out of bounds when he was pressured by Shead.

But, adventure or not, the Wizards did get the win — something they have often not done against a weakened opponent over the past few decades.

The first entry in my notebook for the night — before opening tip — was about how Toronto was missing its top three players. I jotted, "Trap game."

First offensive possession, the Wizards ran a complicated looking horns set that had multiple screens and cuts and guys running all over the place. So they could throw the ball to Davis at the free throw line and get a heavily contested runner that missed. Davis bailed out the possession by getting the offensive rebound, getting fouled and making a free throw.

I was in the process of jotting a note about how the Wizards seemed to be constantly on the edge of committing a turnover when Alex Sarr lost the ball out of bounds trying to make a move inside.

About three minutes into the game, there was a very nice offensive action from the Wizards. The ball arrived to Sarr on the wing. Kyshawn George came up from the corner into a dribble handoff coming towards the middle. He drove with advantage, Jakob Poeltl (Sarr's man) was forced to help, and George made the easy kickout to Sarr for a wide-open three. That's good basketball.

Maybe 10 seconds later, Dybantsa blew up a Toronto dribble handoff and got a breakaway dunk.

Get used to it: Toronto repeatedly brought Young into the action on defense and attacked him. Even when Young gave a good effort (which was most of the time), the other four defenders had to help, which created openings. That's something the Wizards could get away with against a team missing its top three players.

One offensive possession rankled. While Will Riley and Davis tried to figure out how to attack on the strong side, Dybantsa was on the weakside wing, and Bilal Coulibaly and George with both in the weakside corner. And no one cut. Or lifted. Or screened. They…just stood there and watched. Davis bailed out the possession by drawing a foul.

Raptors analyst Jack Armstrong made this observation in the third quarter: "The Raptors are on a back-to-back, but they're the ones making the hustle plays. They look like they're the better conditioned team."

At the 4:55 mark of the third quarter, George had a major size advantage in the post…and took an awkward fading jumper, which he missed. Terrible shot selection in that situation.

At 1:42 of the third, the Wizards had a 3-on-1 fast break that somehow ended up in a Coulibaly charge.

Dybantsa fan boy moment — check out 10:29 of the fourth quarter. Amazing drive and finish by the 19-year-old rookie — WOW power and athleticism.

About three minutes later, Dybantsa made a spinning move while driving and finished with a dunk. Another moment of outlandish athleticism.

In the span of about a minute during the fourth quarter, Young failed to pay attention and got backcut by Shead for a layup. He followed that up by not tagging Walter on a Poeltl missed free throw, which gave Walter a free run into the lane for the offensive rebound.

Young got his dribble picked twice in the final couple minutes of the game.

Terrific game overall from Dybantsa, by the way — 23 points, 12 rebounds, strong defensive effort.

Davis was too much inside for the depleted Raptors — 24 points, 14 rebounds, a steal and two blocks.

George played 40 minutes, scoring 20 points and avoiding the turnovers and fouls that have undermined his impact.

Sarr was good — 13 points, 2 rebounds, 3 assists, and 3 blocks in 22 minutes.

Another poor shooting night for Young. Plus three turnovers. Not so good.

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

PPA is my overall production metric, which credits players for things they do that help a team win (scoring, rebounding, playmaking, defending) and dings them for things that hurt (missed shots, turnovers, bad defense, fouls).

PPA is a per possession metric designed for larger data sets. In small sample sizes, the numbers can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#2828. NFL predictions: Our picks for Giants-Jaguars, the full Week 11 slate

The New York Giants face major test this week when they face the Jacksonville Jaguars. It is also a game that will provide a huge swing in the Giants' expected chances to make the playoffs. Will the Giants upset Jacksonville? See what our Big Blue View staff members think about that game and the rest of the Week 11 action in this week's staff picks.

I think there's a path to a win for the Giants, if they can find it. The Giants are one of the very best teams in the NFL at forcing drives to end in punts. At the same time, the Jaguars will be without their starting center and the Giants are one of the best teams in the League at creating quick pressure. That's important because Trevor Lawrence has been one of the quarterbacks most affected by pressure in the NFL.

At the same time, the Giants have rediscovered the explosive pass with J.J. McCarthy, which has been the weakness of the Jags' defense.

If the Giants can score touchdowns while disrupting Lawrence, they've got the chance to come away with the upset. We've seen the Giants rebound after bad games, as well as play much better than anticipated when they're underdogs. Maybe both will happen here.

The flip side of the coin is simpler and scarier to me: The Giants have one of the worst red zone defenses in the NFL, and the Jaguars have one of the best red zone offenses in the league. If the Giants can't stop them between the 20s, this game could get ugly fast.

Jacksonville is one of the hottest teams in the league with a young and explosive offense that can run the football. Their defense is aggressive but doesn't NEED to bring the blitz — they blitz at about a league-average rate, but Anthony Campanile does an excellent job utilizing simulated pressure to harass opposing quarterbacks. Jacksonville is third in offensive EPA, 4th in defensive EPA allowed, and 1st in Net EPA — they're a juggernaut based on their performance and the advanced analytics.

Still, that doesn't mean the Giants don't have a chance — they just must play efficient football and avoid the catastrophic mistakes that have robbed them of wins. It's possible, but against the most efficient team in the NFL, it will be difficult. John Harbaugh will have the Giants ready and prepared for the game, and I believe it will be more exciting and competitive. Jacksonville is concluding their third straight road game, which could give the Giants a slight advantage at home, but I ultimately believe the better team finds a way to win.

It took 11 weeks, but for the first time this season, the Giants will face a team with a winning record when the 7-2 Jaguars come to town on Sunday. Not only is Jacksonville running away with the AFC South (they lead the division by four games), but they're steamrolling the competition. They've won their last three games by a combined 75 points. This is easily Big Blue's toughest test of the season, so far.

Jacksonville is very good on both sides of the ball. They're fourth in offensive DVOA, third in defensive DVOA, and third in overall DVOA. They also have an excellent field goal kicker with crazy range. If you look at both rosters, it's hard to find clear advantages for the Giants at any position group outside of tight end, and even there, Jacksonville has good players.

Can the Giants win this game? Yes. They're at home, they're getting an extra three days of rest, and as we saw when they played Houston, they aren't scared and can surprise as a big underdog. They'll need to dial it up on defense and pressure Trevor Lawrence into the kinds of mistakes he used to make before Liam Coen got there. They also might have a little extra motivation after letting last week's game against the Commanders slip away at the end.

I won't be surprised if John Harbaugh's team hangs in there and keeps it as a one-score game most of the way. But in the end, until the Giants show me that they can beat a really good team, I can't pick them to do so.

You can talk yourself into believing that the Giants can beat Jacksonville this Sunday. They needed a miraculous last-second 57-yard field goal to beat the Eagles team (with Jalen Hurts) that the Giants defeated (without Hurts). They lost to the Texans team that the Giants beat the following week. The woeful Titans were within a TD against them last week with 5 minutes left. So indeed, it could be a competitive game. Unfortunately, the Jags have also won games by 24, 29, 35, and 23 points this season. They have scored 31 or more in each of their past four games, and over 40 in two of those. The Giants have only scored more than 30 points once, and only then because of a 99-yard pick-6 on the last play of the game.

Trevor Lawrence isn't necessarily playing any better this year than in the past. He's a QB that simultaneously makes great passes and puts the ball up for grabs, yet unlike in years past, he's cut down on the INTs while getting the TDs. Part of that may be due to 5'10" wide receiver Parker Washington (a 2023 6th-round pick), who had a breakout 2025 and is on pace for 1,000 yards. Running back Bhayshul Tuten, a 4th round 2025 pick, isn't quite in the Jahmyr Gibbs – Kenneth Walker class but he's not far below and is a missed tackle machine. A lot of the credit has to go to head coach Liam Coen, who also calls the plays and turned this team around as soon as he was hired. Lawrence, like most QBs, has trouble with pressure, but he is not too fazed by the blitz. Finding a way to disrupt his rhythm is a key to any chance the Giants may have.

On defense, the Jaguars are strong at linebacker with fourth-round 2023 pick Ventrell Miller, one of the league's best (note how many mid-round picks the Jags have hit on), along with Foyesade Oluokun. They also put on a decent pass rush with Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker, and Dennis Gardeck. In the secondary, Travis Hunter is playing more like a No. 2 pick, having mostly given up his evening gig as a receiver.

Are the Giants a serious playoff contender? This is the type of game they can use to make a statement against a team that is in the Super Bowl conversation. I think they'll put up a fight. I also don't think they're there yet.

I want to convince myself to pick the Giants to defeat the Jaguars. I really do. I just can't. The Jaguars are a team with justifiable Super Bowl ambitions. They are a well-rounded team with a high-powered offense, a very good defense, and one of the best field-goal kickers in the business in Cam Little.

The Giants are a good team. They are resilient. They will give the Jaguars their best shot. Maybe, just maybe, it will be good enough to pull off an upset that would go a long way toward ensuring that the Giants make the playoffs.

"Rather than being one player out of 10 in the industry serving compute, we want to be the one player with Palo Alto that delivers secure compute and security capability," Arora told CNBC.

#2824. Cameron Smith’s Tour Path Hinges On Strict PGA Rules

Cameron Smith faces a clear but narrow path back to the PGA Tour following his time with LIV Golf. A specific detail regarding his eligibility has emerged from the new membership structure. While Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm secured official status for the upcoming season, Smith's situation requires meeting strict criteria. The PGA Tour has not softened its stance on players who competed in the rival league. Brian Rolapp, the tour chief, made it clear that rules exist to ensure fairness and competitive balance within the organization.

The conditions for a return remain rigid for any player barred until one year after their last LIV event. For Smith, DeChambeau, and Rahm, that date lands on August 26, 2027. Smith would likely need to fit into Category 1 membership to regain status. This category requires winning the Race to Dubai Rankings between 2022 and 2026, or capturing a Major Championship between 2022 and 2027. Smith won the Open Championship in 2022, which should theoretically qualify him for this tier if he signs up for membership.

Despite the potential pathway, the tour leadership has signaled no intent to bend the rules for high-profile names. According to reports, a special exemption for specific players is improbable for the tour. Although the tour initially provided exemptions via the returning member program at the start of 2026. He noted that this option now appears unavailable. "Rules matter and they will be enforced," Rolapp said. This hardline approach suggests that Smith must rely entirely on his performance in the DP World Tour or a future major win rather than a special invitation to get back on the circuit.

PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp has been vocal about the financial and competitive strategy driving these decisions. Speaking at the Sports Business Journal's Dealmakers event in Manhattan on Wednesday morning, Rolapp compared the current golf landscape to past mergers in basketball and football. He argued that the sports business is not that difficult when the focus remains on the product. "The sports business is not that difficult," Rolapp said. His point is that if the tour provides the best competitive product, fans and sponsors will reward it with their time and attention.

The tour is preparing for a new structure commencing in 2028, which includes the creation of Championship and Challenger series. This shift aims to create scarcity and increase media value. Rolapp noted that U.S. media rights constitute a $30 billion annual enterprise that keeps growing. He noted that money will be reallocated from scripted programs into sports live events, but warned that this trend does not guarantee funding for every property. "It'll go up because more and more money will be reallocated from scripted program and other things that are more commoditized into sports live events, but it doesn't mean it'll feed everything," he said. This financial reality reinforces the need for a competitive field, which is why the tour is enforcing rules that keep the field strong and the product valuable.

The DP World Tour has emerged as a key partner in this ecosystem, offering a platform for players seeking a lifeline. According to Fox Sports, the tour has seen a stack of players agree to play in its events. This arrangement allows players like Smith to remain active and visible while they navigate the PGA Tour's eligibility requirements. The DP World Tour has essentially become the primary venue for these players to prove their worth during the suspension period. Without a clear path back to the PGA Tour, these players must perform well in Europe to keep their careers moving forward.

The situation for Smith highlights the tension between the tour's desire for top players and its commitment to its membership rules. The tour wants the best players playing together, a view Rolapp shared with fans. He stated, "We've heard from our fans and we know they want the best players playing together, and we share that view." However, the mechanism for achieving this is strictly defined by the new membership categories. There is no indication that Smith will receive a special pass based on his past success or marketability.

Smith's path relies on the specific criteria laid out for Category 1 membership. If he has won a Major Championship in the 2022-2027 window, he meets the requirement. His 2022 Open Championship victory is the key factor here. However, he must also sign up for membership to activate this category. The timeline means he will not be able to compete on the PGA Tour until August 2027 at the earliest. Until then, his competitive home remains the DP World Tour or other international events. The tour's refusal to offer special exemptions suggests that this timeline is fixed for everyone, regardless of their star power.

The new structure aims to protect the integrity of the tour while still allowing for a return of top talent. By enforcing the one-year rule and requiring specific performance milestones, the tour ensures that any returning player has maintained their status through competition. Rolapp believes the product must be the tour's most competitive and valuable creation, and the one-year rule with specific performance milestones reflects that belief. The focus is on merit rather than exception. Smith and others in his position must wait for the rules to expire or meet the performance benchmarks to re-enter the fold.

The immediate focus for the tour shifts to the new structure taking effect in 2028. This is when the Championship and Challenger series will be fully implemented. The current season continues with the FedEx Cup Fall, which determines eligibility for the 2027 season. Players like Neal Shipley are currently fighting for their spots in this final stretch. Full Tour status goes to the top 100 in standings after Sunday, whereas players ranked 101-125 get conditional status. The outcome of these events will set the stage for the 2027 season, which precedes the major structural changes of 2028.

#2823. Bill Belichick, Robert Kraft one step closer to Pro Football Hall of Fame induction

Two key members of the New England Patriots dynasty are a step closer to Pro Football Hall of Fame induction.

Former head coach Bill Belichick and team owner Robert Kraft have been selected by the Hall of Fame's respective coach and contributor subcommittees as candidates for induction in 2027.

They are now among 15 total candidates, who are up for the final voting rounds in February. They will be joined by 13 as-of-yet-unannounced players at a later point.

Belichick, 74, emerged from a group of five coaching nominees, beating out the likes of Tom Coughlin, Mike Holmgren, Dan Reeves and Mike Shanahan.

A six-time Super Bowl champion as New England's head coach, who also earned two rings as defensive coordinator with the New York Giants, he won a combined 69% 0f regular season and playoff games between 2000 and 2023 and earned nine conference championships and 17 division titles. Including a previous head-coaching tenure with the Browns, he ranks second all-time in NFL coaching wins with 333 and first with 31 postseason victories; he also is a member of the NFL's 100th Anniversary Team

Seemingly a lock to make the Hall of Fame based on his unrivaled résumé, Belichick was denied the honor of first-ballot induction last year in what is arguably the most controversial decision in the Hall of Fame's history. His exclusion from the 2026 class drew heavy criticism and set the stage for the implementation of sweeping changes to the selection process.

Kraft, 85, garnered the subcommittee's support over fellow contributor nominees Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, Doug Williams and John Wooten.

His ownership saw the Patriots turn from a relative afterthought into the NFL's most successful franchise. Besides winning six Super Bowls and reaching two others, he also oversaw 20 AFC East titles, 23 playoff berths, and only six losing seasons. The club has sold out every home game since he bought it in 1994, and won a combined 66% of games along the way.

To make it into the Hall of Fame, Belichick and Kraft will need to garner at least 80% of votes from the full selection committee at its next meeting ahead of the Super Bowl. The group will first be reduced from 15 to 10, with between three and seven finalists ultimately receiving the honor.

The expectation is that former Patriots tight end Rob Gronkowski will join them among the 15 candidates.

#2822. The Nets have lost their way… Now what?

"I fully anticipated the Nets to be so fired up having us here, they would blow Chicago out. I'm looking at 62-39, so I was wrong," Nets legend Julius Erving said on YES.

"Been in the league 13 years and this… one of the worst games I've been a part of," Julius Randle said after the game. That is the veteran who once talked about shocking the world with the Nets, now stuck on a disconnected young team and wearing a Chicago White Sox hat right after losing 137-107 to the Chicago Bulls.

"I saw selfishness. I saw pointing fingers, and I saw guys that didn't always play hard," head coach Jordi Fernandez said after the loss.

This is who the Brooklyn Nets are: a 3-11 team with no identity. Nothing more, perhaps something less.

Of course, those who have been here long enough have been through agonizing times like a 12-70 season, MeloDrama, when the Nets pursuit of Melo fell flat, and Dwightmare, when the Nets pursuit of Dwight Howard also came short.

There were absolutely miserable days in the post-Deron Williams era, as they watched Boston pile up lottery draft picks, more specifically, Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown. They had none of their own picks, which is what made Sean Marks's early work stand out so much, because he had so little to work with. He was throwing restricted free agent offer sheets at guys like Allen Crabbe (four years, $75 million), Tyler Johnson (four years, $50 million), Donatas Motiejunas (four years, $37 million), and Otto Porter Jr. (four years, $106.5 million).

We know what happened with the Big 3 and we don't need to go back down that road, but ultimately it failed. Kevin Durant criticized the team constructed around him. Marks made two massive trades to get out of the trenches after that predicament, dealing Durant and later Mikal Bridges for picks that might as well be stashed in a Doomsday vault at this rate.

Now? He has too many assets to work with, and it isn't leading to wins, development, or a gritty identity. Fans are waiting for the product to be good, for the Nets to strike, and instead they are staring down another losing season.

Talk about an improbable fall from grace.

The Nets entered Wednesday with very few things to feel good about, but ABA Night was meant to be a night set for those who won two championships and laid the foundation. The reality from those 1970s teams and this one now are night and day, even if times have changed. Dr. J said what everyone was feeling, even if he meant it innocently.

The Brooklyn Nets have dropped to 3-11 after getting blown out by 30 on their own floor, surrendering 120+ points in eight games total and allowing 130+ points for the fourth time this season. It is, in many ways, as miserable a stretch as any of those above.

"I can try to say it in Spanish, because in English they don't understand. So I'll keep trying and find whatever language works. But yeah, our effort was not good."

At this point, a translator won't help. The scoreboard speaks every language fluently, and right now it's shouting that effort has been lost in translation. With Fernandez in Year Three and Sean Marks in his 11th season running basketball operations, the blame can point in plenty of directions.

So where should it go? Frustrations didn't start on Wednesday night.

There is a growing disconnect and stubbornness that shows up in clunky rotations and cautious minutes restrictions. If they are going to be cautious with Mikel Brown Jr., at least distinguish caution from coddling. Seven players got more playing time than him on Monday, and it was only his second game in eight days.

So, if they aren't going to be good (hint: they aren't), it's worth living with the growing pains of developing cornerstones like MBJ at point guard.

The team was otherwise built with positional size, yet as rival scouts told Brian Lewis of the New York Post, "The lineups don't really fit." One Eastern Conference scout put it plainly: "It's like super jumbo right now. Sometimes it's super small, you have like three guards out there. The roster just isn't very clean. … There's small guards or some big guards, but they're guards who need to ball. The lack of shooting on the roster, that can be an issue."

Are the Nets stretching this rebuild out as far as possible? Even scouts looking at the 2025 draft haul see the mess, with one veteran scout saying, "The back end is what the back end is. But yeah, it's tough when you have five firsts and it looks like two sure misses and probably three, more than likely three misses."

Another scout added, "And the other ones, the other first rounders of that five, you wonder are they NBA players. Saraf? Powell? And then Wolf. They probably should have consolidated that and tried to move up."

Rebuilding is one thing; compounding it with avoidable, self-inflicted wounds is another.

What makes this all even harder to stomach is that the Nets are outright awful, and for some reason they carry themselves with an unearned arrogance. Why do they act entitled to patience when this franchise has made the playoffs just eight times since moving to Brooklyn and won only a single playoff series across Marks's entire decade-long tenure?

Flash back to the Milwaukee game when Brooklyn pulled starters in a winnable contest and earned the NBA's first Player Participation fine. After dropping 118 games over the prior two years with Houston holding their pick, there should be a real sense of urgency instead of questionable rotations and questions about effort.

The so-called culture has contradictions piling up even higher. For years, this franchise leaned into progressive milestones, Yet the Nets keep getting pulled into jarring off-court noise around Michael Porter Jr. and his habit of testing dates with Andrew Tate clips. Pair that negativity with something so specific like his anti-vax posture, and it looks glaringly hypocritical next to how the Kyrie Irving situation played out.

On-court merit hasn't come close to justifying the leash leadership continues to get, yet every sign points to Joe Tsai and Marks staying locked in on this slow-drip rebuild at least for the time being. Tsai is a businessman, but his product is spoiled, the people paying are fed up and he hasn't changed anything.

#2820. Kyle Shanahan on the Brian Flores defense: "It's not just a fad"

49ers coach Kyle Shanahan has never beaten a Brian Flores defense. Which might be the most impressive thing that can be said about the Brian Flores defense.

They meet again on Sunday night in Mexico City, when Shanahan’s 49ers play the Vikings, whose defense is coordinated by Flores.

“He’s more unique than all the other 31 guys,” Shanahan told reporters on Wednesday regarding Flores. “He’s the one guy who commits to this and it’s not just a fad for these nine games or whatever. He’s been doing it his whole time in Minnesota. He did the same thing in Miami. He’s as good as it gets at that stuff.

“Anybody who lives in that world as much as he does, it’s usually a matter of time. I think offensive coaches used to like to say that early on, but it’s too many years of it and it’s too many games in this year that they’re sound. They put so much pressure on the quarterback, the play-caller, the O-Line, the receivers, on everybody. A lot of times when you go into an NFL game, the pressure’s really on people on third down and stuff like that because those are things where everything can come and when you play against Brian it’s 70-straight plays of that.”

It’s not easy to beat in part because it’s almost impossible to simulate in practice. As Devin McCourty has said, you think you have a plan and then the game starts and everything changes.

It changes in part because Flores seems to be constantly self-scouting and adjusting, defying the films to create pressure in new ways.

The goal is to eliminate the offense’s built-in advantage that comes from knowing what the play will be by creating confusion for the entire offense. Who’s rushing? Who’s dropping into coverage? Who do I block? If that guy doesn’t rush, what do I do?

It makes for a compelling chess match, with the 49ers needing to find a way to get the Minnesota defense on its heels.

A strong running game is a must. Wearing down the defense physically is required. When inevitable passing situations arise, the quarterback needs to quickly find the open man (if there is one) and get the ball out before the walls close in.

Sometimes, they close quickly. The strategy results in plenty of guys getting a free run at the quarterback, forcing a deer-in-the-headlights response — right before impact.

#2818. Surfing Legend’s Brother Says Family ‘Had Our Suspicions’ About Girlfriend Who Claimed to Survive His Murder

Surfer Kurt Van Dyke lived a seemingly idyllic life in Costa Rica until he was killed in a violent home invasion earlier this year

His girlfriend and another man were arrested last week in connection with his slaying

The family of the beloved surfer says they are shocked by her arrest but were also suspicious about details surrounding the deadly attack, per CBS News

Things weren't adding up for Kurt Van Dyke's family when they learned that the benevolent surfing legend had been tortured and then murdered in a violent home invasion that left his girlfriend largely unscathed.

On Feb. 14, California native Van Dyke, 66, known as "King," was found under a bed at a residence in Hone Creek, near Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, in Costa Rica, with multiple stab wounds and signs that he had been strangled, Costa Rica's Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) announced.

Van Dyke's girlfriend, who has only been identified by her last name, Arroyo, was found zip-tied after the attack but didn't suffer any serious injuries, police said at the time, CBS News reports.

Now, nine months after Van Dyke's brutal slaying, Arroyo and a 34-year-old man with the surname Gutiérrez, were arrested on suspicion of participating in his murder, the country's Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) announced on Nov. 12, Teletica.com, the Los Angeles Times and SF Gate reported.

The man and Van Dyke's girlfriend had allegedly "planned a robbery targeting the American with the intent of obtaining the PINs for bank cards" linked to the Hotel Puerto Viejo in Puerto Viejo de Talamanca that he owned, officials said, CBS reports.

Van Dyke's brother, Peter Van Dyke, told CBS News that he and his family found it "shocking" that she was arrested.

At the same time, however, he said they thought it was "extremely odd" that Arroyo had emerged from the violent attack largely unscathed, but said he "didn't want to make any speculations."

Kurt Van DykeCredit: Kurt Van Dyke/Facebook

"We had our suspicions," he told CBS News.

PEOPLE previously reported that Van Dyke was at a residence in Puerto Viejo with Arroyo when at least two armed men stormed inside, threatened them with a firearm and held them in a room for several minutes before stealing valuables.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

Van Dyke was tortured and beaten when the suspects were unable to access his banking information, OIJ Deputy Director Vladimir Muñoz said, La Nación reported.

The OIJ Deputy Director also said parts of the attack appeared to be "staged," per La Nación.

Born in Santa Cruz, Calif., to a well-known surfing family, Van Dyke grew up "ripping pipelines."

He learned how to surf from an early age from his parents, Gene Van Dyke and Betty Van Dyke, who pioneered the sport in northern California in the 1950s, the Santa Cruz Sentinel reported.

Betty Van Dyke, who died in 2021 at age 89, was one of the first female competitive surfing champions in the world.

Peter Van Dyke told CBS News that he and the rest of the family are relieved that arrests have been made in his brother's murder.

"We're just satisfied with the outcome so far," he told CBS News. "I have faith in the Costa Rican law enforcement. It took them nine months, and I totally understand why."

Peter Van Dyke noted that his brother was one of the good guys.

"My brother was a very benevolent, giving person who would help just about anybody," he previously told the San Francisco Chronicle. "Kurt would never hurt anybody, and he was always there when you needed him."

#2817. Mexico City altitude will affect the kicking game on Sunday night

When the Vikings and 49ers face off in Mexico City on Sunday night, they’ll be playing at the highest elevation any NFL game is ever played at: Estadio Azteca’s altitude is around 7,300 feet. And that could have an impact on the kicking game.

Kickers and physicists alike have agreed that high altitudes can easily add five yards or more to field goal range. The air is thinner at altitude, and in Mexico City the altitude makes the air about 20 percent less dense than at sea level. In Denver, which is about 2,000 feet lower than Mexico City, the air is about 15 percent less dense than at sea level, and Denver’s Mile High Stadium is well known for the boost it gives to kickers.

Vikings kicker Will Reichard has a career-long field goal of 62 yards, and 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro’s career long is 59 yards. Both kickers made their career longs at sea level, and they both should feel confident if called upon to attempt a kick from at least a few yards beyond 60 yards in Sunday night.

Kickoff strategy may also be a factor at altitude. Only 16 percent of all kickoffs in the NFL this season have gone for touchbacks, as teams believe it’s better to try to pin their opponents deep on their own end of the field than boot the ball into the end zone. In Mexico City, it may be hard for a kicker to avoid kicking the ball into the end zone — or kickers might be able to get a higher trajectory on their kicks and make it even easier to pin their opponents deep.

And punts will travel several yards farther, which could be especially exciting for Vikings return man Myles Price, the NFL’s top punt returner, who might be able to reach top speed before the coverage can get to him if 49ers punter Corliss Waitman outkicks his coverage.

There’s a lot of talk before games at altitude about how teams should acclimate so their players don’t get out of breath in the thinner air. But that’s not the only part of the game that players will need to adjust to on Sunday night. The kicking game will be significantly impacted.

#2816. Struggling Colts should start Anthony Richardson Sr. at QB the rest of the 2026 campaign

The consensus among Indianapolis Colts fans seems to be that this current rendition of Daniel Jones should no longer be the starting quarterback for the franchise.

After leading the Colts to an 8-2 start last year, at the helm of a historically elite offense at the time, the wheels have quickly come off for Jones and the franchise. Cracks of vulnerability were beginning to show even before Jones suffered critical injuries late last season, including a fractured fibula and season-ending torn Achilles. Most notably, opposing defenses began to blitz Jones at a higher rate, and started having a greater deal of success.

Jones continues to be pass pressured at a high rate, and while there may be some expected physical limitations, still working his way back less than a year removed from the torn Achilles, Jones' regression doesn't appear to be all physical—as his mental processing and decision-making in-game has also relapsed. He much more closely resembles the turnover prone former failed franchise quarterback hopeful for the New York Giants, than the breakout Pro Bowler that Colts fans saw firsthand for the first half of the 2025 campaign.

Embattled Colts head coach Shane Steichen values the much maligned Jones' continued leadership, preparation, and understanding of the offense, but his on-the-field production so far this season for the 3-7 Colts stinks:

ESPN's Jeremy Fowler recently reported that Steichen sticking with Jones, despite his continued struggles, may speak more to the lack of viable quarterback options behind him:

Colts head coach Shane Steichen's loyalty to Daniel Jones might be less about Jones' poor performance and more about the options behind him. As it was told to me, Steichen simply is not motivated to play Anthony Richardson Sr., the 2023 fourth overall pick who fell out of favor after a strong start to his rookie year. Richardson and No. 3 quarterback Riley Leonard did not have strong training camps in the Colts' view, and it seems that has carried over. Richardson, a 2027 free agent, badly needs a fresh start elsewhere but appears poised for spot duty in Indy at some point this year, given the team's 3-7 record and its trading away of four key players before the deadline. But I just don't see Steichen benching Jones right now unless absolutely necessary.

That being said, if Steichen doesn't believe that Richardson can even supplant this clearly spiraling version of Jones, then what was the point of even keeping him on as the primary backup? They should've just moved him.

Furthermore, even if Richardson Sr. didn't have a particularly strong 2026 training camp, neither did Jones in 2025 Colts training camp when he won the starting job from Richardson Sr. and was named the new starter just weeks before the regular season started.

If anything, Richardson Sr. was arguably the stronger on-the-field performer in 2025 camp, whereas Jones won the job because of his off the field study and practice habits, and mental understanding of Steichen's offense.

I'm not saying Richardson Sr. is going to be the savior either, but at the very least, he could potentially provide this stalling passing offense a much needed spark, especially with his big arm and willingness to throw the ball downfield—which at the very least, is more exciting offense than the "Charlie Checkdown" Jones we've seen.

For a team on a short week missing its two starting offensive tackles, and facing Houston Texans All-Pro pass rusher Will Anderson Jr. on Thursday night, Richardson Sr. could also provide much needed mobility and escapability in the passing pocket, while making the Colts ground game more dynamic and versatile, and harder to defend and predict for the opposing defense.

Coming off the Achilles, this current version of Jones hasn't looked nearly as explosive or comfortable running with the football, so Richardson Sr.'s improved mobility would be a significant upgrade in that regard.

I'm just having a tough time with this one because Jones starting for the 2026 Colts has clearly run its course, and it's hard to see how starting Richardson Sr. could be any worse. The status quo at QB isn't working.

At the very least too, it provides the Colts, who are clearly going nowhere fast, one last extended look at the 24-year-old Richardson Sr., to see if he's made any significant jumps in passing accuracy and progression of reads, and safely close the chapter on his time here—should he falter again.

#2815. A Wolves Retrospective Part One: Kevin Garnett

With the season moving forward at a breakneck pace, it can be difficult to find the bandwidth to focus on anything else. But for people like us, and hopefully many of you reading this, there's no better time to appreciate the moments and players who got us to this place than when the planted seeds are finally bearing fruit.

And with Anthony Edwards' explosive start to the season, where he placed third on the MVP ladder and was heading the scoring race before unfortunately being sidelined by injury, there is no better place to start than with the Timberwolves' sole MVP.

We think there has been some anger from fans recently about how Garnett seems to embrace his Boston Celtics career, but we believe that some love remains from older fans who remember how great KG really was.

On the other hand, there are likely newer fans who don't understand the extent of KG's dominance. In this article, we offer an impassioned defense of why Kevin Garnett peaked as the best player in the world and arguably a top-five player ever.

The easiest place to start is a catch-all. We find it the easiest heuristic to understand exactly what we are dealing with. Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus (RAPM) uses on-off data adjusted across thousands of possessions to attempt to find how much value a player adds over a variety of lineups.

This is then converted into how many points of value a player adds over 100 possessions. Any guesses how much utility Garnett generated during his prime?

In that MVP season in 2003-04, Garnett added NINE POINT EIGHT points per 100, which ranked first in the league and second all time, only trailing 2016-17 LeBron James. This type of impact is easily understood when we look at the team context.

KG came into the NBA as a wiry high schooler, with extreme energy and length that would later make him one of the best defenders we've ever seen. But his feel is largely unappreciated, as he excelled as one of the best ancillary offensive weapons of the 21st century. He is one of the most multiplicative pieces in history, as represented by some truly tremendous lineup data.

In the 2003-04 season, Garnett was off the court for a total of 715 minutes. During those possessions, the Wolves — a 58-win team — put up a net rating 10.3 points below the league average. In the 3,235 minutes that KG played, the Wolves rocketed up to a relative net rating of +9.6.

The obvious response to this is that Garnett was boosted by playing with the starters. After all, the Wolves employed Sam Cassell at the time, a player who earned second-team All-NBA honors that season. And it is true that when Garnett and Cassell played together, the Wolves put up astounding numbers.

Minnesota put up an explosive +11.5 net rating in the 2,535 minutes — 4,760 possessions — that the duo spent together. When both of them were off the court in 403 minutes, the Wolves fell to a precarious -15.8. Similarly, in the 313 minutes Cassell was on without Garnett, the team sported a -4.4 net rating.

However, there were 700 minutes, or 1,288 possessions, if you're picky, that KG played without Cassell. The team's net rating during those minutes? +4.3.

No matter who was on the court during KG's time at the top of the basketball world, they did little to stifle his ability to impact the game at a historic level. His defensive superpowers made him one of the greatest game-changers in the league, but also a team-building cheat code.

Although KG wouldn't officially receive the DPOY honor until his later years in Boston, we refuse to allow this lack of an accolade to diminish how impactful he was at his best in Minny. KG was truly one-of-one, a reactive, processing octopus who would use his tentacles to reach out at any shot attempt and stamp it.

What is lost in KG having so much length is that he also had some of the most miraculous hand speed ever for someone his size. The way he snaps his arms up to block passes or shots looks like a glitch in the system sometimes.

Garnett's intersection of reaction speed, length, and movement let him be one of the best rim protectors ever while being able to guard at the point of attack when switched onto guards or in space when put into the pick and roll.

One area where he struggled, and where his contemporaries, such as Tim Duncan, were able to pass him up, was in strength-based stoppage. I am not explicitly arguing KG over Duncan in this article, but I use Duncan as the other dominant figure at the power forward position in the NBA to illustrate Garnett's strengths. While no one truly stopped the once-in-a-lifetime Shaquille O'Neal, there is a gap in the work Duncan was able to do over Garnett, with both being incredible defenders.

However, Garnett makes up ground through his ability to play in different schemes, compared to Duncan's traditional drop coverage. For example, the greatest offensive engine of their era, Steve Nash, found success solving these coverages in 2007, although his team ultimately fell short.

It is hard to compare because we do not have any Phoenix Suns playoff series against Garnett to compare with, nor was Duncan at his peak when they played, but it is one signal that matches up with the eye test that Duncan's main points he held over Garnett were strength-based, while Garnett held more movement and versatility advantages.

KG getting into a defensive stance | FOX Sports

Garnett's ability to move his feet, atypical for a big, allows for more aggressive and versatile coverages. For example, trapping or hedging toward the ball-handler is much easier when the center can recover quickly. It also enables switching and denies mismatch hunting.

These traits would translate incredibly well to the modern era, but that's not to say he didn't already put up monstrous defensive performances in his own time period. It is unfortunate that we do not get many playoff series from KG after 2004, but he puts up remarkable defensive signals in all of them.

Throughout his career, from 1997 to 2014, KG maintained an opponent-adjusted relative defensive rating of -6.4 when he was on the court, which is remarkable for someone who came into the league so early and left so late. If you isolate from 2004 onwards, he put up marks of:

Unfortunately, KG peaked in the pre-tracking era, so we don't have many individual metrics that represent this impact, but the ones we have are extremely helpful. In his 2004 season, KG averaged five stocks per 100, split between three blocks and two steals. 67% of his blocks were recovered by his own team, which helped Garnett force 0.3 more turnovers per 100 than the league average, an 84th percentile mark.

Furthermore, KG had a 4% STOP% this season, with a stop being any action you take that causes a change in possession (eg. steals, blocks recovered, charges drawn), which ranked in the 97th percentile. Combine these stats with the holistic impact Garnett showed on his teams and the versatility that he could offer to any team that acquired him, and you get one of the best defenders to ever touch the hardwood, period.

Defense is based on three things: eliminating the offensive possession through forcing a turnover, Suppressing the offensive possession through forcing a hard look, and ending the offensive possession through a defensive rebound.

Garnett was one of the best ever at the first two, but adding in that last bit gives him a case for being the GOAT. From 2003 to 2007, KG led the league in defensive rebounds. For five straight years, his lowest defensive rebounding total was 9.2 per game, and in all four other years he maintained an average over ten.

The all-time defensive rebounding leader, with 11,453 in his career, didn't play during the tracking era, but the signals we have from the end of his career are incredible. In his 2014 season, ten years past his peak, he had a 27.9% defensive rebound percentage, which was in the 100th percentile. 100th!!! 32.2% of those rebounds were contested.

He maintained that already ridiculous rate of 26.6% defensive rebound percentage in the playoffs, with a 45.6% contested rebound percentage. Even past his physical prime, KG was still a monster on the defensive glass.

While we already mentioned his portable qualities, Garnett was still a one-man army on defense. In his 2004 season, he carried a defense 2.4 points better than the league average (a 7.5-point swing compared to when he was off), which represents the level of defensive help his teammates provided.

DARKO, an all-in-one metric that combines the box score and lineup data to estimate a player's performance, views the players put around Garnett as, on average, a -1 boost to his defense — in other words, they returned negative defensive value.

Garnett was simultaneously a wrecking crew by himself and one of the most multi-faceted, ecosystem-building defensive players ever.

Often, defenders come with warts on the other side of the ball, especially when it comes to big men. That is being seen with another one of these all-time defenders who resides in Minnesota right now, Rudy Gobert. Fans despair over the lack of an offensive game, but this was never the case with KG.

KG was, in the truest sense, a unicorn in both ability and responsibilities. This may be easily said about players of the past in retrospect, but KG's abnormal offensive duties on his teams didn't go unnoticed at the time either.

Chris Broussard, in his 2004 article for the New York Times (the headline of which really says it all), recounts Game 4 of the Western Conference Finals, in which KG, flanked by an injury-depleted and underperforming Wolves roster, was left to face down the Kobe-Shaq Lakers "virtually by himself". He played a game-high 47 minutes, which he himself felt wasn't enough. Broussard notes that with lead guard Sam Cassell out, KG had become a "7-foot point guard, igniting the offense, then attempting to be a low-post presence as well."

The article quotes Wolves head coach Flip Saunders as saying: "We've never asked [KG] to do more than he's doing right now." And although this was true, it was a temporary exacerbation of a preexisting problem – KG, as a Timberwolf, was systematically overtasked on offense.

In 2004, KG carried a 29.6% usage rate (an estimate of the percentage of total team plays a player used). For comparison, Steph Curry, in his 2014-15 MVP campaign, posted a 28.9% usage rate. He put up 30.2 true shot attempts per 100 (basically how many offensive possessions did he end up taking a shot, combining field goal and free throw attempts), which was in the 98th percentile. And he did this with efficiency 2.9% better than league average — 91st percentile. He also averaged 6.8 assists per 100 – 99th percentile. Overall, he created 47.9 points per 100 – 100th percentile.

Garnett bringing the ball up the court | Icon Sports Media

This was not a one-season phenomenon. From 2003 to 2005, for three seasons straight, KG was in the 100th percentile positionally in points created per game and in points created per 100. Nobody at his position was asked to create offense at a higher volume on a game-to-game or possession-to-possession basis. From 2001 to 2007, a seven-season stretch, the lowest he ever dropped was 97th percentile in either per-game or per-100 points created.

During that span, the highest offensive rating the Wolves posted in a single season was in 2001-02 – a 109 ORTG, good for fourth in the league. Their highest playoff ORTG during that span was in 2003: 106.2, good for ninth out of 16 playoff teams.

Across all games in that span, regular season and postseason, when KG was on the floor, the Wolves ORTG sat at 107.2, a mere 2.4 points above league average. When he went to the bench, however, the offense dropped to an abysmal 97.3, a 10-point swing that saw them plummet to 7.6 points below league average.

Certain fair criticisms can be levied against him, as a handful of limitations prevented him from carrying the Wolves to greater playoff heights on offense.

He lacked the dominant low-post game that many fetishize in older bigs, which suppressed his overall rim scoring. In his '04 MVP campaign, he put up 4.7 rim attempts per 75 (56th percentile positionally), shooting 67% on them. 6'2 Tyrese Maxey so far in the 2026-27 season is averaging 5.8 rim attempts per 75 and shooting 71.4% on them. To be fair to KG, he got his in the height of the dead-ball era.

Hindered by his comparative stringiness and higher center of gravity, his post-up possessions more often than not ended with a tough jumper instead of a layup or dunk. He looked almost anemic at times, trying to create quality looks against contact.

His jumper-heavy diet limited his free-throw rate. He peaked at 6.7 free-throw attempts per game in 2005, though a high conversion rate of 81.1%, especially for a big, stemmed the bleeding. It also reduced his offensive rebounding opportunities. And of course, his penchant for long twos instead of threes suppressed his scoring efficiency.

Garnett skying for the dunk (per Wikipedia)

All this is true, and yet he remains one of the most unique, offensively impactful big men we've ever seen.

KG was ahead of his time. He possessed a genuine center's frame with agility and ball-handling reminiscent of a wing, along with a silky, soft touch that led to some of the most prolific jump-shooting seasons we've ever seen from a big. If he played in today's era, these qualities would no doubt translate beautifully.

In 2004, 74% of his field goal attempts came from either the long or short midrange, 42% from long midrange. Dirk Nowitzki, in the same season, shot 62% of his field goals from either the long or short midrange, and 46% from long midrange. They were similarly efficient.

KG was as versatile a scorer as any big ever. A capable play-finisher, he frequently scored on hard rolls, short rolls, pops, spot-ups, lobs, and other miscellaneous catches with layups, dunks, and jumpers.

Out of the low post and mid-post, although he could get his way to the rim, usually against smaller players, his bread and butter was a lethal midrange game. He could face up and just shoot it, but more often, he would turn and fade, from a variety of spots over both shoulders, off the catch or off the dribble, as he pleased and as the situation called for. He could also go to a hook shot over the top.

He had the stride length and quickness to drive by his man and take it to the rim with an open lane. He could also run the floor in transition or push the break himself off a rebound, which not only helped him score but also led to easy playmaking opportunities.

He was a tremendously gifted, versatile passer for a power forward. At his size, he could see above and pass over smaller defenders, and his ball handling, agility, and ability to process the floor let him pull the trigger quickly when an opportunity presented itself. He could ignite breaks with outlet passes off his rebounds. He could make passes off the dribble to shooters or streakers in transition. He could pass on the roll. He could spray it out of the post when he drew extra attention from help defense, even skipping it cross-court at times to the opposite corner or wing. He could zip it to a cutter or flashing big on the block for easy scores.

In each of the four seasons from 2002-05, KG was 100th percentile at his position in assists per game, and averaged just 2.7 turnovers per game and 5.5 APG over the whole stretch – doubling his assist-to-turnover ratio.

When he wasn't doing the shooting, KG was cleaning up on the offensive glass, grabbing three per game from 2002 to 2005.

KG was a tremendous offensive player during his Wolves peak – not a flawless one, but extremely talented. He consistently found himself in the low-to-mid 20s PPG band, maybe only a tier or two below the upper echelon of big man scorers like Shaq or Dirk and in the same range as someone like Tim Duncan, while being a strong contender for the best big man passer on the planet.

Unfortunately (Wolves fans may not want to hear this), he wasted the better part of his prime on a subpar roster, forced into a suboptimal role. It is partially his fault for not being a dominant force in the low post and taking too many long twos, but he was also no doubt bogged down by the constraints of his teammates. Whatever the cause, he was routinely inefficient in the playoffs, and from 2001-2004, the Wolves never achieved even a +3 opponent-adjusted relative ORTG in the playoffs with him on the court.

Once he moved onto greener pastures in 2008, even though he had started to slip out of his physical peak and his creation volume dipped, his true shooting percentage reached near-career highs, from 53.9% in 2007 to 58.2%. Having more real shooters and playmakers alongside him replaced his tough post-up possessions with easier looks. His rim FG%, which was at 63.3% the year before, leaped to 71.2% on higher frequency. His short and long midrange FG%, which were at 46.1% and 43% respectively the year before, jumped to 49.8% and 47.7%.

There was improvement at the team level too. In 2008, the Boston Celtics posted nearly a +6 opposition-adjusted rORTG in the playoffs with him on the court. Evidently, KG is someone who, while capable of bringing poor offensive teams to somewhat competent heights as a first option, thrives when he is not tasked with being a primary creator for himself. And it seems his team thrives as a result.

Many may look back at the KG years with mixed emotions: They were never able to get over the hump, but it is one of the true exalting feelings of being a sports fan to have the best player in the world playing for your team.

In the same way, Garnett was much of a mixed bag. He lacked some of the things you'd like from a traditional 2000s big man. He didn't have the size or the post game to assert his will on the game through physicality. But he made up for that and then some with a generational motor and other physical tools.

He was never able to carry his team to the championship as the number one option, but he demonstrated an ability to do so, while perhaps being better suited as the number two, pushing the Celtics team to historic heights.

But one thing is for certain if you are a fan of Minnesota. One of the best players to ever touch the rubber ball called this place home. Perhaps another is doing so right now. Sometimes, even with the new era roaring in your face, you can sit down and look at the fields of fruit in front of you and think about the one great tree that was here at the start.

#2814. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2813. Myles Price, NFL's top punt returner, shows he can make an impact on Vikings' offense, too

The Vikings have a big weapon on special teams in return man Myles Price, who is leading the league in punt return average, total yards and touchdowns, and is third in the league in both kickoff return average and total yards. But on Sunday against the Packers, Price showed that he can make an impact on offense, too.

In the Vikings’ win over the Packers, Price got a career-high 33 snaps on offense, and he responded by catching four passes, including the first touchdown of the game on a 38-yard pass from Kirk Cousins. Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell told Paul Allen that the decision to give Price so much playing time was mostly because of injuries to starting receivers Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings, but with the way Price performed, he’ll get more playing time on offense going forward.

“We want to continue to find ways to get Myles involved in the offense,” O’Connell said.

O’Connell said that when the Vikings are as thin at wide receiver as they were on Sunday, there are concerns about getting anyone else injured, and he was worried about seeing Price take hits in the return game.

“With all the injuries the other day, we had no way of getting another player up,” O’Connell said. “There was not another body to have, so we actually went into the game for the first time since I’ve been here with four receivers up. Every time Myles returned a ball, you felt like we could be out of 11 personnel altogether here on one play. He did get banged up a couple times, we tried to feature the bigger groupings, and luckily he was able to return.”

Ultimately, O’Connell believes that when Price has the ball in his hands in the open field, he can make big plays whether on offense or special teams.

“Myles is a guy that we feel very strongly about making that last move, making that last man miss, and being able to score,” O’Connell said.

Expect to see Price do more of that for the rest of the season.

#2810. Inside the looming chess match between Kyle Shanahan and Brian Flores this weekend

The San Francisco 49ers are back in primetime on Sunday night, as they're taking on the Minnesota Vikings in a battle between Top NFC contenders.

San Francisco, sitting at 8-1, is coming off a 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys, where its offense was unstoppable, while the defense had a ton of holes. Minnesota, on the other hand, just traded for Kirk Cousins at the trade deadline and blew out the Green Bay Packers in his first game back.

While Minnesota's offense has raised questions this year, it's the defense that has remained elite under coordinator Brian Flores, who has continued to find different ways for his defense to excel. This year, it's with a blitz-heavy approach.

Flores has been able to neutralize teams all year long. No team has scored more than 25 points against the Vikings, and that lofty defense was what propelled Minnesota while its offense was struggling.

Flores has had head coach Kyle Shanahan's number in the chess match between play-callers over the past few years. Regardless of the circumstances of the previous matchups, this is a perfect opportunity for Shanahan and the 49ers to establish themselves in many ways. It would continue to provide a boost in the NFC race, while also giving Shanahan another game to bolster his Coach of the Year case.

But Shanahan acknowledged the difficulty that Flores and his game plan will provide on Sunday.

"He just, he does it. He's more unique than all the other 31 guys," Shanahan said of Flores. "He's the one guy who commits to this and it's not just a fad for these nine games or whatever. He's been doing it his whole time in Minnesota. He did the same thing in Miami. He's as good as it gets at that stuff. Anybody who lives in that world as much as he does, it's usually a matter of time.

"I think offensive coaches used to like to say that early on, but it's too many years of it, and it's too many games in this year that they're sound. They put so much pressure on the quarterback, the play caller, the O-Line, the receivers, on everybody. A lot of times, when you go into an NFL game, the pressure's really on people on third down and stuff like that because those are things where everything can come and when you play against Brian, it's 70-straight plays of that."

One position that Flores's defenses have done really well to neutralize is the tight end position because of how much the Vikings blitz, forcing another blocker to stay in-line. That's critical with Mike Evans currently not trending to play, leaving George Kittle as the team's top weapon.

But overall, this game will be a chess match between the two brilliant minds who have arguably been the best play callers in the NFL this season. And there's a lot on the line on both sides with the NFC race heating up.
