#2808. Bucks vs. Heat Player Grades: Jakucionis and Herro continue good and bad form as Giannis dominates

On a momentous night when the Milwaukee Bucks and Giannis Antetokounmpo faced each other for the first time, the Miami Heat pulled off a 137-130 win. Frankly, the final score flatters the Bucks, who spent most of the game down ~20 as Giannis diced them up from all over the court and finished with a near triple-double. As for interesting interactions between former teammates on both sides, there really wasn't much to report. Tyler Herro got booed pretty mercilessly, while the reaction to his other three former Heat teammates was pretty lax. Giannis barely interacted with anyone from the Bucks (other than a brief joking interaction with Jericho Sims after Sims fouled him). Frankly, it looked a little awkward for everyone involved. Read our full summary of the game here and catch a six-minute audio recap on the Bucks+ podcast, Bucks In Six Minutes, below.

24 minutes, 8 points, 4 assists, 1 steal, 4/11 FG, 0/5 3P, 0/1 FT, -18

Herro was awful, yet again. Insipid on defence and unable to do anything with the Heat's quick, physical guards as they hounded him up and down the court. I was desperately hoping for a snarling, trash-talking Herro who gave the Heat the business, but he went out with a whimper with the team looked better with him on the bench.

23 minutes, 10 points, 2 rebounds, 5 assists, 2 turnovers, 3/7 FG, 1/4 3P, 3/4 FT, -8

Jaquez was fine. He had his usual backbreaking turnover or two, but otherwise he was kinda just out there and made little impact, positive or negative.

30 minutes, 26 points, 5 rebounds, 1 assist, 2 steals, 1 block, 3 turnovers, 9/16 FG, 2/5 3P, 6/10 FT, -18

Credit where it's due: Kuzma was fantastic. Milwaukee would have lost this game by at least 30 if not for Kuzma's work on both ends. He was about as good as anyone could have asked for as one of two primary defenders on Giannis, and his ability to keep the scoreboard ticking—even if it came drawing a BS foul—was crucial in slowing the Heat's barrage of scoring runs.

21 minutes, 4 points, 5 rebounds, 4 assists, 3 blocks, 2/5 FG, 0/2 3P, -15

Turner didn't do anything that stood out as actively detrimental to the team, but he wasn't a major plus either. Based on our lowered expectations for the big man this season, I would say he played fine. They kept Turner away from Giannis as much as possible, and I thought he did a solid job as a weak-side rim protector.

17 minutes, 11 points, 3 rebounds, 1 steal, 5/7 FG, 1/2 3P, -15

I mean, Ware got most of his when the game was, for all intents and purposes, over, scoring four of his five buckets in the second half. Still, I liked the way he ran the floor and kept his hands ready. I will say that whenever Giannis had a chance to go at Ware, you could almost hear his inner monologue saying, "BBQ chicken."

25 minutes, 20 points, 7 rebounds, 1 assist, 2 steals, 3 turnovers, 6/9 FG, 3/5 3P, 5/6 FT, -14

Burries was great, especially in the third quarter, when he was the only guy who wanted to play with a spark, scoring 12 points on 4/6 shooting, including a sequence where he scored a layup, stole the inbounds pass, and flipped it to a streaking Kuzma for another layup. I thought his defence was a major plus too, as he fought over and under screens on the Heat guards.

25 minutes, 20 points, 3 rebounds, 5 assists, 2 steals, 0 turnovers, 6/8 FG, 3/5 3P, 5/6 FT, +11

Jakucionis with his second consecutive great game. Once again, his pace and burst were far more useful than Herro's finesse. KJ's second-half line is insane: 5/5 from the field, 3/3 from three, and 5/6 from the charity stripe with four assists, two steals, and no turnovers. He made several great passes out of the pick-and-roll, showcasing his ability to create a two-on-one and read the help defender.

17 minutes, 7 points, 4 rebounds, 1 assist, 3 turnovers, 1/5 FG, 0/3 3P, 5/5 FT, +9

Ament wasn't overly involved in the first half, missing both of his three-point attempts. However, there were some encouraging signs in the second half. One facet of Ament's game that's evolving is his feel. They had him sprint up to set middle and side ball screens to see if he could catch it on the slip when the defence was switching, and he got a nice scoring opportunity doing exactly that. Interestingly, they also used Ament a bit as a passing hub at the top of the key as screening actions occurred around him; he hit LeVert on a nice dime while playing that role.

16 minutes, 1 point, 2 steals, 0/5 FG, 0/3 3P, -19

17 minutes, 4 points, 6 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 turnovers, 1/3 FG, +12

Sims was the other primary defender on Giannis (along with Kuzma), and he was solid enough. Attacked the rebounds hard and even made some nice passing reads.

14 minutes, 11 points, 3/5 FG, 3/5 3P, +17

Green got most of his opportunities off roll-and-replace actions, where the point guard (mainly Jakucionis) created a two-on-one in the pick-and-roll, forcing Green's man defender to rotate over and tag the roller, leaving him open for a split second from three.

Obviously, the game plan centred on defending Giannis. I have always said that the first step to stopping Giannis is having a defender who can at least trouble him one-on-one, and then you're able to help opportunistically as opposed to every time down. The Bucks don't have that guy, so their plan was basically to turn GA into a passer, and he wrecked them doing exactly that. There's nothing you can do about that, but I at least liked that Jenkins chose to take something away and didn't let him score and pass; he shot just four times in the first half. I also suspect Sims started the last game to prepare for this one—and that starting won't be regular—but I could be wrong.

Inactive: Kam Jones, Cormac Ryan, Pete Nance, Ousmane Dieng, Bogoljub Markovic, Ryan Rollins

The Bucks do not have a passable Giannis defender on their roster. Kuzma and Sims did their best and competed admirably, but neither was enough to really make him work.

Jericho Sims still has a major issue with illegal screens.

I hate to say it, but the Heat's GTA-themed court looked stunning (see below). This was a one-night thing; we won't see it ever again.

Unlike last season, when they were among the top teams in shooting percentage, the Bucks this season cannot seem to find a rhythm, and it is frustrating. Shot 15/43 in the first half last night and rank 29th on the season (42.9%).

Giannis did not shake hands with any members of the Bucks at the end of the game. A few nights before, he said this was "just another game."

The Bucks are back in action tonight as they take on the Portland Trail Blazers at home. Watch at 7:00 p.m. CST on MY24.

#2805. Ben Johnson sees Bears' 4.2 yards per carry average as "a deceiving statistic"

League wide, NFL teams average 4.2 yards per rushing attempt. The Bears also average 4.2 yards per rushing attempt. Bears coach Ben Johnson doesn’t much care about that.

What Johnson does care about is that the running game is efficient, and Johnson would like to see better efficiency than he has seen so far from his offense. Johnson noted that an occasional long run can skew the yards per carry average, and if there are too many runs getting stuffed for no gain, that’s a problem. On the flip side, a one-yard run will bring down any team’s average, but it’s a great play if it happens on fourth-and-goal at the 1-yard line.

“I don’t see it as bigger chunk runs, necessarily. The yards per carry is a deceiving statistic in a lot of ways,” Johnson said. “We run the ball a lot in the red zone, and when you’re down there a four-yard carry is really an explosive.”

Johnson said what he cares more about is efficiency. Many teams look at running success rate, which means the percentage of runs on which a team gains at least 40 percent of yardage needed on first down, at least 60 percent on second down, or at least 100 percent on third or fourth down. The Bears’ success rate this season is 49.2 percent, and Johnson says that’s not good enough.

“We go off efficiency, and we’re under 50 percent efficient running the ball. We set our bar higher than that. We want to be closer to 55 percent, so we’ve got some work to do and all our guys know it,” Johnson said.

Ultimately, Johnson wants to see rushing first downs and rushing touchdowns. Yards per carry is secondary to that.

#2803. The Lakers finally slowed down Luka Doncic — for one night

After a seemingly endless flurry of efficient 40- and 50-point masterpieces, fatigue finally caught up to him. His legs felt the weight of carrying the team without Austin Reaves, who has been sidelined for three straight games. His shot was finally off.

It took him playing on the second leg of a back-to-back following a game that began at 8 p.m. and went into overtime the night before.

But Doncic was finally not quite himself Wednesday.

The Slovenian superstar finished with 29 points (2-for-12 shooting from beyond the arc), five rebounds, seven assists, two steals and nine turnovers in the Lakers' 109-97 loss to the Jazz, which snapped their nine-game winning streak.

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Utah Jazz in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"Yeah, I mean, honestly I just got to do way better than this," Doncic said. "This is unacceptable for my part. I got to lead the team in better ways. So just, like I said, got to look at this game, got to move on and learn from this."

Doncic proceeded to pick apart his performance.

"Well, just a little bit of everything," he said. "Obviously the shots, the turnovers. Those [are] two [of the] specifics. I think defensively, we're in a good space. Just offensively, I got to lead the team better than this."

It was an exceedingly rare relative off night for the 27-year-old amid an MVP-caliber start to the season. He entered Wednesday's game leading the league in scoring with 38.8 points per game on a career-high 39.8% shooting from beyond the arc — while carrying the Lakers to the best offensive rating in the league.

But alas, after having the best start in modern NBA history, he finally sputtered a bit.

It happened after Doncic had a 36-point, seven-rebound and seven-assist performance less than 24 hours earlier as the Lakers clawed their way back from an 18-point deficit to beat the Hornets in overtime on Tuesday, 118-114.

Lakers coach JJ Redick acknowledged that the load Doncic has been carrying without Reaves is astronomical.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

"The shot creation that is required from him, I think it takes its toll," Redick said. "…So you know that's the luxury of having two really elite creators, and obviously when they're both in the lineup, it makes things a little bit easier."

Doncic has the highest career usage rate in NBA history and he's nipping at the heels of the highest single-season usage rate ever. It's a load that has been exacerbated without Reaves, who averages 24.7 points per game, and is considered day-to-day after sustaining a left heel bruise against the Bucks on Nov. 11.

Quentin Grimes compensated for Reaves' absence Tuesday by exploding for a career-high 47 points.

But Wednesday, Doncic didn't get enough offensive assistance to offset his less-than-brilliant performance. Grimes, who was the team's second-leading scorer, finished with 20 points, going 1-for-6 from the field in the fourth quarter. Walker Kessler had 10 points on 3-for-7 shooting and 11 rebounds.

When Jake LaRavia was told Doncic took responsibility for the Lakers' loss, he balked.

Luka Doncic handles the ball during a game against the Utah Jazz in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"Yeah, of course he's going to say that," said LaRavia, who had four points, six rebounds and two assists. "It's obviously not on him. It's a team game. Yeah, I mean he's obviously been carrying the offensive load, so if there's ever bad shooting nights, it's on the rest of the team to kind of help be better on offense and help make shots and stay in rhythm offensively."

And when Doncic's battery dipped in his third game in four nights following a brutal turnaround at Crypto.com Arena, the 3-13 Jazz were able to steal a game against the 13-3 Lakers.

Doncic had been playing so stunningly well that a 29-point performance could come across as a relative stinker.

But a bit of exhaustion finally took a toll on the epicness of Luka magic for one night.

"Yeah, that can't be an excuse," Dončić said. "All NBA teams play 82 games, so that can't be an excuse. I got to do way better. I feel that we had some open shots we didn't make, but it's one game. We got to move on."

#2802. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2800. Troy Aikman’s Latest Dig at Joe Buck Sets Up an Awkward Super Bowl at the Stadium Where They Clashed

The countdown to ESPN's first Super Bowl is on, but the network's top broadcast booth keeps grabbing attention for reasons that have nothing to do with football.

Troy Aikman took a jab at his longtime broadcasting partner, Joe Buck, during his weekly appearance on Dallas sports radio station 96.7 The Ticket, in a clip posted to X on Thursday, November 19,

With host George Dunham's usual cohost out sick, Aikman, 59, joked, "Well, I know Joe's always wanted a one-man booth; I'm wondering if you've always wanted a one-man radio show?"

The quip is a far cry from what Buck, 57, said just two months ago.

"Troy Aikman knows that I have his back…We had a lot of shared experiences…He knows I'm his biggest fan, vice versa," he told Front Office Sports in September.

As First for Sports previously reported, Buck signed a six-year extension with ESPN worth $108 million. Aikman, meanwhile, is still working without a new deal. Both men arrived from Fox in 2022 on five-year contracts after two decades together there, and Aikman's agreement is set to run out after the Super Bowl.

The uncertainty has complicated a broadcasting partnership spanning decades.

The tension spilled over on October 12, when the pair argued before the Buffalo Bills–Los Angeles Rams game at SoFi Stadium. "I'm not the reason you don't have a contract," Buck reportedly told Aikman during the exchange, according to The Athletic.

The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback, who won three Super Bowls during his 12-season NFL career, has made it clear he's thinking about what comes next.

"I'll broadcast through this season and I'll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens," he said, per The Athletic.

First, though, the two will have to share a booth on football's biggest night, and in a familiar setting. Super Bowl LXI is scheduled for Sunday, February 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium, the same venue where their argument took place. Per ESPN, it will be their seventh Super Bowl together.

ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro admitted this week that the media coverage of the feud has been "disappointing," but he isn't worried about what viewers will see on air.

"These guys are professionals, and they're delivering every week," Pitaro, 57, said, on stage at the SBJ Media Innovators conference, per a clip Sports Business Journal shared to X. Pitro added that he would "fully expect that to continue that through the season and through the Super Bowl."

#2799. Bills Week 11 Power Rankings: Do power rankings matter heading into a divisional game?

Despite a convincing win over the New York Jets, national analysts remain divided on whether Buffalo deserves the NFL's top spot. The Buffalo Bills walked out of MetLife Stadium with a 31-12 victory over the New York Jets, but apparently a 19-point divisional win isn't enough to impress everyone.

Heading into Week 11, Buffalo remains firmly entrenched among the NFL's elite, with four of our eight tracked national outlets ranking the Bills No. 1 and the remaining four placing them at No. 2.

Interestingly, two outlets moved Buffalo in opposite directions following Sunday's victory. ESPN dropped the Bills from first to second, while Sports Illustrated bumped them from third to second.

The result? Buffalo's average ranking remained exactly where it was last week: 1.50.

While national analysts might disagree about which team deserves the top spot, there's little disagreement that the Bills belong in the conversation.

ESPN drops Buffalo despite another convincing victory

Perhaps the most interesting development this week came from ESPN, which moved Buffalo from No. 1 to No. 2 following its victory over New York. It's not as though the Bills struggled to put points on the board. Buffalo scored 31 points, generated 389 yards of offense, and kept the Jets out of the end zone entirely.

Was it a flawless performance? Absolutely not. The Bills converted just two of their 10 third-down opportunities, and the defense allowed New York to sustain several extended possessions.

However, Buffalo also produced three second-half touchdown drives totaling just seven plays and 2:49 of possession.

James Cook rushed for 157 yards, including a 74-yard touchdown, while DJ Moore contributed 90 receiving yards and a score. Buffalo found ways to win comfortably without needing everything to go perfectly.

Power rankings aren't simply about the previous week's final score. Analysts consider the overall body of work, strength of opponents, and how teams stack up against other contenders.

Still, dropping a team after a 19-point divisional victory certainly raises some eyebrows.

USA Today FINALLY showing Buffalo some respect

Now here's an outlet we've been watching closely. USA Today hasn't exactly been Buffalo's biggest supporter throughout the season. In fact, the Bills sat at No. 9 entering Week 8 before beginning a steady climb.

The Bills moved from No. 9 to No. 6 entering Week 9, then made an impressive four-spot jump from No. 6 to No. 2 heading into Week 10. FINALLY, some respect!

Following Buffalo's victory over the Jets, USA Today kept the Bills at No. 2 for Week 11.

While USA Today isn't quite ready to crown the Bills the NFL's best team, the steady climb suggests Buffalo has done enough to change the perception of its overall performance.

And considering how long we've been watching USA Today rank Buffalo lower than several other national outlets, seeing the Bills maintain their place near the top is certainly worth acknowledging.

While Buffalo continues battling for the top spot in the national rankings, its next opponent finds itself at the opposite end of the conversation.

The Miami Dolphins enter Week 11 with considerably less confidence from national analysts.

USA Today dropped Miami five positions, from No. 27 to No. 32, while FOX Sports also placed the Dolphins last in its rankings. ESPN, NFL.com, and CBS Sports each ranked Miami No. 30.

It's a striking contrast between two AFC East rivals heading into their Week 11 matchup. Buffalo is receiving serious consideration as the best team in football. Miami is being evaluated among the league's worst.

However, divisional games have a way of making power rankings feel irrelevant once the ball is kicked off. The Bills cannot afford to overlook Miami simply because national analysts have little confidence in the Dolphins' current trajectory.

Buffalo has an opportunity to continue building momentum, and another convincing divisional victory would only strengthen its case among the NFL's top contenders.

The biggest remaining question isn't whether Buffalo belongs among the NFL's elite. The national rankings have largely settled that debate. It's whether the Bills can continue proving they deserve to be considered the very best.

With the struggling Dolphins coming to Buffalo, the Bills have another opportunity to make their case.

#2798. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2796. A Vice City rout: Heat defeat Bucks 137-130 in collab with ‘GTA VI'

A Vice City rout: Heat defeat Bucks 137-130 in collab with 'GTA VI' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

A loss on Vice City night never made sense.

The Miami Heat routed the Milwaukee Bucks 137-130 on Wednesday during a one-night-only promotional collaboration with Rockstar's "Grand Theft Auto VI," which launches in the U.S. at midnight Thursday.

Miami rolled out a new court at Kaseya Center with pink, blue and black colors matching its special-edition jersey. The words "Vice City" replaced the usual Heat logo in mid-court, while a "VI" with a palm tree featured in the corner of each paint.

Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo led the way for Miami in a night that meant a lot to both players. Antetokounmpo faced the team that drafted him for the first time, while Adebayo went head-to-head against former teammate Tyler Herro and Co.

Antetokounmpo posted a game-high 27 points on 7 of 11 shooting to go with 13 rebounds, nine assists, one steal and a block.

Adebayo followed suit with 26 points on 7 of 15 shooting to go with four rebounds, two assists and two steals. Adebayo dominated the first half, while Antetokounmpo took over in the second.

Davion Mitchell added 24 points on a hot 6 of 7 clip from long range to help Miami move to 9-6 after a slow start. Milwaukee fell to 1-14 as Kyle Kuzma scored 26 points to lead the team.

Milwaukee closed the gap in the final quarter once Miami pulled most of its starters, but the Heat had been in control since the end of the first.

Beyond the game, fans had access to a limited-edition Vice City merch and apparel collection at team shops throughout the arena. There were also unique cars on display for fans to see and a photo spot with the "VI" logo.

Vice City is the fictional name of the game's city that loosely represents Miami, while Leonida is the fictional Florida-inspired state the city is based in. Other prominent in-game locations are based on the Everglades and the Florida Keys.

"GTA VI" has been expected to be the biggest game of the decade since its initial trailer release in December 2023. The previous installment, based in a fictional Los Angeles and surrounding areas, released 13 years ago.

#2794. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.

#2793. Jared Goff: Jahmyr Gibbs is a special player, special guy, special teammate

Back in August, the Lions signed Jahmyr Gibbs to a three-year contract extension.

The 24-year-old running back currently leads the league in rushing yards (1,000), rushing touchdowns (11), yards from scrimmage (1,384), and total touchdowns (13).

In his Wednesday press conference, quarterback Jared Goff praised Gibbs for his outstanding performance so far in 2026.

“You look at the numbers he’s doing, it’s like you hear his name mentioned with [Hall of Famer] LaDainian Tomlinson it seems like every week. And obviously we know about that guy and yeah, he’s unbelievable,” Goff said, via transcript from the team. “He really is. He’s a special player. He’s a special guy, special teammate. The work he puts in I think gets unnoticed sometimes. He’s a worker and has elevated his game from last year to this year in a lot of ways that you guys have obviously seen and it’s paid off. It’s been great for him and he’s playing really well.”

Goff added that there’s plenty the public doesn’t see when it comes to Gibbs’ competitiveness.

“He’s very competitive,” Goff said. “Anytime there’s a competitive situation in practice, he wants the ball, he wants to make someone look silly, he wants to make somebody miss and he wants to make the play. And when he doesn’t, he gets upset and that’s kind of what you like to see when he makes a mistake or misses a block. He’s truly upset about it and that’s a sign of a good player and a guy who’s striving for greatness.”

It’s also worth noting that Gibbs leads the league in rushing attempts (199) and touches (240). His previous career high in touches came last year with 320, which he appears poised to blow through.

#2792. The Seahawks must put Drew Lock on the Russell Wilson plan

It's interesting that the Seattle Seahawks first acquired Drew Lock in the Russell Wilson trade on March 8, 2022. That deal sent Wilson from Seattle to the Denver Broncos, along with a 2022 fourth-round draft pick, in exchange for Lock, tight end Noah Fant, defensive lineman Shelby Harris, 2022 and 2023 first-round picks, 2022 and 2023 second-round picks, and a 2022 fifth-round pick, and it set the Seahawks up for future success in ways few could have predicted at the time. Seattle got Devon Witherspoon, Charles Cross, Boye Mafe, and Derick Hall out of those picks, while Lock didn't quite make the cut.

He was Geno Smith's backup in 2022 and 2023, signed with the New York Giants for the 2024 season, and signed a two-year, $5 million deal to come back to the Emerald City in 2025. Not much came of it in 2025, as Sam Darnold had enough on the ball to help the Seahawks to their second Lombardi Trophy, but things have obviously been different in 2026. Darnold was injured early in the season opener against the New England Patriots, and Lock finished that 13-10 win, and a 31-7 Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals, looking very much like the NFL's next reclamation quarterback. He completed 35 of 48 passes (72.9%) for 422 yards (8.8 yards per attempt), four touchdowns, no interceptions, a passer rating of 127.3 (the NFL's highest among quarterbacks who took at least 20% of their teams' snaps), and an EPA per pass of +0.43 (the NFL's fourth-best).

Still, it made sense that a (relatively) healthy Darnold returned to the field in Week 3 against the Washington Commanders. Dan Quinn's defense looked like an easy out, and the Lock story was more about the Seahawks having a top-tier backup than any sort of quarterback controversy. In that 33-31 upset loss, Darnold gave us the full Sam Darnold Experience, completing 31 of 45 passes for 379 yards, four touchdowns, two interceptions, a passer rating of 105.7, and an EPA per pass of +0.05.

From Week 4 through Week 8 as the starter, Darnold completed 95 of 164 passes (57.9%) for 1,086 yards (6.6 YPA), six touchdowns, seven interceptions, a passer rating of 72.4, and an EPA per pass of -0.18 — down there in the mid-thirties with Deshaun Watson, Cam Ward, Jalen Hurts, and Jacoby Brissett. Darnold's injuries were clearly affecting him, and this was especially true when he tried to throw outside the pocket, which was a big factor in the Seahawks' Super Bowl run. This season when throwing outside the pocket, Darnold has completed 13 of 35 passes for 162 yards, two touchdowns, one interception, a passer rating of 59.5, and an overall EPA of -12.14 — ninth-worst in the NFL.

Basically, because of his physical limitations, Darnold was put on a quick-game plan by offensive coordinator Brian Fleury — his average time to throw went from 3.14 seconds in Week 3 to 2.32 seconds in Week 7, and 2.67 seconds in Week 8.

I asked Darnold about this right after Seattle's 34-17 Week 8 loss to the Chicago Bears — a game he finished despite a quadriceps injury and a cracked rib.

"Yeah, I think for me, it's all about when I get the ball out quick," he said. "It's all about knowing where to go with the football. And I think, again, just being decisive, knowing when I need to move on in the progression and doing that. Talking about this game specifically, you gotta watch the tape, obviously, but I feel like there were opportunities to get the ball out, and I just didn't."

Fair enough, but when your passing game is that limited, it's a problem. Especially when your run game has been behind the sticks all season long.

So, Lock was back under center for Seattle's 17-3 Week 9 win over the Arizona Cardinals, and last Sunday's 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, and the work was similarly strong. In those two games, Lock completed 33 of 45 passes (73.3%) for 415 yards (9.2 YPA), three touchdowns, no interceptions, a passer rating of 123.8 (fourth-best in the NFL), and an EPA per pass of +0.22 (fifth-best).

By the way, Lock's EPA per pass of +0.33 is the NFL's highest among quarterbacks with at least 50 dropbacks. And he's the quarterback who allows the Seahawks to run their entire offense at this point in time. Whether Darnold's issues are tied to injuries and/or other things, he's not able to do that right now.

"Oh my gosh, yeah," Mike Macdonald said of Lock's two touchdown passes out of scrambles against the Raiders. "He's got that ability to extend plays and not put the ball in danger, which is cool. We turned it over twice, but those were really early in the play. Great plays, man. It was awesome."

"Yeah, we just talked about creating plays," Jaxon Smith-Njigba said after the Raiders game. "Drew's a creative player, great player, can move around, great athleticism. So, just sticking with him, knowing that his eyes are downfield trying to make a play. Just being there for him."

What Smith-Njigba said of Lock in the wake of Darnold's possible return revealed even more.

"Man — unbelievable player, great player. Not only how he played incredibly, but just what he does off the field and in the huddle and how he commands his troops. True professional, and [I] love sharing the field with him."

And how about an endorsement from Devon Witherspoon?

"Ah man, it's dope. See Drew come out there and do the things he does. We watch him in practice all the time. I call him the Locksmith, because it seems like he's just got all the damn coverages. To see Drew play the way he's played, given the situation he's in, you can't ask for anything better than that. He comes out here and he works every day. We see the looks that we give every day in practice, man.

"We've got all the confidence in the world, because we know he put in the work to do it."

By the way, Lock has done all this with injuries to his throwing elbow and his oblique muscles.

Okay. What do I mean when I say in the headline that the Seahawks need to put Lock on the Russell Wilson plan? Let's take a trip in the Wayback Machine.

I started covering the Seahawks with credentials in 2010, which means that I got to see the genesis of the Pete Carroll plan, and the creation of the Legion of Boom. I also got to see what happened in 2012 after the team signed Matt Flynn to a three-year, $19.5 million contract with $10 million guaranteed, and selected Russell Wilson with the 75th overall pick in the third round of that draft.

Wilson made his supremacy at the position evident from the start. At his rookie minicamp, he was making bang-on throws 40 yards downfield. As training camp turned into the preseason, I started hearing from veterans on the team that Wilson was the quarterback they trusted. He was the one they wanted to load the wagon behind. And that eventually happened, because Carroll understood the value of momentum, and that the best player must win the job, regardless of position.

Macdonald has said all the right things publicly about Darnold as his starter. But he's also smart enough to know that with his team outside the playoff picture right now at 6-4, and a bye week to get everyone on the same page, this would be the ideal time to make the right call.

And regardless of the reasons why, the right call is to give Drew Lock all the starter's reps. The difference in performance has been all the difference.

#2791. Todd Monken: Getting flexed into Sunday night is really cool for our players

If someone had told you at the beginning of the season that the Week 12 game between the Browns and Raiders would get flexed into Sunday Night Football, you probably would have responded with some healthy skepticism.

But with the way the season has unfolded, that’s exactly what’s happened.

With the Browns at 6-4 and the Raiders at 4-6 — and now starting the league’s No. 1 overall pick at quarterback — the two clubs make for one of the most compelling matchups of Thanksgiving weekend that wasn’t already in a standalone window.

Browns head coach Todd Monken told reporters on Wednesday that getting flexed is “really cool for our players.”

“I said it at the beginning of the year. I mean, you want to be on Thursday Night, Sunday Night, Monday Night — you want to be flexed, means you’re having a good year,” Monken said, via transcript from the team. “As nice as it is to have a one o’clock schedule every week, I mean, I said that, early in the [year]. I mean, you’re on a trajectory to be fired at some point because you’re at one o’clock every week. So, you’re fighting like hell to get to where you’re on national TV. So, if people are going to watch football, and more importantly than that, an opportunity to get to seven [wins].”

Monken also agreed that it’s a good test for the Browns as a young team.

“I think you earn where you’re at in the present moment, and that only lends itself to what’s in front of you and how important that’s going to become,” Monken said. “You know, getting the bye at 6-4 and putting yourself in position where the rest of the games matter, and especially the one coming up.”

This will be the Browns’ first Sunday night game at home since 2019, which should make for a rowdy atmosphere on the shores of Lake Erie.

“Oh, it’s a huge advantage. Huge advantage,” Monken said of the anticipated environment. “Making it hard for the opposing offense, cadence-wise, being able to function, and making an advantage for us when we’re on offense. I mean, it’s a huge advantage, and it should be playing at home.”

#2790. Game Preview: Knicks at Timberwolves, November 19, 2026

It wasn't long ago that a Knicks vs. Timberwolves matchup almost felt like a mini-rivalry—one of the few the Knicks had against a team from the Western Conference.

Given the East Coast vs. West Coast of it all, and the LeBron vs. New York effect, the Lakers made for a fun matchup. The Spurs and Knicks have had some tough battles, including the 1999 Finals and the 2024 Christmas Day game, and that pseudo-rivalry was elevated to a new level with the 2026 Finals. But whenever the Knicks and Timberwolves played each other over the last two seasons, it felt like there was more on the line than just the game. It was a battle for narrative, not just bragging rights. Which team won the Karl-Anthony Towns trade? How would former Knicks Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo play against their former team? Now, with the Knicks having won a championship and Randle moving from Minnesota to Brooklyn, this matchup no longer feels as personal.

That doesn't mean that it'll be a bad game. Nor does it mean that the Timberwolves won't be a tough opponent. At 11-4, they enter Thursday night with a better record than the Knicks despite being without star guard Anthony Edwards since he underwent knee surgery on October 29. And contrary to expectations, their success hasn't been a result of LaMelo Ball putting up insane offensive numbers. Their scoring has been incredibly balanced, with Ayo Dosunmu averaging 18.6 PPG, Ball averaging 17.7 PPG, and Jaden McDaniels averaging 17.1 PPG. Even without a single player averaging more than 20 PPG, they've managed to have the 12th-highest offensive rating.

Where they've remained elite sans Edwards, though, is on the defensive end. The Timberwolves, thanks in large part to four-time Defensive Player of the Year winner Rudy Gobert, have been incredibly dominant defensively. As of today, they have the best defensive rating in the league at 104, two full points better than the second-place Celtics. They rank third in the league in opponents' field goal percentage, first in opponents' three-point percentage, and force the sixth-most turnovers per game.

The Knicks, who haven't completely gotten past their early-season shooting struggles, may have a tough time scoring against the Timberwolves. Even with the recent play of Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Landry Shamet, and Miles McBride supplementing Karl-Anthony Towns' dominant season, the Knicks still find themselves outside the top 10 in three-point percentage and near the bottom of the league in field goal percentage. That doesn't mean the Knicks won't be able to score, though. They have two very clear advantages heading into tonight.

One advantage is that they'll have the two best players on the court. The Knicks can say this in a lot of games, and that hasn't stopped them from getting off to a disappointing 8-6 start. And this matters less in the regular season than it does in the postseason. But this should still bode well for the Knicks. Brunson won Eastern Conference Player of the Week to kick off November and hasn't really looked back. Even against a tough Raptors defense, he came through and put together back-to-back quality games. And you can make the argument that Towns hasn't had a single game this season where he hasn't been great in one way or another. The big man has also had some monstrous games against his former team, averaging 29.0 PPG, 14.3 RPG, and 3.7 APG while shooting 61.7% from the field and 56.3% from three. And in two of those three games, Towns scored 32 or more points and grabbed 13 or more rebounds.

The Knicks' second advantage comes on the offensive boards. The Timberwolves give up the 12th-most offensive rebounds per game. Some of that is a direct result of their defense forcing so many misses. But with the Knicks being a top-five offensive rebounding team, Towns, as well as Andre Drummond and even Jordan Clarkson, could have big nights on the boards, making up for what could be an inefficient shooting night.

This will be a good test for a Knicks team that has earned seven of its eight wins against teams that are .500 or worse. The Timberwolves are 7-2 at home, deploy a dominant defense predicated on forcing players into the rim-protecting monster that is Gobert, and have a balanced offense that often scores just enough points. But expect the Knicks to lean on their two big horses. Brunson has also had some nice games against the Timberwolves and LaMelo Ball-led teams. And Towns has dominated just about everybody this season. We also can't forget that the Knicks themselves have a good defense, which could test a limited Timberwolves offense. The Knicks come away with a low-scoring, ugly win led by Towns to improve to 9-6.

#2789. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2788. Detroit Lions pass rush not 'a one-man band,' even before Aidan Hutchinson's injury

The Detroit Lions will miss Aidan Hutchinson dearly. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard told his unit as much earlier in the week.

But Sheppard said Thursday, Nov. 19, that Hutchinson's season-ending knee injury is not a deathblow for a Lions pass rush that's been one of the best in the NFL all season.

"It hasn't been a one-man band anymore," Sheppard said. "I know that's what we're used to here and, 'Oh, everything goes through Aidan.' Listen, he generates a lot, but I think you either haven't been watching the game or you're only watching Aidan if you think he's the only person that's been applying pressure this year."

The Lions rank fourth in the NFL in sack rate (9.38%) and third with 32 total sacks. They're the only team in the league with three players with six sacks, and even after losing one of them − Hutchinson − Sheppard said he has faith in the group that will be led by Alim McNeill (6½ sacks), D.J. Wonnum (6) and Tyleik Williams going forward.

Hutchinson tore the ACL in his right knee on the opening drive of last week's 35-10 win over the New England Patriots.

"Can't just rely on scheme, can't just rely on one player. It's going to have to be all of us," Sheppard said. "Luckily – unfortunately but luckily, kind of, like I said, looking at everything, what can I pull from this? Pulling from the last three or four seasons. I know for myself personally having to adjust and adapt on losing high-caliber, top-end players, especially on the defensive side, has been something we've done and we'll continue to do and do it at a higher rate than we've done, I'm hoping this time."

Sheppard said he received his first text from injured linebacker Jack Campbell before last week's game against the Patriots.

Sheppard declined to share details of the message but said he wanted "to make it known that happened because I hadn't heard from him until then, so that really excited me, man."

"I miss the hell out of Jack, if I'm being honest," Sheppard said. "But his teammates have done a tremendous job making sure that he knows that we're doing this clearly for him."

Campbell was injured on a tackle in the fourth quarter of the Lions' Nov. 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings. Neither he nor the Lions have shared any in-depth updates on his recovery since they said Nov. 4 that he regained full movement in his lower body and was "continuing to make progress with movement" in his upper body.

"Still sending thoughts and prayers out to Jack and his wife, Megan, his son and his family as he continues through his recovery process," Sheppard said. "I was excited to get a text from him for the first time on game day, so that kind of fired me up a bit there. I was very thrilled about that."

Drew Petzing said he "put no thought" in the ritual he has with tight end Sam LaPorta that went viral this week when the Lions posted video of the offensive coordinator head-butting LaPorta in the chest.

"I put no thought into it when it started, and then it just kind of became a routine," Petzing said "When you're my height, it's a pretty natural thing to do when people come up to you because it's just like you're right there and it felt right."

In the video, Petzing high-fives LaPorta on the Lions sideline, then leans in to headbutt him in the chest as Lions receivers Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown look on. Williams laughs hysterically in the video, then tells LaPorta he's going to greet the tight end the same way.

LaPorta told Williams he and Petzing do it every week.

On Thursday, Petzing said he got a chuckle out of Williams getting a laugh at him.

"Yeah, I enjoyed the clip," he said. "I'm glad Jamo enjoyed it, as well."

After a spike in punt return touchdowns last season, when there were a total of 15 punt return TDs across the league − the most since 2012 (18) − NFL teams have struggled to generate big plays in the return game this year.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are the only NFL team that's allowed a punt return touchdown this season, and Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp said a number of factors are contributing to the decline of explosive punt return plays.

"I always say to returners, I mean, if you want to hit a home run, then swing the bat a lot of times," Fipp said. "The more times you swing the bat, the better your odds of getting a home run. Now, you might strike out more, too, but people don't worry about that. They talk about the one. So returns are down, punts are down in the NFL, so the fact that that number's down a little bit doesn't totally surprise me."

Teams are averaging fewer than four punts per game for the third straight season, according to Pro Football Reference, and the fifth time in NFL history as they've become more aggressive trying to convert fourth downs and kick long field goals. Fipp said teams also are punting more from midfield when they do punt, which leads to more touchbacks.

Though the Minnesota Vikings had an 86-yard punt return touchdown against the Bucs in Week 1, Fipp said that play was more a one-off than an indication Tampa has problems defending punt returns.

"In order to get a touchdown return, there's a lot of things that have to come together all at the same time," Fipp said. "It's both you doing a good job executing, but there's also some things that had got to fall into place for you, too."

Dave Birkett covers the Lions for the Detroit Free Press. Contact him at dbirkett@freepress.com. Follow him on Bluesky, X and Instagram at @davebirkett.

#2786. Cowboys roundtable discussion: Christian Parker, Christian McCaffrey, and Tennessee Titans

Every week, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer's perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jorge Guajardo, Dyllan Rivers, Tom Ryle and Sean Martin.

Mike – The biggest responsibility falls squarely on Christian Parker here. Players have to execute, maintain their assignments and make tackles, but when your defense surrenders a franchise-record 584 yards and 46 points at home, that's a complete failure of coaching.

Kyle Shanahan repeatedly exposed Dallas with misdirection, poor defensive positioning and mismatches that Parker simply had no answers for. Parker is being outcoached every week, and the decision to strip him of play-calling duties tells you everything about how badly things have gone.

Jorge – Both. Pairing a rookie DC with this roster is a bad combination, and the results show every week. From a player standpoint, watching the film there are some guys not playing through the whistle, with some jogging while players appeared to be still in the mix.

As for Parker, he's in way over his head, just like his head coach. Now, I think something needs to be said for good coaching. I think good coaching gets you to hustle and finish every play. Good coaching arms you with the knowledge to take the right angles to stop a certain play; good coaching puts you in positions to succeed, but none of that is apparent on this defense. Yes, the players also have responsibility. So this is a result of a match made in hell with Parker and a poor defensive roster.

Tom – Really, that's the only answer that makes sense. It's a perfect storm of ineptitude and it is threatening to sink Dallas. There are some talented players on the defensive side of the ball, but a combination of misuse and not everyone shouldering their share of the load is nullifying it. And let's not forget the role the head coach plays in the motivation arena. I don't know what is going on in the locker room, but I can't help but worry that Schottenheimer is on the verge of losing it – if he hasn't already.

Sean – All the respect in the world to Von Miller, but this was on coaching. It's being kind to only use the last three weeks as a sample size, but just in this stretch where the Cowboys are 1-2 against two losing teams and a 49ers team they let break records on them, the explosive plays allowed are outrageous.

Look elsewhere around the NFL, and games are being decided by razor thin margins even between teams you might expect to have a little more of a gap. Explosive plays are earned through a clear, visible effort from coaches to put players in those positions. Christian Parker's defense is the antithesis to this. Whenever an offense needs a huge play, even for a touchdown, they can get it.

Dyllan – All of the above. Christian Parker can't control Elijah Garcia and James Houston chasing down a phantom running back 40 yards the wrong direction instead of containing the Deebo Samuel reverse. But Parker can decide to not call a zero blitz in the most crucial moment of the game, leaving Von Miller one-on-one with Christian McCaffrey. The perfect blend of mediocrity and misery has found its way to the Cowboys defense.

Mike – For me, this comes down to poor coaching, dreadful defensive discipline and Christian Parker repeatedly putting his players in positions to fail. Having a 37-year-old Von Miller isolated against McCaffrey in coverage is baffling and the best example of my statement of Parker putting players in positions to fail, he has to take responsibility for allowing such a ridiculous mismatch. The Cowboys continually lose their assignments, take poor tackling angles and fail to communicate, but these are recurring problems that should be getting corrected on the practice field. When the same mistakes happen every week, it's no longer just poor execution, it's poor coaching.

Jorge – In a game where the Cowboys gave up three plays over 65 yards that all ended in TDs, it's hard to say that this is where the game was lost. However, the offense had clawed back to within one score; it was a 2nd-and-9, and a stop gives you a chance. You would think that in a game where your defense has already given up two disastrously long plays, you wouldn't ask your 37-year-old, pass-rushing specialist linebacker to cover a back like CMC in his prime, right? Wrong.

That's exactly what Christian Parker did. A lot of people have said it was just a great counter from Shanahan to route CMC right at Miller. My counter is they're right. Shanahan is a great coach with an incredible feel for the game, its moments and his roster. Christian Parker is not. How are you not prepared for that alternative? There never seems to be any contingencies with this team, and it's defense. They simply run what they run, fail because their plans never survive contact with the enemy, and they have nothing prepared for the possibility that their plans may not work. Parker left Miller out to dry.

Tom – It is beyond embarrassing how the Cowboys just let one or more players absolutely go off on them every week. The topic of Schottenheimer's job security is a popular one, but the seat is far hotter under Parker. A well run team would likely write him off as a failed one-year experiment and start planning for the next DC. That would hardly be helpful for the players to have to go into the third new system in three years, but what is the point in prolonging the bleeding?

Unfortunately, that part about a well run team really doesn't apply for Dallas. Worse, there is no likelihood that is going to change.

Sean – Maybe we should have just known better to not have hope during another frantic fourth quarter comeback by the Cowboys, but for all the ones in the past that felt pointless and hollow, this one against the 7-1 49ers actually felt real. The offense earned back a legitimate chance to retake the lead down by six, the comeback had legs. Then in the blink of an eye, McCaffrey is literally running so free that a Dallas defender couldn't even dream of touching him. There was a 0% chance to make a tackle on that play, zero.

It was sickening, inexcusable, and to answer your question, yes the most baffling decision of the game.

Dyllan – I don't believe having Von Miller man up against Christian McCaffrey is something the 31 other defensive coordinators in the NFL would ever dream of doing, especially in clutch time. As far as the other explosives, it's coming from a blend of losing the schematic chess match, poor tackling, and players simply making bad decisions. The fundamentals are missing for the second year in a row. The explosives will continue for as long as the most basic elements of defense are lost.

Mike – Absolutely. Anything less than a convincing victory against Tennessee would be deeply concerning, and losing this game should effectively end any serious conversation about Dallas making the playoffs. Brian Schottenheimer needs to have this team prepared, aggressive and ready to take control early. More importantly, the defense must finally show it can handle an opponent without surrendering ridiculous explosive plays.

Jorge – The Cowboys will almost certainly make this a game, as they did against Indianapolis. The defense can only play solid for an entire half, so expect this to go down to the wire. Tennessee is not in the business of winning football games this year; I mean, neither are the Cowboys, although there is an illusion of it, but that's a different story. That said, if the Cowboys lose to Tennessee on Sunday, the season is over, and the staff will pay with their jobs come season's end. What a terrible season.

Tom – To your last question, yes, it would be the effective end of things. I just don't see this team as having the resiliency to come back from that level of embarrassment, and while I agree that they will probably win, it is not a given.

So we may see the flickering hopes for making something out of this year resting on Parker/Mike Pettine figuring things out. That is not good. The play-calling change change might shake things up and get a different fire lit under the players.

Sean – I don't even want to slap a must win label on this one, because that also carries the connotation of a team building towards a goal by getting such wins, and the Cowboys don't have that right now. They could win the next two and the only realistic take to have about it is that the team's best case scenario is a repeat of last year, playing well through a stretch in November and that's it.

Even if they get these two wins, they would need one more to match last year's win total and two to pass. The most likely two that Dallas can win are against their own division to end the season, and that's just the worst sequel of all time at this point when it comes to not taking the bait over beating bad division opponents.

Beating the Titans would make Thanksgiving a little more enjoyable to not feel like absolutely all hope is lost by the holiday, but I think that's about it.

Dyllan – Simply put, losing any more games against bad teams effectively ends the season. The "easy wins" need to be easy while Dallas also needs to steal potentially two out of three games against Jacksonville, Seattle, and the Rams. The Giants are helping the Cowboys stay alive, so Dallas needs to capitalize on the gift.

#2785. How Damian Lillard has boosted Trail Blazers in promising return from Achilles injury

The fear, when we saw Damian Lillard sitting there with a thousand-yard stare after falling to the ground early in Game 4 of the Milwaukee Bucks' first-round series against the Indiana Pacers in the 2025 NBA playoffs, was that we might never see him again.

A ruptured Achilles tendon has altered, if not derailed, plenty of NBA careers. What would it do to a small guard with more than 35,000 NBA minutes on his odometer who was entering his mid-30s?

What if that — that false step, that unsatisfying whimper of a finish to his time in Milwaukee, an era that felt like an error almost from the moment it started — was the last time we'd ever see Lillard looking like what he'd been for the previous 13 years: among the most dangerous shooters of all time, a generational scoring threat from the second he crossed half-court, one of the 75 greatest players in the league's history?

An awful lot's happened since then: the shocking waive-and-stretch that ended Lillard's time in Milwaukee (and, more or less, Giannis Antetokounmpo's time there); his subsequent re-signing with the Portland Trail Blazers, the home he never really seemed to want to leave; an entire season spent rehabilitating and recovering, in hopes of giving himself a shot at becoming himself once again.

"All the time off I had, I had to take advantage of it," Lillard recently told NBC. "Not just look at how far out I was and just try to chill or whatever. I had to make sure that every day counted. I was diligent in the process of my rehab, and then when I got back on the court, the weight room, making sure I was balanced on both legs. And then, once it got back to just hooping, that was the easy part — it was just a matter of shaking off the rust."

Fourteen games into his first action in 18 months, Lillard still hasn't totally shaken it all off and returned to the level that made him a nine-time All-Star and seven-time All-NBA selection. Entering Thursday's matchup against a Bucks team that now looks very different from the one for which he last played, he's averaging 20.1 points, 4.4 assists and 3.0 rebounds in 29.1 minutes per game, and shooting 39.6% from the field — all at or near career lows. He's driving to the basket less frequently than he has since 2013; just 15% of his field goal attempts are coming at the rim, far and away the lowest share of his career. Nearly 60% of his shots, conversely, are coming from 3-point land — by far the largest share of his life in the NBA.

He's had nights to forget in the early going, like scoring nine points on 3-for-13 shooting in a blowout loss to the Memphis Grizzlies, or finishing with nine on 2-for-15 shooting in Monday's loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves. Those two single-digit performances, by the way, are already as many as Dame has had in any whole season since 2014.

Dame's also had moments to remember, though. Like dropping 25 points with a half-dozen 3-pointers in 24 minutes on the Phoenix Suns in Portland's season opener, his first live action in 543 days …

… or knocking down a side-step dagger in the right corner to hand the Los Angeles Lakers one of just three losses they've suffered on the season …

… or punctuating a 13-point third quarter against the Oklahoma City Thunder with a vintage, swashbuckling just-inside-the-logo buzzer-beating pull-up triple over the outstretched arms of 7-foot-3 rookie Aday Mara:

"I knew he was gonna shoot," Blazers two-way guard Chris Youngblood told Conor Bergin of Blazer's Edge after the win over OKC. "I was like, 'If this goes in, this crowd is about to go crazy.'"

Even amid the fits-and-starts with his finishing, Lillard has helped give Portland fans plenty to go crazy about in a pleasantly surprising start to the season — one in which he's been a lot more than just a nice story.

The Blazers enter Thursday at 9-5, in sixth place in the Western Conference, with the NBA's No. 8 offense and No. 10 defense, according to Cleaning the Glass. (The last time the Blazers ended a season in the top 10 on both ends of the floor: 2014-15.) They've taken down Luka Dončić's Lakers in L.A. and Nikola Jokić's Nuggets in Denver, swept a two-game baseball series from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's Thunder at Moda Center, and looked like a team capable of building on last season's return to the playoffs, ownership misadventures and personnel shuffling be damned.

Dame's done it in part by working his way into a new normal — one in which he's no longer the sun around whom the entire organization orbits, but rather one component of a constellation in which All-Star forward Deni Avdija often shines brightest.

Heading into the season, one of the main questions hanging over the Blazers was how first-year head coach Micah Nori would craft an offensive ecosystem that kept everything copacetic despite introducing two decorated All-Star on-ball playmakers (a returning Lillard, an incoming Ja Morant) alongside Avdija, who rose to prominence and helped return Portland to the postseason by becoming the league's highest-volume driver and establishing new career highs in usage, shot attempts, touches and time of possession. The early returns were positive: The Blazers are plus-19 in 66 minutes with Avdija, Lillard and Morant sharing the floor, scoring a scorching 125.9 points per 100 possessions in their minutes with both Dame and Ja taking a smaller slice of the total offensive pie.

The overarching experiment got paused when Morant went down with a hamstring strain, leading Nori to shuffle his starting lineup — first by sliding fourth-year guard Scoot Henderson into Morant's spot, and then, with Scoot struggling, swapping in 6-foot-6 forward Sidy Cissoko for a bigger, more defensively sound look. Portland's allowing just 106.5 points-per-100 with Cissoko on the court alongside ace defensive center Donovan Clingan and swingman Toumani Camara — a near-best-in-the-league level of point prevention.

Removing one ball-handler from the mix has somewhat reduced the need for offensive sacrifice, but Lillard has continued to keep up his end of the bargain. He is finishing 27.7% of Portland's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover — his lowest usage rate since 2014-15, when he was setting up LaMarcus Aldridge. His on-ball percentage — literally the share of his floor time that he has the ball in his hands — is the second-lowest of his career.

Dame has never averaged fewer touches or a lower time of possession, spent less time operating in the pick-and-roll, or spent more time lurking as a catch-and-shoot option. Just under 19% of the offensive possessions Lillard has finished this season have come while spotting up away from the primary action, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking data — more than twice as much as in 2022-23, the final year of his first stint in the Pacific Northwest.

"Being on this team and having less responsibility than I had before, I don't have to make every play," Lillard told Sean Highkin of the Rose Garden Report. "I don't have to score every basket. I just came into this season mostly focused on how I could impact winning. I know that at the end of games, I'm gonna have to make shots and make plays and make free throws. But over the course of a game, I think the load is just lighter."

Deploying Lillard as a different sort of threat in a smaller-scale role has proven useful to the overall offensive operation for the Blazers, who are scoring like a top-five offense with Dame on the floor — and like a near-top-10 unit when he's on the floor without Avdija, which were minutes in which Portland's offense died last season.

Last season, even with Avdija ascending as a downhill menace, primary playmaker and point-producing weapon, the Blazers finished the season just 20th in offensive efficiency, due partly to struggles with ball security (dead last in the NBA in offensive turnover rate, with 90 more live-ball turnovers than any other team in the league), shot-making (27th in team 3-point accuracy, 29th from midrange, 21st in overall effective field goal percentage) and half-court execution (just 29th in points per half-court possession). The arrival of Lillard has helped: Portland has turned the ball over less frequently, generated a higher share of its shots from 3-point land, shot better in the midrange, and scored more efficiently in the half-court with Dame on the floor this season.

Even with Lillard not quite at the peak of his shot-making powers, his presence opens things up for the rest of the offense. With him on the floor, nearly 53% of Avdija's 2-point baskets have come via assist — 20 percentage points higher than when Dame sits. The driving lanes that were so often so congested last season are open a bit wider with defenses needing to account for Lillard, who ranks eighth in the NBA's gravity metric — a stat aiming to quantify "how much a player pulls defenders towards them [...] how much attention they draw compared to what the spacing on the floor predicts" — just south of one high-volume superstar scorer in a ball-handling timeshare (Donovan Mitchell) and two designated sharpshooters playing off high-usage primary creators (Klay Thompson, Duncan Robinson).

That company feels illustrative of the space Lillard currently finds himself occupying: not peripheral, still vital, but more of a complement than a centerpiece. (He still can shift into primary mode, though; on Tuesday, with Avdija sidelined by a sore left foot, Dame scored a team-high 25 points with five assists against the Timberwolves, pushing the NBA's No. 1 defense to the brink in a game that Portland nearly, and perhaps should have, won.)

Plenty of superstars over the years have struggled to find comfort moving into that space. Perhaps due to the time away, though, Lillard seems to be navigating the shift fairly smoothly.

"Obviously, for the sake of rhythm and timing, you want to be on the ball sometimes, which I am," Lillard recently told Sam Amick of The Athletic. "But I think it just lessens the load of having to sometimes beat two guys, or get into the paint and do too much when we've got so many guys that can do that. I can space the floor, give guys space, and also catch and attack on the second side. It's been a process, kind of finding the spots, and it's becoming more natural. But it's been great as far as how I feel physically, how I'm able to play late in games, the effort and energy I'm able to give defensively throughout games. And I think it's a more sustainable way for us to handle the game."

Eighteen months ago, we wondered if we'd ever see Dame look like Dame again. While the jury's still out on that, what he's been so far — in terms of his combination of scoring and shooting efficiency, and by metrics like win shares per 48 minutes, box plus-minus, value over replacement player and player efficiency rating — nets out to something like a top-20 guard in the league. Just a month after coming back from one of the most devastating injuries an NBA player can suffer, that's not nothing … and, with a little more time, a little bit of luck and a lot more hard work, it's also not where Lillard's return is going to stop.

"This early in the season, I still feel like I'm getting it back completely — just that rhythm, and taking bumps, and moving at the pace of the league," Lillard told NBC. "But I'm feeling better and better. [...] I've just got to keep it rolling, and keep doing what I'm doing."
