#2784. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2783. Joe Burrow can become the first QB ever with 4+ touchdowns in 6 consecutive games

Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is on a remarkable streak of four-touchdown games. If he does it again on Monday night, he’ll do something no player in NFL history has done before.

Burrow has at least four touchdowns (combined running and passing) in each of the last five games. A four-touchdown game against the Commanders on Monday night would give Burrow an all-time NFL record six straight four-touchdown games.

Currently, Burrow and Peyton Manning are tied for the record, with five consecutive four-touchdown games. Manning did it in 2004 with the Colts. Burrow’s last five games have featured:

Four touchdown passes in a 38-18 win over the Steelers.

Three touchdown passes and one touchdown run in a 34-17 win over the Falcons.

Five touchdown passes and one touchdown run in a 43-36 win over the Titans.

Four touchdown passes in a 35-13 win over the Ravens.

Four touchdown passes in a 31-24 win over the Dolphins.

Burrow is the MVP favorite, and with 2,795 yards and 27 touchdown passes through nine games this season, he’s closing in on 3,000 yards and 30 touchdowns, which only four quarterbacks have done within their first 10 games of a season: Tom Brady in 2007, Aaron Rodgers in 2011, Manning in 2013 and 2014, and Patrick Mahomes in 2018. That’s good company for a quarterback to be in, and Burrow is playing right now at a level few quarterbacks have ever reached.

#2782. Detroit Lions pass rush not 'a one-man band,' even before Aidan Hutchinson's injury

The Detroit Lions will miss Aidan Hutchinson dearly. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard told his unit as much earlier in the week.

But Sheppard said Thursday, Nov. 19, that Hutchinson's season-ending knee injury is not a deathblow for a Lions pass rush that's been one of the best in the NFL all season.

"It hasn't been a one-man band anymore," Sheppard said. "I know that's what we're used to here and, 'Oh, everything goes through Aidan.' Listen, he generates a lot, but I think you either haven't been watching the game or you're only watching Aidan if you think he's the only person that's been applying pressure this year."

The Lions rank fourth in the NFL in sack rate (9.38%) and third with 32 total sacks. They're the only team in the league with three players with six sacks, and even after losing one of them − Hutchinson − Sheppard said he has faith in the group that will be led by Alim McNeill (6½ sacks), D.J. Wonnum (6) and Tyleik Williams going forward.

Hutchinson tore the ACL in his right knee on the opening drive of last week's 35-10 win over the New England Patriots.

"Can't just rely on scheme, can't just rely on one player. It's going to have to be all of us," Sheppard said. "Luckily – unfortunately but luckily, kind of, like I said, looking at everything, what can I pull from this? Pulling from the last three or four seasons. I know for myself personally having to adjust and adapt on losing high-caliber, top-end players, especially on the defensive side, has been something we've done and we'll continue to do and do it at a higher rate than we've done, I'm hoping this time."

Sheppard said he received his first text from injured linebacker Jack Campbell before last week's game against the Patriots.

Sheppard declined to share details of the message but said he wanted "to make it known that happened because I hadn't heard from him until then, so that really excited me, man."

"I miss the hell out of Jack, if I'm being honest," Sheppard said. "But his teammates have done a tremendous job making sure that he knows that we're doing this clearly for him."

Campbell was injured on a tackle in the fourth quarter of the Lions' Nov. 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings. Neither he nor the Lions have shared any in-depth updates on his recovery since they said Nov. 4 that he regained full movement in his lower body and was "continuing to make progress with movement" in his upper body.

"Still sending thoughts and prayers out to Jack and his wife, Megan, his son and his family as he continues through his recovery process," Sheppard said. "I was excited to get a text from him for the first time on game day, so that kind of fired me up a bit there. I was very thrilled about that."

Drew Petzing said he "put no thought" in the ritual he has with tight end Sam LaPorta that went viral this week when the Lions posted video of the offensive coordinator head-butting LaPorta in the chest.

"I put no thought into it when it started, and then it just kind of became a routine," Petzing said "When you're my height, it's a pretty natural thing to do when people come up to you because it's just like you're right there and it felt right."

In the video, Petzing high-fives LaPorta on the Lions sideline, then leans in to headbutt him in the chest as Lions receivers Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown look on. Williams laughs hysterically in the video, then tells LaPorta he's going to greet the tight end the same way.

LaPorta told Williams he and Petzing do it every week.

On Thursday, Petzing said he got a chuckle out of Williams getting a laugh at him.

"Yeah, I enjoyed the clip," he said. "I'm glad Jamo enjoyed it, as well."

After a spike in punt return touchdowns last season, when there were a total of 15 punt return TDs across the league − the most since 2012 (18) − NFL teams have struggled to generate big plays in the return game this year.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are the only NFL team that's allowed a punt return touchdown this season, and Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp said a number of factors are contributing to the decline of explosive punt return plays.

"I always say to returners, I mean, if you want to hit a home run, then swing the bat a lot of times," Fipp said. "The more times you swing the bat, the better your odds of getting a home run. Now, you might strike out more, too, but people don't worry about that. They talk about the one. So returns are down, punts are down in the NFL, so the fact that that number's down a little bit doesn't totally surprise me."

Teams are averaging fewer than four punts per game for the third straight season, according to Pro Football Reference, and the fifth time in NFL history as they've become more aggressive trying to convert fourth downs and kick long field goals. Fipp said teams also are punting more from midfield when they do punt, which leads to more touchbacks.

Though the Minnesota Vikings had an 86-yard punt return touchdown against the Bucs in Week 1, Fipp said that play was more a one-off than an indication Tampa has problems defending punt returns.

"In order to get a touchdown return, there's a lot of things that have to come together all at the same time," Fipp said. "It's both you doing a good job executing, but there's also some things that had got to fall into place for you, too."

#2779. LeBron Log No. 5: Popcorn in hand, a viral chorus and ‘basketball AI'

LeBron Log No. 5: Popcorn in hand, a viral chorus and 'basketball AI' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James spent Monday night in street clothes.

He still managed to argue a call with popcorn in his hand, practice his golf swing during a timeout and reject a report about himself before the Sixers left Brooklyn with a win.

That followed a Sunday afternoon in which James passed Jason Kidd on the NBA's career assists list and received an unusual description from Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle.

Welcome to the fifth edition of the LeBron Log.

James sat out the Sixers' 135-123 win over the Nets because of low back and sciatica management.

It was his fourth absence through 15 games. James has yet to play both ends of a back-to-back this season after logging nearly 33 minutes Sunday against Indiana.

He watched Monday's game from the end of the Sixers' bench in a yellow hat and an "Ohio Baby" sweatshirt. James snacked from a small bag before switching to popcorn.

When Joel Embiid believed he was fouled on a first-half drive, James stood and pleaded his case to official Jacyn Goble without putting down the box. He also joined conversations between teammates and officials during several timeouts.

James found another way to pass a third-quarter stoppage. As "Hot To Go" played inside Barclays Center, he practiced his golf swing near the bench.

His most pointed contribution came on Instagram.

An ESPN story by Dave McMenamin cited a Sixers source who said James had asked the coaching staff to remain patient while he worked toward finding his rhythm and conditioning by December.

James reposted ESPN's graphic and rejected the account.

"🧢! Those words never came out of my mouth!" he wrote.

The Sixers improved to 4-0 without James. They have beaten the Bucks, Hornets, Raptors and Nets in the games he has missed.

Brooklyn pulled within five points during the final five minutes Monday, putting the Sixers in another clutch game.

Philadelphia has reached 10 clutch wins more quickly than almost any team since the statistic began being tracked in 1996-97. The 2026-27 Sixers are the second team in that span with at least 10 such victories through their first 15 games.

The other was the 1997-98 Atlanta Hawks, who had 12.

James was also on the last team before Philadelphia to open a season with at least 10 consecutive clutch wins. The Lakers started 13-0 in those games last season.

James did not play in the Sixers' latest close finish, but he has now been part of the last two teams to start at least 10-0 under those circumstances.

Before Sunday's game, Carlisle explained why he tries to limit his play calls against James.

"LeBron James is one of the reasons we try not to have play calls, 'cause he knows all of them," Carlisle said. "He's a walking NBA basketball AI machine. That's what he is."

James followed with 15 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds in the Sixers' 131-124 win.

His pass to VJ Edgecombe for a layup with 1:19 remaining gave him 12,092 career assists and moved him past Kidd for third in NBA history. Only Chris Paul and John Stockton remain ahead of him.

Noah Levick wrote more about James' milestone and the anticipation behind his passes.

When told what Carlisle had called him, James appreciated the description.

"So, yeah, Rick is great," James said. "He's one of the greatest coaches of all time, and I've had my battles with him over the years. That's super humbling coming from a guy like that."

Philadelphia has found its soundtrack for James' biggest home moments.

The Sixers have played the viral "LeBron, LeBron, LeBron" song after several of his baskets, including his late putback against the Knicks on Oct. 30.

The refrain comes from a version of Steve Lacy's "Oh Yeah?" that replaces "Come on" with James' name. The Baylor University Men's Choir performed its own rendition, helping the song spread across social media.

Lacy later joined in. During an Oct. 15 concert at Freedom Mortgage Pavilion in Camden, he performed the LeBron version as the crowd sang along.

James has noticed Philadelphia's use of it.

"I've seen it. I've heard it. It's pretty hilarious, to be honest," James said. "I heard it towards the end of a game when we were winning. I made a play, and I heard that song. I was just chuckling to myself on the inside."

#2778. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2776. A badly timed shock - the story of Matos' Swans exit

Vitor Matos attempted to ingratiate himself with Swansea City fans by pointing out in a couple of press conferences how many days remained until the south Wales derby.

There is some irony, therefore, that confirmation of his exit has come a little over a week before Swansea's first meeting with Cardiff City in two seasons.

The timing of Matos' departure is far from ideal, and not just because the fixture which matters most to Swansea supporters is just around the corner.

The loss of Matos has come as a shock to a club sitting sixth in the Championship, while it has left many fans feeling the pain of separation.

With Matos gone, the Swans are unexpectedly left trying to figure out where to turn next.

Managers have come and gone with some regularity at Swansea in recent times, with the Welsh club now looking for an eighth permanent boss since they were relegated from the Premier League eight years ago.

Even during the glorious spell when Swansea went from the basement division in 2004-05 to seven seasons in the top flight between 2011 and 2018, there were numerous changes in the manager's office.

Yet few, if any, of the various managerial departures was more surprising than Matos' swift exit.

A little over a week ago, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe spoke to the media at length and was fairly emphatic as he brushed off questions about the prospect of Matos being tempted away any time soon.

Matos, meanwhile, had been due to speak to BBC Sport Wales to assess his first year as Swansea boss on Monday of this week.

Vitor Matos' Swansea had 23 points from 10 league games this season - and were two points clear at the top of the table - after victory at Millwall just over a month ago [Getty Images]

The interview was arranged at the tail-end of last week. On Sunday evening, however, Matos told Swansea's media staff that it needed to be postponed.

Even then, there was no suspicion that the chat was being scrapped because he was not going to make it to the 12-month anniversary, which was due to come on 24 November.

By Monday evening, however, word began to get out that Strasbourg were keen on Matos – and that he wanted to go.

The 38-year-old spoke to players and staff about his decision at the training ground on Tuesday, with a suggestion that he was emotional at times as he attempted to explain his reasons for walking away.

The loss of Matos was especially unexpected because everything seemed to be going along nicely at Swansea.

Usually there are signs of a managerial change on the horizon, either because a team are struggling or because things are going so well that rival clubs are circling.

Matos' exit is in the latter category, but there is still surprise that he has gone at this particular point.

Yes Swansea endured a first difficult run of the season just before the international break, with four defeats in five games.

But only one of those losses came as the result of an alarming performance – at Queens Park Rangers – and Swansea might easily have taken points from their losses against West Ham United, Portsmouth and Birmingham City.

Had that happened, they might well be top of the league now – as they have been during two spells this season – rather than three points off the summit.

Would Matos have walked away had Ross Stewart scored late on at Fratton Park, or if Marko Stamenic had avoided a match-turning red card in what proved to be his final game in charge at Birmingham?

Did he not back himself to revive the sparkling form which earned Swansea seven wins in their first 10 league games of the season?

There was no sign of an imminent departure as Vitor Matos performed a chin-up gesture following Swansea's defeat at Birmingham on 7 November [Huw Evans Picture Agency]

They are questions which will never be answered.

What we can say for certain is that Swansea remain firmly in the mix to achieve something significant this season, and yet Matos - who was given a new deal running until 2030 as recently as July - decided he wanted out.

He has opted instead to take charge of a team who lie 13th in the French top flight, albeit one who expect better and who - crucially, perhaps - are a sister club of Chelsea, with all their financial might.

For Swansea's owners, whose Premier League ambition seems pretty clear, Matos' decision must be somewhat galling, particularly given the support he has been given since they took something of a punt on him last November.

The messy manner of his move, which was announced by Strasbourg long before it was confirmed by Swansea, has quite clearly not gone down well either.

Many of the managers who have opted to leave Swansea in recent memory – the likes of Roberto Martinez, Graham Potter, Steve Cooper and Russell Martin – could claim they were not given all the tools they wanted during their respective stints in Wales.

They could argue that they had to move on because Swansea's ambition did not match theirs, or that they would be given greater backing elsewhere.

But it would be hard for Matos to make that case given that Swansea have spent significantly in recent transfer windows, and that their squad – as the long-serving Jay Fulton suggested earlier this season – looks as deep now as it has any point since the end of the Premier League era.

Swansea 'acknowledge' Matos' move to Strasbourg

Swansea's decision-makers are now left trying to figure out who might be able to maintain the momentum built up by Matos.

In the short term, Ashley Williams will hold the fort alongside three other long-serving former players, Joe Allen, Leon Britton and Kristian O'Leary.

The temporary coaching team will go straight in at the deep end, with fifth-placed West Bromwich Albion to come this Saturday before a trip to Middlesbrough, who are second, next Tuesday.

The south Wales derby follows at the end of a brutal Championship week.

Might a new permanent boss be in charge for Cardiff? That depends on how long Swansea need to identify their targets – and to get an agreement over the line.

Swans CEO on transfers, finances and Snoop's next visit

As ever, Swansea's fans will expect a new boss who is committed to playing possession football.

It would also make sense, given the squad Matos built, to find someone who is as committed to a high-pressing game as the Portuguese was.

Who will that manager be? A string of names have already been linked, and Swansea will not be short of applicants for what is an attractive job.

Jamestown Analytics is likely to be involved in the selection process, given that Swansea's deal with the data specialists covers coaches as well as players.

For the moment, forecasting which candidate will emerge from the crowd is difficult.

The only certainty is that Matos' exit has left Swansea's hierarchy with a big decision to make.

#2775. Bears-Lions Thanksgiving audience will be huge — and it could have been even bigger

Last year, both of the early Thanksgiving Day games broke the prior record for NFL regular-season audience size. This year, the all-time record of 57.2 million from the Chiefs-Cowboys game is likely safe.

With one small tweak to the schedule, it perhaps wouldn’t be.

In 2025, Packers-Lions attracted an incredible 47.7 million viewers. This year, the looming battle between the 7-2 Bears and 7-2 Lions should approach (if not match . . . if not beat) that number.

The problem is the second game. The 2-7 Eagles are in soft-tank mode. The 4-6 Cowboys have disintegrated into defensive disarray. While it will still attract a very large audience given the captive audience and the usual Thanksgiving routines, it likely won’t approach 50 million.

While the NFL has granted a permanent hammerlock to the Lions and Cowboys for the traditional Thanksgiving afternoon games, a simple tweak would have set the stage for Bears-Lions to break 50 million — and perhaps to threaten last year’s record.

Here’s the idea. Why not install flexibility to flip the start times of the afternoon games?

It’s no different than the usual Sunday-afternoon flex, like the one that happened this weekend when Steelers-Eagles moved from 4:25 p.m. ET to 1:00 p.m. ET and Jaguars-Giants slid to the higher-profile slot.

On Thanksgiving, the late-afternoon game always does better than the early one. In some years, the Lions game could be viewed as more attractive than the Cowboys game. This year would be one of those years.

It’s something to consider. Getting an annual Thanksgiving Day game doesn’t mean owning the window. And given the NFL’s current willingness, on and after Week 12, to flex from Sunday to Thursday or Sunday to Monday, why not reserve the right to acknowledge that, for the two afternoon games on Thanksgiving, the “best” one should be played in the higher-profile slot?

#2774. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2771. Swansea 'acknowledge' Matos' move to Strasbourg

Swansea City have belatedly confirmed that head coach Vitor Matos has left the Championship club by saying only that they "acknowledge" Strasbourg's statement over his move to the French side.

Strasbourg announced the appointment of Matos as their new boss on Wednesday evening.

Around 23 hours later, Swansea issued a statement of their own featuring only one line on Matos.

"Per RC Strasbourg's announcement, Swansea City acknowledges that Vitor Matos and his coaching staff have left the club," the Welsh club said.

Swansea's statement initially misspelled Matos' first name, as Victor rather than Vitor. The same error was made in Strasbourg's English language social media announcement of his appointment on Wednesday.

The 'mistake' was quickly updated on the Swansea's website. When asked whether the misspelling had been deliberate, a Swansea spokesperson declined to comment.

Swansea say former captain Ashley Williams will lead a temporary coaching team tasked with filling the void left by Matos' departure.

"Swansea City can confirm club greats Ashley Williams, Leon Britton, Joe Allen and Kris O'Leary – a quartet boasting over 1,400 appearances in black and white – will be at the helm for Saturday's game against West Bromwich Albion," the club's statement added.

"Additionally, head of academy goalkeeping Paul Whitfield has stepped up to the senior set-up, with the group taking today's (Thursday) training session at Fairwood.

"The club wants to place on record its thanks to Ashley, Leon, Joe, Kris and Paul for making themselves immediately available without hesitation, and we are grateful to have people with such a great passion for Swansea City guiding us through this period."

Ex-captain Ashley Williams has been assisting Wales boss Craig Bellamy since September, but has never held a senior managerial role [FAW]

Strasbourg are expected to pay Swansea a compensation fee thought to be in the region of £5m for Matos, who has left despite agreeing a new contract running until 2030 in July.

The 38-year-old spent just under a year at Swansea, having left his role as Maritimo boss - after only 12 games in charge - to succeed Alan Sheehan as the Championship club's head coach in November 2025.

Four members of Matos' coaching team - Diogo Medeiros, Toze Mendes, Goncalo Ricca and head of goalkeeping Pedro Pereira - are also expected to leave Swansea.

A badly timed shock - the story of Matos' Swans exit

Allen and Williams return to the club to join an interim coaching team alongside fellow former players O'Leary and Britton.

O'Leary and Britton are the only remaining members of Matos' backroom staff, with academy goalkeeping coach Paul Whitfield temporarily stepping up to first-team level.

The hastily assembled coaching group will lead Swansea while the club searches for Matos' permanent successor, with their first game in charge coming when West Bromwich Albion visit on Saturday.

Swansea then go to Middlesbrough next Tuesday before hosting Welsh rivals Cardiff City on Sunday, 29 November.

"Our focus is firmly on this weekend's fixture against West Bromwich Albion and collectively working to continue to drive the club forward," the Swans' statement added.

Swansea's long-awaited statement on Vitor Matos' exit – or should we say Victor – is about as cold as they come.

The Welsh club are unhappy over various aspects of Matos' move to France.

Without saying as much, they have made that abundantly clear.

Barely a week ago, Matos was his usual chirpy self at Swansea's Fairwood training base, as he chatted to BBC Sport Wales about Marko Stamenic's three-match suspension and which of his injured players might be fit to play against West Bromwich Albion this Saturday.

By last weekend, Strasbourg had made their move for the Swansea head coach – and suddenly Matos' plans for West Brom were forgotten.

His surprise departure all happened very swiftly and, as Swansea's statement shows, has left a sour taste for many within the club.

The wait for the Swans to say anything was not a result of bitterness towards Matos.

BBC Sport Wales understands the Championship side - unusually in this sort of situation - did not know Strasbourg's announcement was coming on Wednesday, and they were particularly surprised when it did given that they did not believe the process of finalising Matos' move had been completed.

It all amounts to a sorry end to a reign which brought plenty of progress, and had promised much more.

#2770. AMD dives on short-seller report of alleged China exposure

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."

Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."

The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

#2763. ‘It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround

'It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers created their two cleanest late-game looks several hours before they needed them.

During Wednesday morning's shootaround in Orlando, Nick Nurse had the Sixers work on offensive material they had not consistently used this season. They tested one of those actions during the first half, returned to it throughout the closing minutes and watched it produce the shots they needed to complete a 17-point comeback.

"We worked on some stuff this morning that we hadn't used before, and they ran all that stuff very, very well and very calmly and with composure," Nurse told reporters.

The Sixers have earned six of their 13 wins after trailing by double digits. They are also 11-0 in games that reached clutch time.

Relying on comebacks is not a sustainable plan. The repeated late-game situations, however, have forced a new roster to respond to different lineups, coverages and responsibilities while the season is still young.

Each close finish gives Nurse more information about which players and actions hold up when possessions tighten. Wednesday gave him a new option.

Anfernee Simons' clinching three in the Sixers' 121-116 win over the Magic was the final result of that preparation.

"That last play, we ran that play in the first half," Simons said. "We worked it a couple of times, and in the second half we ran that play every single time down the stretch, and it worked every time.

"It was a play we ran through. [It's gratifying] especially when it's working consistently and you're getting different shots out of it and the opposing team just don't know what to do.

"We just continue to run the play and get the open shots we need."

NBC Sports Philadelphia video producer and Sixers Talk podcast co-host Kevin Rice broke down how the Sixers used its different options to keep Orlando guessing.

The action begins with two players stationed near the elbows. A player on the opposite elbow then sets a screen for the player up top, who receives the ball while moving around it.

The Sixers ran the set three consecutive times during the first half. None of the possessions reached the primary option. Each still produced a quality opportunity.

On the first, Joel Embiid cleared LeBron James out of the area and directed Simons around him for a dribble handoff. Simons received an open three-point look.

Orlando took away the handoff the next time down but left Embiid one-on-one against Wendell Carter Jr. Embiid created enough room to retrieve his own miss and convert an and-one opportunity.

The third attempt pulled Orlando's defense into the paint. Two passes moved the ball through the collapsing coverage and created an open three for VJ Edgecombe.

"We had a little thing where he comes flying off behind Joel, and he doesn't get to do that that much, right?" Nurse said of Simons. "So tonight he gets the opportunity to do it, and it was very good for us on a number of plays."

The Sixers changed the action late without abandoning its initial Horns alignment. Simons moved through the lane to help form a Spain pick-and-roll involving James and Embiid.

On the first late possession, Simons remained near the play after James gained a matchup against Carter. Orlando struggled to sort out its assignments, leaving James open for a 19-foot jumper with 54.8 seconds remaining.

After Jalen Suggs made one of two free throws, the Sixers returned to the same setup. This time, Simons relocated to the left corner after James drew Carter on a switch.

James drove into the paint. Suggs lost track of Simons while responding to the penetration, and James sent the ball toward the corner.

Simons buried the open three to give the Sixers a 119-113 lead with 15 seconds left.

"Bron just penetrated the paint," Simons said. "It kind of got some confusion, and when I was on the dunker and kind of spaced out to the corner, I ended up finding myself wide open for the three, and Bron found me."

The Sixers entered the night without Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, their two leading scorers. Simons made his first start with Philadelphia and recorded 18 points in the city where he grew up.

His final basket also illustrated why Nurse believes the Sixers have more to uncover with him.

"When he's out there, they gotta be really careful," Nurse said. "So I think there's some drives he creates, and just about every time he lets it go, whether he's on balance or not, you think it's going in, and that is a big deal. Like, that is a big deal.

"And again, I think we're still a ways away from really unlocking him to being even more part of some of the things we can do with him to create more shots."

Philadelphia is now 11-0 in clutch games. The finish in Orlando provided a more specific explanation than experience or shot-making alone.

The Sixers installed a set in the morning, explored its counters and trusted it when the game tightened. James supplied the patience to read Orlando's coverage. Embiid occupied the middle of the action. Simons moved without the ball, and Edgecombe remained ready to shoot.

James said his heart rate drops when close games increase the pressure on everyone else.

"I mean, experience," James said. "A guy that's seen every situation this league has to offer. It's nothing I haven't seen. And, you know, in the moments where people's heart rate goes up or anxiety goes up, mine is pretty low. It's actually lower, you know."

The Sixers still have more actions and reads to learn as Nurse becomes familiar with his new personnel, but their latest win showed their innate ability to adapt in big moments.

"I think we're still a long ways away from knowing all the reads and all that stuff because it's just a little early, right?" Nurse said.

Brian Schottenheimer confirmed Mike Pettine will take over as the Cowboys’ defensive play-caller on Sunday. He replaces defensive coordinator Christian Parker, who will retain his title.

“Christian Parker is a huge part of what we’re trying to build here and that he is our defensive coordinator,” Schottenheimer said Wednesday, via Todd Archer of ESPN. “He is our leader. Parker, 34, arrived in January as a first-time play caller, leaving Philadelphia after two seasons as the Eagles’ defensive passing game coordinator. Pettine arrived before Week 5 as a senior defensive assistant to help Parker, whom he brought into the NFL with the Packers in 2019. He was defensive coordinator with the Jets, when Schottenheimer was on staff, and also served in that role with the Bills and Packers.

Pettine was head coach of the Browns from 2014-15.

“When I look at this situation, we’re all committed to trying to get it right,” Schottenheimer said, “and so we’re making adjustments like we’ve made. We’ve made adjustments. We’ve adjusted some scheme. We’ve adjusted some personnel. We’ve adjusted some play time. This is just another adjustment where we’re trying to get right.”

Schottenheimer made clear several times that he still believes in Parker and still believes Parker has a future with the Cowboys.

“CP has a very, very bright future as a coach, but more specifically, a very bright future here as our defense coordinator,” Schottenheimer said.

Seven things Solak thinks for NFL Week 11: Takes on four QBs, Lions, Rams, morehttps://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/50505355/week-11-seven-things-solak-thinks-burrow-mvp-rams-lions

I think … Vikings-49ers is the coolest game of the seasonThe Vikings have had a fraught three weeks. Everyone was excited to see them face the Lions in Week 8 — the best offense they'd faced in a while. Detroit stuck it to 'em with a sick schematic wrinkle for which the Vikings were not prepared — multiple tight ends lined up in the backfield as quasi-fullbacks to pave open rushing lanes.…This is quite literally the best against the best. The 49ers lead the league in points per drive (3.0), success rate and EPA per play on offense. The Vikings lead the league in points per drive (1.24), success rate and EPA per play (if you eliminate the Bucs' rainstorm game against the Falcons, which is cheating, but I don't care) on defense. It does not get better for offensive football than what the 49ers are doing right now. It does not get better for defensive football than what the Vikings are doing right now. Snap the pool stick, toss it down at midfield and let's see who survives.

Not only are these the most effective units on their respective sides of the ball — there's actually some structural similarity between the two. The Flores defense has been exhaustively covered this season, but if you've missed them to this point of the season: The Vikings are blitzing on 72.3% of opposing dropbacks through 10 weeks. I shouldn't need to tell you where that ranks among league defenses, but just in case: It's first.

To blitz that much sounds deranged (and likely is), but Flores has greatly deepened the meaning of blitz packages in the modern NFL. He doesn't blitz to get the quarterback down, but blitzes to force the ball out fast to predictable hot reads. He blitzes to keep the back and tight end in protection and limit the pass-catching options the opponent can deploy. For many defensive coordinators, the blitz is an end to itself — they want to get to third-and-long so they can blitz. For Flores, the blitz is a means to many different ends depending on the opponent and context.

Let's consider the route distributions. Opposing offenses get all five routes into the concept 31.2% of the time against the Vikings, which is the lowest number in any season as far back as I have data (2017). The aggressive blitz fronts — with five or six (or seven or eight) bodies on them — keep backs and tight ends in the formation to protect, which makes the Vikings all the more dangerous when they drop bodies into coverage and only bring four on the rush. Against the Vikings' four-man rush, opposing quarterbacks are averaging an eternity to throw the ball (3.34 seconds, highest in the NFL Next Gen Stats database) and still suffer a 44% pressure rate, which leads the league.

Flip the coin to the other side, and you'll discover that no offense gets five routes into the concept more often than the San Francisco 49ers. On 72.5% of Brock Purdy's dropbacks this season, the 49ers have five eligible in the concept — that's tied for the highest rate of any offense over the past two seasons with … the 2025 49ers.

Why so many players out in the concept? It is indicative of a change that's been underway in San Francisco's offense since the Christian McCaffrey trade in 2022.

When you employ McCaffrey, you don't keep the back in to protect. Are you out of your mind? Have you seen this guy catch passes? The only season of the past five years in which the 49ers have been below 72.5% in five-out rate was 2024, when McCaffrey was hurt for much of the year. When the Cowboys called up a Cover 0 blitz in Week 10 in a got-to-have-it spot late against the 49ers, San Francisco had no issue getting McCaffrey into the route and quickly throwing him the ball against a defensive end (Von Miller) peeling off into coverage. A 74-yard touchdown later, the game was over.

This peeling defensive end is a big part of how the Vikings like to deal with pass-catching backs, mind you. No edge rusher drops into coverage more often than Andrew Van Ginkel. But for as special of a Swiss Army knife as the Gink is … do you like him dropping with McCaffrey in space?

Much as Flores throws additional bodies at the offensive core to force players into protection, the 49ers throw as many eligible bodies as possible into the route to force defenders to win in coverage. Because the ball can go to George Kittle and McCaffrey at high volumes, it's hard to play man coverage against 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan — your linebackers and safeties will be victimized — so you have to drop into zone, which pulls players out of your blitz packages. Purdy has been blitzed on 29.1% of his dropbacks, 27th among 37 qualifying quarterbacks this season.

When I say "five receivers in the route," you might instinctively think about spreading the defense out — and you'd be right. But the 49ers, critically, do not play from spread formations. No offense has been more condensed in the entire Next Gen Stats era than the 2026 49ers, who have an average formational width of 18.9 yards — a full yard tighter than second place (the 2025 49ers at 19.9 yards).

This has been another big leap in the 49ers' offense since they acquired McCaffrey. From 2017 to 2021 — B.C, or Before Christian — the 49ers were in condensed sets on 42.3% of their offensive snaps. After the McCaffrey trade, that number leaps to 61.2% — easily the highest among offenses.

The condensed sets serve several purposes. They allow the 49ers to get extra blockers into the run concept more easily — they wouldn't have nearly as complex of a running game otherwise. They allow pre-snap motions to hit faster across the formation, which strains how well a defense communicates — linebackers have to see a lot more when all 11 players are in the offensive picture. They all but guarantee opposing cornerbacks have outside leverage on the 49ers' wide receivers (otherwise out-breaking routes would be far too easy to complete), and that outside leverage opens up runways for the deep crosses, posts and in-breakers than Shanahan tends to favor.

The McCaffrey of it all is very simple: He's the 49ers' slot receiver. He's their player to win on option routes inside the numbers, to run little safety-valve routes through the middle of the field. But because he lines up in the backfield, the 49ers don't actually need to create a slot alignment with a nice wide formation. It would be a waste of space.

Condensed sets have drawbacks, and the first is the blitz issue. When all 11 offensive players are pulled into the core of the formation, all 11 defensive players follow. For a coach like Flores, who wants to (and has shown the ability to) blitz every single player from every possible alignment, condensed sets are a dream. It's far easier to disguise a blitz when all of the bodies are close together anyway, and the path to the quarterback is inherently shorter for cornerbacks and safeties — the most surprising and often most devastating of the potential blitzers. The league is blitzing condensed sets at a 38% clip this season relative to 29.6% for all other formations. To condense against Flores feels like playing into his hand.

Because Flores blitzes so much, his defense is also the most condensed defense, just as the 49ers' offense is the most condensed offense. He wants as many players close to the ball as possible so that the blitz paths are shorter, just as Shanahan wants as many players close to the ball as possible so that the motion paths are shorter. Flores has at least five men in his defensive front on 79.2% of his snaps this year (highest in the Next Gen Stats era) and at least six men in the defensive front 35.8% of his snaps, second only to the 2025 Vikings. It doesn't matter if these bodies are defensive tackles or safeties or anything in between — Flores crowds your space.

This is why the 49ers/Vikings game is so interesting to me. Shelve the actual efficiency stats for now. No two units put as much formational strain on their opponent pre-snap as these two units. And no two units throw as many bodies at their opponents as these two units. Shanahan and Flores are dictators — not in the political despot sense, but in the playcalling sense. Elite offense against elite defense is often cast as unstoppable force against immovable object, but this matchup is more unstoppable force against unstoppable force.

This will be a true clash of football minds with six, seven layers of counterpunches and curveballs. I have absolutely no idea who will win. Play ball!

49ers might have just outsmarted the Vikings with unique travel plan for Week 11 NFC showdown in Mexico Cityhttps://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/49ers-outsmarted-vikings-unique-travel-plan-week-11-nfc-showdown-mexico-city/

The 49ers outsmarted the Rams with their travel plan in Week 1, and they might try to do the same this week against the Vikings in Mexico City. Mexico's capital creates a unique challenge for NFL teams because it sits at an elevation of about 7,350 feet. To put that in perspective, Denver has the highest altitude of any NFL city at 5,280 feet, over a quarter-mile of elevation below what the 49ers and Vikings will be dealing with in Mexico.

When you're playing at an altitude that high, it's not easy to get acclimated, so the 49ers have decided to spend their entire practice week in Colorado Springs at Air Force Academy's Falcon Stadium, which sits at 6,621 feet.

Niners coach Kyle Shanahan was raised in Denver, so he knows how difficult it can be to adjust to high altitude, which is why he decided to move the team's base to Colorado this week.

"I think it helps," Shanahan said this week, when discussing practice at a higher altitude. "I grew up mainly in Denver, and I always know how bad it would be for me. It didn't matter how good a shape you're in. Like, when I came home from college, you'd run up the stairs and be out of breath. It takes some time to get used to it. It just is what it is with altitude. I know when you go to play in Denver, it's always a challenge, and I know Mexico City's higher than Denver. It's not make-or-break by any means, but I do think it makes you a couple percent better."…On the Vikings' end, they won't be making any changes to their practice location to prepare for the high altitude in Mexico. Instead, the Vikings will spend the week at their practice facility in Eagan, Minnesota, which sits at an altitude of 945 feet.

Minnesota might not be adjusting its travel schedule, but the team did install an altitude chamber to help players acclimate.

The chamber allows the players to get a workout in at a "high" altitude, but riding a stationary bike or running on a treadmill isn't exactly the same thing as practicing actual football.

Defensive coordinator Brian Flores previously coached a game in Mexico City as a member of the Patriots' coaching staff in 2017 — a game New England won 33-8 over the Raiders — so he has some first-hand experience with what the trip will be like. During an interview on Tuesday, Flores admitted he'll probably have to change his substitution patterns since the high altitude will likely cause his players to get winded faster.

"There's less oxygen, it's a tough place to play," Flores said of Mexico City. "It's certainly taxing. As a staff, we're already talking about, 'Hey, we're going have to rotate these guys and everybody's going to have to be ready to play.' And so, yeah, it's certainly something that we're going to have to deal with."

Minnesota Vikings have made a calculated bet that could give them a significant advantage vs. San Francisco 49ershttps://atozsports.com/nfl/minnesota-vikings-news/minnesota-vikings-have-made-a-calculated-bet-that-could-give-them-a-significant-advantage-vs-san-francisco-49ers/

Jim Rutberg, a climate-specialized pro endurance coach, noted that the two best windows for athletes to travel at altitude are the day before or a week-plus in advance.

"From a practical standpoint, arriving the afternoon or evening before a competition the following day is probably the best option for time-crunched athletes. If you have the time to get out to altitude a week before your event, that would be good too. In the latter case, the time at altitude will not give you enough time to acclimate, but it does give your body time adjust respiratory habits, reduces the stress of traveling immediately before racing, and gives you time away from normal life to focus on good habits, recovery, and thoughtful eating. The worst timeframe is arriving 2-4 days before your event, because you're more likely to be feeling the impact of disturbed sleep, fatigue from travel, and dehydration in this timeframe."

Here's where the Vikings could end up getting an advantage. There are real arguments to be made about both approaches, but one team is going to sleep in their beds for the entire week, and the other will be in a hotel the entire time. That alone gives the Vikings a leg up, but paired with the element of sleeping in a hotel, the 49ers could also be dealing with altitude sickness while they are going through the acclimation process. That's not good when it comes to game preparation.

Head coach Kevin O'Connell highlighted how they went about their decision-making process to leave on Saturday.

How a rocket scientist is fueling the NFL's best defensehttps://www.nbcnews.com/sports/nfl/rocket-scientist-fueling-nfls-best-defense-rcna610015

The Minnesota Vikings' defense is the type of unit that unleashes pure terror on its opponents, a whirring buzz saw of blitzes coming from all levels of the field and entirely unpredictable.

It leads the NFL in total touchdowns allowed (just 12 scores this season), average points allowed per game (14) and total number of sacks (37) — a testament to making life quite miserable for opposing quarterbacks.…But one of the untold secrets of their success might be that acclaimed defensive coordinator Brian Flores happily accepts input from all corners, and that includes rocket scientists. In this case, it's the team's assistant defensive backs coach, Chenzo Funari, who until a few years ago was working on SpaceX's combustion devices group and the company's Starship system.…The Cleveland native — whose first love was football until he suffered several significant knee injuries as a teenager (and came to grips with his 5-foot-5 frame) — first left SpaceX for a job at TaylorMade Golf, then a couple of months later applied for a volunteer coaching position at Youngstown State University in Ohio.

It involved plenty of nights sleeping on air mattresses and a complete lack of certainty about what came next in his professional journey. But Funari said he saw one thing clearly: Working on defensive schemes was similar to working on rockets. And his background allowed him a unique perspective to deliver some valuable insight to teams.

"Something starts as an idea, a concept," he said. "Then you design it on the computer, you get it manufactured, built and then you test it. So there's a big process of the idea and the final product that you see on the rocket."

"And to me, I view it as the same [with football], what these guys are able to do and the life that they bring to our defense," he added. "Everyone calls it chaos, and schematically it's, 'How do we take those ideas and communicate them in a way that allows us to bring that to fruition?'"…As for Flores, the defensive guru known for his exotic blitzes and frenetic schemes that catch teams completely off guard, he was taken aback a couple of years ago when the fresh-faced analytics hire with a science background handed him a research packet on an opposing quarterback.

"I think some of the information can be overwhelming and hard to really drill it down," Flores said. "But when I got this information from Chenzo, it made a lot of sense. He's got a football background, as well, and he's able to tie the whole thing together."

Flores said now whenever there's a situation that involves running numbers, whether it's defensive fronts or coverages, he puts it through the "Chenzo Filter" for a discerning look.

"We're always looking for an advantage. We're always looking for an edge," Flores said. "And so, from that day on, it was like, 'Chenzo, you're in these meetings every week.'"

Harrison Smith, now in his 15th NFL season, all with the Vikings, is the team's longest-tenured player and a safety who works directly with Funari on a daily basis.

Smith said that Funari knows the game "inside and out at a high level" and that his story is one that could be instructive to others on the importance of crafting your own pathway to success.

"I think kind of the fairy-tale type of takeaway is to follow your dreams," Smith said. "But I think there's a reality within that that he also built himself for this dream. He's qualified for this dream. He has the skill set for this dream. And I imagine building rockets was another dream that he had, as well."

Now an assistant defensive backs coach, Funari (and his many supporters) says the sky is the limit for where he goes from here.

He said that could mean being elevated to a position group coach or, perhaps one day, a coordinator or even an NFL head coach.

"It's never too late to do what you think will kind of bring you joy in life," Funari said. "And always chase a passion."

Vikings defensive tackle Levi Drake Rodriguez is eager to celebrate his roots by playing in Mexicohttps://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/11/18/vikings-defensive-tackle-levi-drake-rodriguez-eager-to-celebrate-his-roots-playing-in-mexico

The third-year player has the rare opportunity to play in the country his ancestors emigrated from three generations ago. Rodriguez was born and raised in Georgetown, Texas, about 30 miles north of Austin.

"I'm excited. On Monday in the weight room, I had Latino music going crazy, blaring, you know, and some of the guys were kind of fed up with it, but I did not care," Rodriguez said during a virtual news conference with Mexican media. "So, just having that music playing, man, and getting our minds right for how rowdy it's going to be over there in Mexico City. Man, I'm excited. It's going to be a lot of fun. Can't wait."

Selected 232nd overall in the seventh round of the 2024 draft out of East Texas A&M, Rodriguez has become quite the success story for the Vikings and their scouting department and coaching staff.

The 6-foot-2, 307-pound Rodriguez played football and baseball at an NAIA school, Southwestern Assemblies of God, before transferring to East Texas A&M as the program transitioned to the FCS level.

Rodriguez worked his way into the defensive line rotation last season for the Vikings (7-2), posting 43 tackles, including eight for loss, and five quarterback hits. He became a starter this year and has been on the field for 60 percent of the snaps for a dominant group led by defensive coordinator Brian Flores.

"I don't know if anyone knows the mind of Brian Flores, if I'm being honest. It's very unique, very intricate. He's watching everything," Rodriguez said. "Just seeing how much passion he has for football — he just wants to put us in the right position to be successful."…The Vikings won't arrive in the Mexican capital until Saturday night, but Rodriguez said he plans to make the most of his short stay in his ancestral homeland.

"It means a lot just to get closer to that root that's inside me, this heritage. I think it's just going to be awesome. You know, I can't wait to eat over there, can't wait to listen to good music," he said. "Hopefully we get a mariachi band over there — just, you know, being fully engulfed in that culture for the 24 hours we do have over there."

Kirk Cousins, Vikings reunion could be just getting startedhttps://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/kirk-cousins-vikings-reunion-could-be-just-getting-started

Even though Cousins is under contract through 2028, the deal was structured to spark a release after one season, with Cousins getting a $10 million payment on the back end aimed at sticking the Falcons with $8.7 million in 2026.

A base salary in 2028 of $78.655 million becomes fully guaranteed on the fifth day of the 2027 league year, along with a $1.345 million base salary in 2027. Although that works out to $80 million over two seasons (which puts the average closer to the bottom of the veteran quarterback pay scale than the top), the current structure imposes a ridiculously high cash and cap obligation for 2028, when he will be 40.

So the deal will need to be revised. And Cousins will have leverage, if he continues to do what he did on Sunday.

That said, he possibly will realize that it's not the time to maximize his leverage. He did that in 2024, when he opted for a multi-year financial commitment that he mistakenly viewed to be a multi-year playing commitment. And then the Falcons pulled the rug out from under him by drafting Michael Penix Jr. roughly six weeks after the ink dried on the new deal.

And, frankly, the Vikings could decide to devise a plan for swallowing the proverbial poison pill and paying $40 million per year for two more season. The impact of Cousins's return on the Minnesota offense would justify trying to devise a solution.

#2752. NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman addresses playoff scheduling, venue issues

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The NWSL Championship returns to the nation's capitol for the first time since 2022, but the league looks a lot different than it did just four years ago.

The field of NWSL teams has expanded from 12 to 16 since 2022, which will increase to 18 teams by 2028. Attendance and viewership records are at an all-time high, as are team valuations after the NWSL fetched a staggering $205 million for the league's 18th team in Columbus, Ohio.

"Today, we're bigger, stronger, more visible, and more ambitious than ever before, and the next five years are going to redefine what's possible," NWSL Commissioner Jessica Berman said during her annual end-of-season address on Thursday, Nov. 19, ahead of the 2026 NWSL Championship game between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday.

But all expansion comes with growing pains, particularly in infrastructure and scheduling conflicts, a problem that's repeatedly reared its ugly head throughout the 2026 postseason.

"I don't think anyone was more frustrated or disappointed with that outcome than the NWSL," Berman said of scheduling challenges. "Obviously, we want our players and our game to be showcased on the biggest stages."

March 21: Houston Dash midfielder Kiki Van Zanten (12) controls the ball as Boston Legacy FC defender Jorelyn Carabalí (16) defends during the first half at Shell Energy Stadium. Houston won the game, 3-0.

The Spirit were expected to move their semifinal matchup against the Utah Royals from Audi Field because their home venue was already booked for a NCAA Division III college football game the same day. The Spirit ended up to playing at Audi Field after last-minute negotiations pushed back the Secretaries' Cup's start time, but there were both soccer and football lines on the field as the Spirit punched their ticket to its third consecutive title game.

Kansas City Current's semifinal win over Gotham FC was relocated from Sports Illustrated Stadium's 25,000-seat home venue to a 5,000-seat arena at Icahn Stadium due to poor field conditions attributed to an international rugby doubleheader held at Sports Illustrated Stadium weeks prior."Yeah, it's nothing you really want to see in the future," Kansas City Current midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo. "Hopefully it's a learning experience for the league and the stadiums involved because we do deserve to have these stadiums ... I think we handled the situation really well and didn't really let it take too much of our energy. We just knew we had to show up and play like any other weekend."

Berman acknowledged there's "a lot of lessons learned from this past season" that will help the league avoid similar scheduling conflicts in the future. She reiterated the NWSL's ongoing commitment to building infrastructure to ultimately dictate where teams play and ensure conditions are up to par.

There were no purpose-built facilities for women back in 2022 when Berman took over as NWSL Commissioner. The Kansas City Current changed that in 2024 with CPKC Stadium, the first stadium built exclusively for women's soccer. By 2028, 13 teams will have purpose-built training facilities.

"We have a huge advantage obviously of having our own stadium so we're always going to be priority in it, which is nice. The standard is that everyone else will get that eventually," Kansas City Current forward Michelle Cooper said.

Building facilities, however, doesn't happen overnight and solving infrastructure problems can sometimes take "up to 50 to 70 years," Berman said. But she said shared ownership is a way the league will look to influence scheduling in the interim. That was the driving force behind awarding the 17th and 18th team in the league to Atlanta and Columbus franchises, whose ownership groups also have a MLS counterpart.

"We are focused on identifying ways to either control or influence where we play," Berman said. "On the control side, of course, this is the reason that Boston and Denver were admitted into our league. They're building purpose-built stadiums, and when those open in the next couple of years, we will be in a meaningfully different place in terms of creating optionality across our league."

Atlanta City FC will play in Mercedes-Benz Stadium with Atlanta United, while Columbus NSWL team will share ScottsMiracle-Gro Field with the MLS' Columbus Crew. It will become a benchmark as the league continues to expand, Berman said.

"Having shared ownership with MLS teams that own their stadium gives us the opportunity to have more influence over our schedule," Berman said. "We've been at this before. I'm incredibly proud of the progress we've made, and it's clear we have more work to do."

#2745. Bill Belichick, Robert Kraft advance to final round of Hall of Fame voting

Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft will have another chance at election to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2027.

The Hall announced on Thursday that Belichick has been chosen as the nominee in the coach category while Kraft is the nominee in the contributor category. That was also the case last year, but neither of them were elected.

Belichick’s failure to get enough votes for election created a particular outcry given the six Super Bowl titles he won while coaching Kraft’s Patriots from 2000-2023.

The Hall of Fame overhauled selection procedures in the wake of last year’s election. The size of the selection committee was cut in half from 50 to 25 and there is no longer be a separate category for senior players.

Belichick and Kraft will join 13 player nominees for consideration by the committee. That list of candidates will be reduced to seven before a final vote with 80 percent approval needed for election.

#2742. Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return

Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia.

The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating.

Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer's blockbuster trade stole the show.

George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston's 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter.

The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward.

The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons.

Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout.

George's return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years.

Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series.

Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed.

"It was good to see Paul," Maxey said. "I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we'll see him again."

Maxey then added one important qualifier.

George instead scored from nearly everywhere.

"He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies," Maxey said. "He played within the game, too. That's what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight.

"PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn't even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that's on us."

Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways.

"He really had it going," Nurse said. "He'd post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight."

George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game.

"This building can be very electric as well," George said. "It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment."

One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player.

During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it.

"There was a fan being an a–," George said. "The ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it, instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do.

"And so, yeah, then I rolled him a middle finger in return."
