#2733. How LeBron James dissected Pacers defense down the stretch

How LeBron James dissected Pacers defense down the stretch originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

As he overtook Jason Kidd for the third-most assists in NBA history, LeBron James piloted the Sixers' offense down the stretch against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday.

With Joel Embiid sitting out and Tyrese Maxey getting a breather on the bench, James took over in the fourth quarter. He did so by spamming the same action over and over again.

The set consisted of James getting a ball screen from a guard – either VJ Edgecombe or Anfernee Simons – at the top of the key. After setting or ghosting the screen, the guard would short roll towards the basket.

When the Pacers blitzed or hedged the screen, James found the guard. The Sixers could then attack a 4-on-3 or 3-on-2 situation.

Twice, Edgecombe and Simons scored off the roll.

When the Pacers helped to the roller, that opened up the shooters in each corner.

James directed traffic on offense to ensure that the Sixers spaced the floor properly. Here, he waved Dean Wade out of the dunker spot and into the corner. Edgecombe promptly hit him for an open three off the short roll.

After all of the Sixers' success, the Pacers eventually switched the ball screen. That left the 6-foot-4, 173-pound Quenton Jackson on James, who has five inches and 77 pounds on him.

Jackson and James had already gone head to head on Sunday.

In the first quarter, James set a ball screen for Edgecombe which the Pacers switched. Edgecombe fed James in the post and the Pacers doubled him to support Jackson. James punished them for it.

They didn't double James after the switch in the fourth quarter. This time, James backed Jackson down, backed him down again and backed him down some more before scoring inside.

James' strength abusing matchups against smaller defenders after switches has been a safety valve for the Sixers' offense. Guards struggle to stop him from getting to the basket. When defenses send help, he picks them apart with his otherworldly passing ability.

That combination forced the Pacers to pick their poison. From the 9:55 mark in the fourth until the Pacers switched to a zone defense (after James bullied Jackson) with just over 6:00 left, the Sixers scored 13 points out of this action across seven possessions. That's a stellar 1.86 points per possession.

James, who's scoring a career-low 15.1 points per game so far this season, might not be the elite bucket-getter he was for most of his career. But he's still brilliant at conducting highly efficient offense that pressures a defense's pain points.

#2728. Cowboys DC Christian Parker calls losing play-calling duties 'not an ideal situation,' says he'll 'cross that bridge' on future with team

A day after Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker was stripped of defensive play-calling duties, the young coordinator spoke to reporters about what he called a "significant" personal disappointment. In a press conference on Thursday, Parker said he initially pushed back on losing the responsibility but accepted that the decision had been made.

"Not an ideal situation for me personally, but it's what's best for the team," Parker said, via multiple reporters.

Parker told reporters that the new arrangement with senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine, who will now take on the play-calling, is "only awkward if you make it that way." The young defensive coordinator added that he considered not staying with Dallas, but decided to stay on.

"In my opinion, that would have been running from it," Parker said of leaving.

However, when asked about his future with the Cowboys, Parker left more up in the air: "We'll cross that bridge when we come to it," he said.

Parker, who is in his first year as the Cowboys' DC and his first year as an NFL play-caller in general, saw his short tenure calling the shots come to an end on Wednesday after the team's early struggles. Play-calling duties for the Dallas defense has gone to Pettine, who was brought on as a senior defensive assistant last month to give the 34-year-old Parker some support.

The move came after the latest dismal showing from the Cowboys' defense, a 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers where Dallas allowed 584 offensive yards — the most the team has given up at home in the franchise's long and storied history.

Postgame, Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer ripped the defense's effort as "atrocious", the latest sign of Schottenheimer's frustration with his young DC. Owner Jerry Jones said Tuesday that he was discussing Parker's role after the performance, before the team ultimately settled on keeping him in the position but reducing his duties.

Part of the problem is that Sunday's loss was just the latest winnable game ruined by poor defense. The Cowboys started the season by failing to get a fourth-quarter stop in a loss to the New York Giants, which Parker admitted was "unacceptable." Dallas then allowed the Baltimore Ravens to get a seven-second game-winning drive in Week 3, before a defensive collapse in Week 8 led the Arizona Cardinals to score four touchdowns in a row to eventually win in overtime. In Week 9, the Cowboys blew another big lead against the Indianapolis Colts and only narrowly avoided disaster.

Schottenheimer and Jones will now hope that Pettine's guidance can salvage the season, with Dallas currently holding a 4-6 record.

#2727. Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory

Observations after Sixers come back for strong shorthanded victory originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stretched their winning streak to four games and snagged a strong road win Wednesday night over the Magic.

They earned a 121-116 victory in Orlando to improve to 13-3 on the season. The Magic dropped to 6-8.

Joel Embiid had 26 points, seven assists, six rebounds, three blocks and two steals.

VJ Edgecombe posted a season-high 24 points, eight boards and six assists.

LeBron James scored 22 points and Anfernee Simons added 18.

Magic star Franz Wagner had 27 points, 11 assists and eight rebounds.

The Sixers had a long injury list in Orlando. Tyrese Maxey (right foot soreness), Jaylen Brown (left hamstring strain) and Dean Wade (left hamstring soreness/tightness) were among their players out. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters in Orlando that Brown will be re-evaluated when the team returns to Philadelphia.

Orlando was without star forward Paolo Banchero (right high ankle sprain).

The Sixers will start a three-game homestand when they face the Bucks on Saturday afternoon. Here are observations on their win over the Magic:

The Sixers' undermanned starting lineup was Edgecombe, Simons, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, James and Embiid.

After scoring 37 points in the Sixers' win over the Nets, Embiid had a subpar start. He began 1 for 6 from the floor and committed a turnover that led to an Anthony Black dunk.

The Sixers' lineup looked exactly like a unit that hadn't built any chemistry yet. The team was not sharp early on either end of the floor.

Desmond Bane drained a long three-pointer to give Orlando a 27-12 advantage. Orlando made 11 of its first 14 field goals and led by as many as 17 points in the first quarter.

Labaron Philon Jr. and Justin Edwards joined the Sixers' rotation. So did two-way contract players Tacko Fall and Caleb Love.

Philon impressed in the first quarter, converting two floaters and a corner three. The rookie passed his previous NBA scoring high of five points and finished the night with 10 on 4-for-5 shooting.

Fall played 10 minutes and posted two points, three rebounds and three blocks. He slammed in a dunk and rejected two shots early in the second quarter. Credit to Fall for giving the Sixers a good backup center performance and doing his job as a rim-protecting ultra-big man.

The Sixers' zone defense also helped them eat into the Magic's lead. The zone seemed to disrupt Orlando's offensive rhythm and it was active enough to prevent the Magic from consistently creating high-quality looks.

Edgecombe's buzzer-beating mid-range jumper cut the Sixers' deficit to 69-64 after two quarters.

The Sixers pulled within a single point on multiple occasions in the third quarter, including on a Philon three late in the period. They trailed by five points after the third.

Fall continued to play well early in the fourth quarter. He deterred the Magic's drivers from getting all the way to the rim as the very large back line of the Sixers' zone defense and made eye-catching hustle plays on both sides of the ball.

The Sixers outscored Orlando by seven points on the night with Fall on the court. Soon after Embiid subbed back in, he evened the game at 104-all with two free throws. Jabari Walker swished a three to finally push the Sixers in front.

The Magic regained a late lead with a Jalen Suggs three. James then drove and kicked the ball out to Edgecombe, who nailed one of his customary clutch jumpers to put the Sixers back on top.

No matter the night-to-night personnel, the Sixers have been fantastic at the tail end of close games. They're now 11-0 in clutch situations, which the NBA defines as games within a five-point differential in the final five minutes.

The Milwaukee Bucks are fresh off the front end of a back-to-back as they host the Portland Trail Blazers—who have been waiting in Milwaukee—tonight. In a word, the Bucks are struggling, currently on an 11-game losing streak. Of their last ten losses, only three games saw Milwaukee lose by single digits. They lack consistent center play, are one of the league's worst defensive teams, and lack a viable, consistent first option on offense. Those issues showed up in a particularly grim loss to Miami last night, where Miami led by as much as 30 before the Bucks' garbage-time comeback. In any event, Milwaukee gets another chance to right its wrongs tonight against a Blazers team that has just lost two straight.

They've also been elite on defense, partly because of their premier shot-blocker Donovan Clingan and defensive Swiss Army knife Toumani Camara, but also because of their emphasis on defending the perimeter and cleaning the glass. Portland has held opposing teams to just 33.1% shooting from the field, good for fourth in the league. Portland could really give Milwaukee, which has relied on spurts of momentum rather than consistent production, a real headache if they don't start hot.

In the latter game, LaMelo Ball stole Clingan's inbound pass and finished it with a fast-break layup to take a one-point lead with less than three seconds left. Portland has slowed down due to injuries—missing star guards Ja Morant and Shaedon Sharpe—and their hot-shooting start has slowed. Deni Avdija: Questionable (foot inflammation)

If Camara starts out shooting well, Milwaukee could have a much harder time stopping Portland's dynamic offense.

Who: Milwaukee Bucks (1-14) vs. Portland Trail Blazers (9-5).

Kasparas Jakucionis' hot streak stops, and he's stifled against the Trail Blazers' backcourt. Portland's defense is especially tough. The Bucks' backcourt will have to deal with All-Defensive Second Team member Toumani Camara, defense-first wing Sidy Cissoko, and prolific shot-blocker Donovan "Cling Kong" Clingan. Jakucionis has been playing very well, but I expect him to take a step back against Portland's elite defense.

#2716. Christian Parker considered not staying with the Cowboys

The Cowboys have removed play-calling duties from defensive coordinator Christian Parker. Parker initially considered leaving the team. He decided not to.

Parker told reporters on Thursday that he decided to process the “significant” disappointment by remaining in his job, albeit with the most important role taken away.

“That would have been running from it,” Parker said as to the possibility of resigning.

As to whether it will be awkward moving forward, Parker said, “I think it’s only awkward if you make it, and we don’t have to make it that way.”

But it will be awkward. The defensive coordinator isn’t fully coordinating the defense. And it’s not like the situation in Denver, where the head coach assumed the play-calling duties from the coordinator. Parker’s biggest responsibilities were given to someone other than the head coach — a consultant who arrived just last month.

The cleanest approach for the Cowboys, given the team’s obvious lack of confidence in Parker, would have been to fire him. But that would have come with a buyout of the balance of his contract. And owner/G.M. Jerry Jones doesn’t like paying coaches to not work.

Jones likely hopes Parker will eventually realize that the situation isn’t sustainable and (as the lingo goes) “self-select.” That avoids the buyout and conclusively ends the inherently awkward situation.

#2713. Lions quietly had $60 million clause put in Aidan Hutchinson’s contract before devastating injury

The Lions made sure they didn't leave themselves exposed when they signed Aidan Hutchinson to a $180 million extension last year.

In the aftermath of Hutchinson's season ending after he tore his ACL celebrating a sack Sunday, the Lions are set to receive salary cap relief due to injury insurance.

The four-year pact includes a clause protecting against injuries in the 2026-28 seasons up to $60 million, according to the Detroit Free Press.

Aidan Hutchinson of the Detroit Lions falls with an injury while celebrating a sack in Munich, Germany, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

The Lions reportedly were allowed to insure up to $45 million for injuries suffered between May 31, 2026 and May 31, 2027, including $12 million of his $15 million signing bonus, his $28.41 million option bonus that registered earlier this year and his $1.2 million base salary for this season.

That insurance can ultimately help the Lions since teams can receive future cap credits for insurance payments that cover injured players' contracts, per the Free Press.

The outlet projects the credit for the remainder of the 2026 season would be more than $5 million.

The Lions (7-2) have $32.9 million available in cap space for this season and are projected for $36.6 million in cap space in 2027 before any credits could be applied, per overthecap.com.

Teams insuring mega contracts like Hutchinson's is a common practice across sports leagues but it's not a given.

Aidan Hutchinson of the Detroit Lions falls with an injury in Munich, Germany, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, during an NFL game against the New England Patriots. Getty Images

The Lions, for example, reportedly did not insure quarterback Jared Goff's or linebacker Jack Campbell's extension in recent years, according to the Free Press.

"It's becoming more and more expensive, I think, because the insurance companies have had to pay out on a few of these things," ex-Lions president Rod Wood said last year, per the outlet. "So it gets into a financial decision about how much. It's like any other insurance, you don't ever want to have to collect on it, but the premiums are real expensive while you're waiting to collect on it."

Hutchinson is a sensational talent but has struggled to stay on the field over the last three seasons.

His 2024 season ended after five games due to a fractured left tibia and fibula, and he appeared in all nine games this season before being shut down.

Hutchinson had six sacks for the NFC North leaders, and they face the Buccaneers on Sunday.

#2712. Swanson: One frigid night against the Jazz doesn't change the fact the Lakers are legit

I don't know who needs to read this, but it's probably all of Lakers Nation.

Shots not falling doesn't mean the sky is.

So the Lakers couldn't quite match the UCLA football team's 10-game winning streak, but that doesn't make them any less of a pleasant surprise — or extinguish hope for a magical season of their own.

Playing three shorthanded games in four nights is a defense for poor offense in Wednesday's 109-97 loss to the Utah Jazz, in which the Lakers' nine-game winning streak petered out after they shot an uncharacteristic 38.2% (34 of 89) from the field and 27.3% (nine for 33) from three-point range.

Read more: Tired-looking Lakers can't make their shots in loss to Jazz

"You're only as good as your last game," posited center Walker Kessler, who was good for only 10 points Wednesday.

But you're also only human. And nobody's perfect, no — but the Lakers are 13-3 and tied for the NBA's best record out of the gate with the Philadelphia 76ers.

They lost for the first time in November, and they weren't happy about it because they are one of the NBA's best teams and they expect more and better from themselves: "I asked the guys who in here feels like they played well tonight," coach JJ Redick said, recounting his postgame locker room address. "Nobody raised their hand."

They should expect a lot. Because the Lakers are legit.

Only a few saw the vision this summer when the Lakers splurged on Kessler. The dynamic and exceedingly polite 7-foot-2 Georgian was the centerpiece of a newly assembled roster of younger shooters, happy-in-their-roles players who fit around Luka Doncic like round pegs in a round cylinder.

Short a suitable backup big, the Lakers otherwise loaded up with a big bucket of wings and you didn't see it before, but Wednesday aside, you've liked what you're seen since.

And you can't help but have noticed that the NBA's landscape has shifted, as it tends to.

There's a world where the Lakers could reach the NBA Finals without having to get past both the San Antonio Spurs and the Oklahoma City Thunder, who've been beset by injuries.

Redick started the season talking about wanting the Lakers to be a "championship-level team."

"I don't like the word 'contender,'" Redick said at practice on Oct. 10. "But being a team that can make a run and can play in the playoffs and can play different ways in the playoffs, those things take time and it doesn't mean you're going to be in the NBA Finals. It's just not the way this works, particularly with the way the playoffs work in terms of just matchups and what you can exploit and what you can't exploit versus certain teams. But I think because of our talent, because of our fit, because of our depth, I really like our team."

Doncic with a fitted roster is dangerous.

He's not 7-foot-4 like Spurs star Victor Wembanyama, not touted as an out-of-this-world talent — but many nights, Doncic is the best player on this planet, a magician who is plenty dangerous when armed with a competent roster.

See pages 20-24 of Doncic's playbook of spells, it'll recount how he and fellow guard Kyrie Irving led his Dallas Mavericks team of perimeter defenders and rim-protecting lob threats — Derrick Jones Jr. and P.J. Washington, Daniel Gafford and Dereck Lively II — to the franchise's first NBA Finals since 2011.

That team didn't have to go through Wembanyama's Spurs, you say?

I say San Antonio — 12-3 and due to meet the Lakers for the first time on Nov. 27 — is beatable.

You know how we know? We just watched the New York Knicks do it.

With a well-tuned roster playing complementary basketball, the power of friendship and a former Mavericks point guard — a concoction much like the Lakers' current mix — the Knicks beat the Spurs in last season's NBA Finals 4-1.

These Lakers are a work in progress and a reservoir of potential.

They're proving among the league's best offensive teams and also its most chaotic defensively. After Wednesday, they led the league in steals (10.8), were third in blocks (5.8) and forced turnovers (18.8) — creating additional possessions for their genius, generational playmaker.

Little wonder the Lakers are averaging 120.9 points per game, second-most in the NBA.

Or that even after Wednesday's relatively ho-hum 29-point outing — after which Doncic was critical of himself: "I just got to do way better than this. This is unacceptable from my part" — he still is averaging an astounding 38.1 points per game. That's seven points more than anyone else in the league. He's also connecting for 7.6 assists per game, eighth-best in the NBA.

And they're all so serious about getting better, about getting it right.

Read more: How three emergency centers helped Lakers survive the Hornets without Walker Kessler

"We're winning games, but so much of it is really about 'What's working? What's not working?'" said newcomer Matisse Thybulle recently. "It's the same conversation you have when losing, but there's just a little bit more uneasiness about it (when you're losing). It's a nicer problem to be solving while winning, but it's still the same thing. Wins right now are great, but wins in the postseason are better."

So relax. Cue up your favorite video game and let Wednesday's loss go. The Lakers aren't going to win 81% of their games this season. But they have the potential to win the big ones when it counts most.

"Frankly, you play 82 games. You're going to have some poor shooting nights," Redick said. "And you can't sit up here and be like, 'Oh, we're going to be about the process,' and then not be about the process when we lose. We'll take a look at everything …"

What's working? That's what's working. The Lakers' own clear-eyed view of their intended destination.

For over 30 years, the couple remained married while raising three daughters together.

Tiger Woods, a 15-time major champion who shared a close bond with the broadcaster, offered a tribute that speaks to Hicks' character. Woods praised his warmth, professionalism, and friendship in a public message. "Dan Hicks was beloved by all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him. His kindness, warmth, and presence will be deeply missed," Woods wrote.

Hicks was behind the microphone for some of the most defining shots in history, including Woods' miraculous birdie putt at the 2008 US Open. He famously shouted, "Expect anything different?!" as the ball dropped to force a playoff. His career spanned decades, starting with NBC Sports in 1992 before he took over as lead golf commentator in 2000. He also called the Olympics and Notre Dame football, showing a rare versatility that few broadcasters ever match.

The reaction from his peers shows just how much he meant to those inside the booth. PGA Tour stars Billy Horschel, Max Homa, and Jordan Spieth all paid tribute to the man who covered their games. Horschel remembered receiving a supportive personal note from Hicks during the time his wife fought alcohol addiction.

NBC's Cara Banks posted a message on X that captured the feeling of a team losing its leader. "Hard to imagine working without you, but somehow we will, and hope to do you proud. Goodbye Dan," Banks wrote. She said she was shocked, as were everyone who worked alongside him. Hicks leaves a legacy.

Hannah Storm, Dan's entire family, and their three daughters receive sincere condolences from everyone at GolfMagic.

#2710. After record-breaking contract, Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey is having his worst season

In April, the Cowboys signed kicker Brandon Aubrey to a four-year, $28 million contract, making him the highest-paid kicker in NFL history. That decision has not aged well.

Aubrey, who missed an extra point in Sunday’s loss to the 49ers, is having the worst season of his NFL career this year.

Aubrey has made just 79.2 percent of his field goals this season, the worst mark of his career. And he’s made just 92.6 percent of his extra points this season, also the worst mark of his career.

Those numbers aren’t just bad for the highest-paid kicker in the league, they’re bad for an average kicker. The league average field goal success rate this season is 84.5 percent, and the league average extra point success rate this season is 95.2 percent. Aubrey ranks 21st in the NFL in field goal percentage and 24th in extra point percentage.

Aubrey does still have a strong leg, as evidenced by the 60-yarder he hit against the Ravens. But in today’s NFL, plenty of kickers have strong legs, and many of them are kicking long field goals more accurately than Aubrey is: On field goals from 50 yards and longer, Aubrey is 5-for-10 this year. There’s nothing special about making 50 percent of your kicks from 50 yards out; there are 25 kickers in the NFL who have made more than 50 percent of their field goal attempts from beyond 50 yards this season.

Ups and downs for kickers aren’t unusual, but this is by far the lowest “down” of Aubrey’s career. And it’s happening after the Cowboys made him the highest-paid kicker in NFL history.

COWBOYS: Dallas strips defensive coordinator of play-calling duties

"Not an ideal situation for me personally, but it's what's best for the team moving forward, so that's how we're moving forward," Parker said.

Though Parker will no longer call the plays for the defense, he remains the Cowboys' defensive coordinator. Schottenheimer said in his press conference on Nov. 18 that the DC will continue to lead meetings and walkthroughs for the unit.

"I want to be very, very clear that Christian Parker is a huge part of the solution," Schottenheimer said.

Parker, who is in his first season with the Cowboys this year, took over a Dallas defense after an abysmal 2025 that was among the worst in franchise history. Through 10 games, he was unable to right the ship as the unit's play-caller.

Dallas has allowed 28.2 points per outing, which is third most in the NFL, and 393.8 yards per game, which is the most in the NFL. Only the 2-7 Philadelphia Eagles and 3-7 Indianapolis Colts have fewer takeaways than the Cowboys' eight so far this year.

The former Eagles passing game coordinator and defensive backs coach said his future in Dallas past 2026 is uncertain after the change to his duties.

"We'll cross that bridge when we get there," Parker said.

Parker was more verbose during his Nov. 19 media availability than Cowboys defensive tackle Quinnen Williams was one day prior.

The four-time Pro Bowler delivered the same six-word response to 12 different questions reporters asked him on Wednesday, Nov. 18: "I'm gonna keep that to myself."

Williams' method of repeating the same response is not a new tactic at NFL press conferences.

His six-word refrain was reminiscent of the four-word response (and its variations) former Patriots head coach Bill Belichick used five times in a row during a 2014 press conference: "We're on to Cincinnati." It was also similar to the seven-word repeated response from former NFL running back Marshawn Lynch later that same season: "I'm here so I won't get fined."

Williams first joined the Cowboys in 2025 as part of a trade deadline deal with the New York Jets that included a 2027 first-round pick as part of the Jets' return. Dallas signed the defensive tackle to a three-year, $105.9 million extension before this year, his first full season with the team.

Through 10 games playing in Parker's defense, Williams leads the NFL with 15 tackles for a loss. He also has three forced fumbles, one pass defense and is halfway to matching a career high with six sacks so far.

The Cowboys are 4-6 and second place in the NFC East. They're coming off of a Week 10 loss to the 49ers in which they allowed 46 points and 584 yards of total offense. Dallas will host the Tennessee Titans for Week 11 on Sunday, Nov. 22.

#2707. Celtics star Jayson Tatum accepts fault for derailment vs. Nuggets: ‘That’s on me’

Jayson Tatum let the Boston Celtics down Wednesday night, as they suffered their first set of consecutive losses this season.

After outperforming three-time league MVP Nikola Jokić with a 20-point first half, Tatum went ghost. He played all 12 minutes of the third quarter but attempted just one shot and committed four turnovers. Denver mounted a 14-point comeback, capitalizing on Tatum's second-half disappearance.

In the fourth quarter, Tatum's ice-cold trend continued. He shot 1-for-5, missing his last three shots before delivering Boston one final costly blow by receiving a technical foul as the Celtics trailed, 103-101, over an incident with referee John Goble in the final 6.4 seconds of the game.

"I should've just probably gave the ball to the ref closest to me," Tatum admitted to reporters after Boston's 105-101 loss, per CLNS Media. "I thought that John was looking at our bench. I should've just found the ref closest to me and just gave them the ball. So that's on me."

Denver's Jamal Murray shot and made the technical free throw, sending Boston packing.

DENVER, CO – NOVEMBER 18: Celtics fan looks on during the game between the Boston Celtics and the Denver Nuggets on November 18, 2026 at Ball Arena in Denver, Colorado. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Garrett Ellwood/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Tatum's incident with Gobble unfolded after Murray's go-ahead jumper put the Nuggets ahead three points. The Celtics called a timeout, and as Tatum retreated to the sideline, he tossed the ball toward Gobble, standing near midcourt. Referee Eric Dalen subsequently blew his whistle in response and assessed Tatum the game-sealing technical foul.

Understanding the gravity of the mistake, along with Tatum's remorse in hindsight, he also expressed some confusion, sharing his follow-up encounter with Dalen.

"I told Eric, I was like, I wasn't mad," Tatum said. "It wasn't a foul on me. We just called a timeout. John Goble called timeout and pointed at our bench. I thought he was looking this way, but they called a tech. So for me, just find the female ref that was there or the other ref, whoever was probably closest, and I should've just gave them the ball."

Tatum's technical foul was untimely, but it would've been salvageable had he not blown a flat tire coming out of the players' tunnel after halftime. As the undisputed superstar in the driver's seat this season, Tatum needs to give the Celtics much more. He painted half a masterpiece before completely defacing the canvas, piling up miscues and reverting to his passive self at moments that demanded a Tatum takeover instead.

Tied at 95-95, Tatum nearly traveled while trying to escape Jokić and Christian Braun. He handed the ball to Neemias Queta before demanding it back with Braun defending him in the post. But rather than exploit the mismatch he had drawn for a much-needed go-ahead bucket, Tatum allowed Braun to poke the ball away, resulting in a costly turnover.

The perfect storm led Tatum and the Celtics right to Gobble and Dalen.

That marked Tatum's third technical foul this season.

"I'll go back and watch it," Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla told reporters. "But we just can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret a certain type of way. So we just gotta be better there."

His fourth-quarter run-in with the officials wasn't the only thing Tatum took responsibility for. He recognized the negative impact his underperformance had on his teammates, with every decision carrying added weight as Boston's No. 1 option. The Celtics waited and waited, but Tatum never returned to his earlier self that saw him shoot 8-for-16 with six rebounds in less than 19 minutes during the first half.

That's the Tatum the Celtics need for four quarters.

"The four turnovers or something I had in the third quarter really just put us out of sync," Tatum said. "And in those situations, I gotta communicate better, I gotta execute better, I gotta take care of the ball, and I think that really put us in a hole, and it was kind of the turning point of the game — the second half."

#2705. Dodgers Reportedly Sign Former Top 100 Prospect With Elite Changeup

The Los Angeles Dodgers have reportedly signed right-handed pitcher Tink Hence to a minor league deal, per MiLB Central's Chase Ford.

Hence was MLB Pipeline's No. 77 prospect in 2025 and ranked as high as No. 64 on the Top 100 list. He was drafted by the St. Louis Cardinals in the second round of the 2020 MLB Draft and spent six seasons in the organization. He was outrighted in August and elected free agency.

Hence has a 3.50 ERA across five minor league levels. He finally reached Triple-A last season, but struggled. He had a 6.64 ERA in 19 games. He has worked mostly as a starter in his career, but worked out of the bullpen more last season.

He is far from a finished product, but this is a low-risk, high-reward move for the Dodgers. He is a former Top 100 prospect and could thrive with help from the coaching staff within the Dodgers organization.

#2704. Raiders’ plan for Fernando Mendoza starts with four yards on first down

Fernando Mendoza took responsibility for all six sacks the Seahawks hung on him Sunday. Klint Kubiak might want to get a word in before the rookie quarterback owns up to the Raiders' run game, too.

There's a reason the Raiders coach included himself among the people who need to do a better job helping Mendoza. By the time the rookie quarterback is trying to escape a free rusher on third-and-9, Kubiak has already had two chances to make his life easier.

That became priority number one as Kubiak and the Raiders began preparing Mendoza for his second career start on Sunday against the Broncos.

Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak speaks during a press conference after an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks in Las Vegas, Nov. 15, 2026. AP Photo/David Becker

"Just coach and player working together. Just getting him into the right calls," Kubiak said. "He did a great job, and it's always on myself to help the whole operation be better."

Start with what four yards on first down would do for everybody in Denver. Against Seattle, Ashton Jeanty carried eight times for 15 yards in the first half. Mendoza completed 11 of 13 passes before halftime, and even at that clip, it was an awfully hard way to move the ball.

Give Kubiak second-and-6 and he can hand it to Jeanty again. He can also show that same handoff, pull a linebacker toward the line and give Mendoza a throwing lane behind him.

Give Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph second-and-10 often enough, and he can afford to let somebody else worry about Jeanty while his best pass rushers get after the quarterback.

Why leave Mendoza in the same spot for those players to find him? Some of his best throws Sunday came when Kubiak rolled him out, something the Raiders got away from in the second half. And with Mendoza's live arm and Tre Tucker's speed, there's reason to dial up a deep ball. Get a safety to give Tucker another five yards of cushion and see what that does for Jeanty underneath.

The uncertainty about Brock Bowers' ankle complicates things. Take him off the field, and Kubiak loses a pretty good target on those rollouts. He can still move Mendoza around, take his chances downfield, and make Denver honor the run.

It takes more than calling a run to get those four yards. If a defensive tackle drives a guard into the backfield, Jeanty has to make his first cut before he reaches the line. Give him room to press the hole and make the linebacker commit, and now he has a say in where the play goes.

Seattle Seahawks safety Julian Love (20) and defensive tackle Rylie Mills (98) tackle Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty (2) on Nov. 15, 2026. AP Photo/John Locher

The communication inside matters just as much on passing downs. Say Denver walks two linebackers up over the center. Mendoza and his linemen have to agree on which one the protection accounts for. Kubiak can help by giving him a receiver breaking quickly into the space the other linebacker leaves if he comes. Then it's on Mendoza to deliver the ball.

"All of those sacks were on me," Mendoza said. "I believe the offensive line played great, and I'm excited to get back out there this next Sunday."

An admirable sentiment. The tackles can still do him a favor by running the edge rushers past him, and the guards by leaving him somewhere to step up.

Mendoza's first film session as the starter gave him and his coaches a chance to sort through all of it. Kirk Cousins could bring 14 seasons of Sundays to those conversations. With Mendoza, even the way he relays the call in the huddle merits a second listen.

"Detailed, detail-oriented. Asks questions. He's a professional," Kubiak said of Mendoza. Becoming the starter means "definitely more things, more questions, more conversations that are geared to him."

"I would say it was a little bit more leaving no stone unturned, making sure we cover all the coaching points, as there can be no assumptions made because this is my first time doing this," Mendoza said.

Fernando Mendoza (15) of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before a game against the Seattle Seahawks at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

And then making sure mistakes get corrected.

"I'm looking forward to getting those right," Mendoza said of the adjustments.

The complication is that Joseph gets to watch the Seattle tape, too. A pressure Mendoza spent Wednesday learning to recognize might look familiar Sunday, right up until the linebacker he expects to rush drops underneath his throw. Kubiak can give him that look in practice and make him find his second receiver.

Come Sunday, that picture might look entirely different.

"So, the learning just gets accelerated when you're doing it," Kubiak said.

Mendoza is not running from that challenge.

"I believe getting thrown in the fire is the best way to learn, and the Seahawks and the Broncos both have considerably elite defenses," Mendoza said.

There's a good way to tell Sunday whether the work paid off.

"Well, the proof always comes in the production on the field, so we get another week to go produce," Kubiak said.

Watch the scoreboard for the down and distance when Mendoza breaks the huddle. If it says third-and-3, that rookie suddenly has an awful lot of the playbook at his disposal. So does the guy talking into his helmet.

#2703. Fantasy Basketball Rookie Report: Tiered rankings for top 1st-year players one month into the 2026-27 NBA season

Rookies are usually a patience game, but this class is producing in November. To compare their value across formats, I averaged each rookie's Yahoo Fantasy 9-cat and standard points ranks into a composite. Both rankings are league-wide, not rookie-only, so a rank of 66 means 66th in fantasy value — not 66th among rookies.

The two formats reward different strengths: efficiency and balanced contributions matter more in 9-cat, while volume drives points-league value. The composite offers a snapshot across both, while the gap between ranks shows which format suits each player best. I also included true shooting percentage, which accounts for 3s and free throws to give a fuller picture of scoring efficiency than field goal percentage alone.

Here's the first rookie report of the 2026-27 season.

Boozer is the best rookie in the class by composite (40.5) and in 9-cat (47th), and his 34th ranking in points is only behind Darius Acuff Jr. among rookies. He's at 9.4 boards and 5.3 assists with 16.6 points in 31.1 minutes, and that kind of big-man passing is rare, especially for a first-year player. The 40% shooting is the one number holding him back, but 88.9% from the line and 1.9 3s a game lift his true shooting to 53.5%. His 14.1% rebound rate is the highest of any rookie on this list.

I touted Bulls F Caleb Wilson as the player with the highest ceiling, but Boozer looks like he could be right there as a consistent double-double threat with the added bonus of high-end playmaking for fantasy managers. A cool record that he's pacing toward: he'd be the first rookie forward to average 15-10-5, and only the second rookie to do it since the "Big O" Oscar Robertson in 1960-61.

Lendeborg is right behind Boozer, ranking 42nd in points and 87th in 9-cat for a 64.5 composite as one of the most complete rookies in the class. He's at 20.8 points on 46.4% shooting with 7.3 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 1.1 steals, and his 26.4% usage rate shows Golden State is running things through him. His 58.1% true shooting is the best of the five rookies who use at least 24% of their team's possessions. He gets to the line nearly six times a game, so there's a floor even when the shot isn't falling. With Stephen Curry out, expect Yaxel to build on his early-season success as the primary engine of Golden State's offense.

Everyone in this tier is shooting under 42%, but their true shooting sits around 53%, so the damage is smaller than it looks. The question is what each one gives you while the shot comes around. For Acuff, it's points, assists and 3s: 26.0 points, 7.0 assists and 3.3 3s in 36.7 minutes, with a 32.5% usage rate that is like a veteran's workload. Despite his ball-hog persona, he's assisted on 34.2% of his teammates' baskets while on the floor — the highest rate of any rookie and 15th in the NBA. The price is 41% shooting on 22.6 attempts (52.9% true shooting) with 3.9 turnovers and limited stocks. Even with that, he's 88th in 9-cat, which is a strong result for a rookie shooting this poorly and shows how much his counting stats carry him. In points leagues, he's 24th, so he's a top-30 player there and a clear starter across formats.

Wilson is out 4-6 weeks with a right metacarpal fracture, but his 10 games before the injury were strong: 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds, 1.8 steals, 0.9 blocks and 2.3 3s in 30.8 minutes. That scoring-stocks-and-boards profile is the hardest to find amongst this specific rookie class. If Norman Powell gets traded (his contract is movable), Wilson would become Chicago's primary scorer. Combine that with his versatility and he'd be a player well worth trading for and stashing on IL.

Peterson's route to fantasy prominence is through scoring, assists and 3s. It's happening sooner than expected, as his opportunity share is expanding with injuries to Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. It's left him as Utah's second scoring option, with a chance to be the primary one until they return. He's at 16.5 points, 2.2 3s, and 1.1 steals in 30.6 minutes and he shoots 84.0% from the line. He also protects the ball better than the other high-usage rookies in the top two tiers, with a turnover rate of 10.4 per 100 possessions, compared to 13.0 to 16.9 for the rest. Peterson's sporting a 29.2% usage rate with Markkanen off the floor (19.9% with him), so a natural jump in production will push Peterson into a top-100 asset in 9-cat and top-75 in points pretty quickly.

Thomas is the most efficient scorer in this tier, with 13.4 points, 2.6 3s and 1.2 steals in 23.9 minutes on 47.5% shooting. The second-rounder has been one of the Cavs' best weapons off the bench, connecting on 44% of his 3s, while 54% of his shots come from beyond the arc. He's seeing a healthy 21% usage rate but only turns it over 1.2 times a game. There aren't many ways for him to hurt you, which explains why he's the highest-ranked rookie in this tier in 9-cat. He's a good add in 12-team leagues.

Aday Mara is picking up steam, averaging 12.5 points, 7.7 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 1.5 blocks in 26.5 minutes over his last six games while shooting 68% from the field. He's scored in double figures in all six contests, raising his season averages to 9.2 points, 6.5 boards and 1.7 blocks. The recent production makes him worth a look for fantasy managers seeking rebounds, blocks and a field-goal percentage boost, though his 57.7% shooting from the line remains a drawback. At 50% rostered, shallow league managers should consider him, especially given Isaiah Hartenstein's injury history.

Dybantsa is the most interesting gap in the class: 216th in 9-cat and 85th in points. He's playing heavy minutes (33.8 per night), and at 16.3 points, 6.6 rebounds, 2.3 dimes and 1.3 steals per game, the volume is there. What's missing is efficiency, at 41.6% from the field and 71.9% from the line, which hurts a 9-cat build far more than it does in points leagues. That's more of a shooting problem than a role problem, so I'd buy him now in points leagues and be more patient in 9-cat.

Wagler's main fantasy value comes at the free-throw line and 3s, where he shoots 85.9% on 5.5 attempts per game while averaging 12.5 points overall. The 37.0% shooting is an issue, and he's not providing much beyond scoring (6 combined rebounds and assists per game). However, it's a long season and the Clippers will likely increase his minutes and usage as the season progresses.

These four are 12-team options to keep on your watchlist or get a jump on before your leaguemates do.

Lendeborg and Boozer claim the top spots one month into the season, with Acuff's counting stats pushing him into the top tier. He is, after all, the best points-league rookie by a wide margin. Peterson and Mara's growing roles give them upside, and Dybantsa is one of my trade targets for points leagues. Be on the lookout for Flemings now that CJ McCollum will miss four weeks, and the more the Bucks lose, the more Burries' minutes will increase as the season goes on.

I'll update this report monthly as roles and production settle. Until then, prioritize steady minutes and production over draft pedigree.

#2700. NFL odds, betting, storylines: 2 underdogs to back in Week 11

What do NFL underdog bettors have in common with a certain billionaire tech-company CEO? Let's just say both have had a brutal couple of weeks.

Speaking specifically of the former group: NFL underdogs have won exactly four of 29 games the past two weeks. And they've covered precisely eight point spreads.

That pencils out to a 27.6% success rate.

Think that's dismal? Check this out: NFL underdogs catching four or more points since Week 9 are 1-16 SU and 4-12 ATS.

So how should an NFL underdog bettor approach Week 11, which sees eight of 13 favorites laying more than six points? Carefully. Very, very carefully.

Fact: The Broncos are on a 7-1 SU and ATS run, winning and covering their last five in a row.

Fact: Exactly one of Denver's seven victories was lopsided (a 30-16 rout of the Cardinals in Arizona in Week 8).

Here's what else is true: The Broncos have not scored more than 30 points all season; they've exceeded that plateau just three times since the 2025 campaign kicked off. And, according to the folks at SportsOddsHistory.com, they haven't covered the spread in six consecutive games since starting the 2009 season 6-0 ATS.

Speaking of history, while Denver is on a 4-0 heater in this bitter AFC West rivalry, it has defeated the Raiders by more than 10 points exactly once in 18 meetings since the start of the 2017 season.

The Raiders' point-spread record in the last 21 head-to-head matchups with Denver: 16-5.

I get it, the NFL is a constantly evolving beast. What happened three weeks ago means a whole lot more than what happened 10 years ago. Still, the Raiders have been a disaster for the better part of two decades, and yet Denver has pounded them out one time in the last nine years.

Want to focus on recently? Yes, Las Vegas is 1-7 since starting out 3-0. But it is still 6-4 ATS overall and 3-2 SU and ATS on the road. Also, a week ago with a rookie quarterback making his first start against the defending Super Bowl champs, the Raiders took a 10-7 halftime lead. It didn't hold up, but the result was still respectable (21-13 loss).

Finally, while the Broncos are 21-5 since the start of last year, only four of those wins were by more than eight points. The opposing quarterbacks in three of those blowouts? Jake Browning (currently out of the league), Jacoby Brissett (now on his seventh team) and Trey Lance (one of the biggest first-round busts of all time).

Since Kellen Moore took over in New Orleans at the start of last season, the Saints have won 10-of-26 games. Not great, right?

But the Saints have been taken to the woodshed just twice in 17 games. And both defeats were against the same division rival at home (24-10 loss to Atlanta in Week 12 last season; 45-24 loss to Atlanta in Week 4 this season).

Remove those two games, and New Orleans is 9-7 SU and 11-5 ATS in its last 16 contests — including 5-3 SU and 8-0 ATS in true road games.

The Saints' results as visitors this season: 31-30 overtime loss at Detroit as 7-point underdogs in Week 1; 24-17 win in Baltimore as 7.5-point underdogs in Week 2; 34-27 win at the Giants  as 1.5-point underdogs in Week 6.

Looking solely on this season, New Orleans has been competitive in every game but the 21-point "Monday Night Football" loss to the Falcons. What about the 23-13 home setback to Minnesota the following week? It was 13-13 going to the fourth quarter.

This is a long way of saying I trust the Saints to hang around in Chicago on Sunday.

I know the Bears emerge from their bye week on a four-game winning streak. And that the offense has been humming since Caleb Williams returned from a three-game injury absence, putting up 31, 30, 34 and 27 points.

But I also know that while the offense has averaged 28 points in the last four contests, the defense has yielded 23.8 points in the last five. And while the Bears opened the season with a 59-37 beatdown of Carolina followed two weeks later by a 27-7 thrashing of Philadelphia, they have since recorded just one victory by more than 11 points.

Perhaps most significantly, take a look at Chicago's closing stretch: at Detroit (Thanksgiving Day), vs. Jacksonville, at Miami, at Buffalo, vs. Green Bay, vs. Detroit and at Minnesota.

I wouldn't be the least bit surprised if the Bears aren't entirely focused on New Orleans this week. And even if I'm wrong about that, the fact remains Chicago is navigating uncharted waters here: It hasn't been favored by more than a touchdown since Week 16 of the 2020 season — and hasn't been a double-digit favorite since Week 9 in 2018.

#2699. Jayson Tatum’s soft technical foul cost the Celtics the game, and it was completely avoidable

The Boston Celtics had one last chance to tie the game against the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday night, trailing by three with six seconds remaining. Jamal Murray had just extended Denver's lead with a tough mid-range pull-up, and the Celtics called timeout after the ball swished through the net. As his team was walking to the huddle, Boston star Jayson Tatum threw the ball towards the official at center court. He was given a technical foul, and it ultimately cost his team the game.

The Nuggets beat the Celtics, 105-101, after the controversial technical was given to Tatum. The ESPN broadcasters agreed that Tatum deserved the technical, but fans online are still fuming after what they perceive as another soft tech for Tatum.

Tatum could have just handed the ball to the official next to him. Instead, he threw it in frustration to the official at halfcourt who wasn't looking for the ball. Watch the play here and decide if this was really worth a tech with the game on the line yourself.

Nikola Jokic knew it should have been a technical foul by the letter of the law right away. Jokic sprinted for the refs to beg for a T on Tatum, and they were already in the process of giving him one.

Section V, subsection P of the NBA rulebook describes what warrants a tech in this instance:

The deliberate act of throwing the ball or any object at an official by a player, coach, trainer, or other team bench person is a technical foul and violators are subject to ejection from the game.

Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla didn't use the tech as an excuse for why his team lost the game.

A few days earlier, Tatum was given an even stranger technical foul for clapping.

All Tatum had to do was give the ball to the ref standing next to him, and the Celtics would have had one more possession to try to tie the game. This might seem like a soft technical foul in that situation, but it was also easily avoidable.

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Prince William led tributes for Harry Kane as Wembley honoured the England captain on reaching his record-breaking 126th cap against Croatia on Thursday.

Kane, who became the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the Ballon d'Or last month, celebrated another remarkable feat as he surpassed legendary goalkeeper Peter Shilton as England's most capped player in history.

After walking out with his four children for kick-off, followed by his England team-mates, the Bayern Munich forward first held his Ballon d'Or trophy aloft to Wembley's buoyant crowd, soaking up the celebrations.

Shilton approached the England captain to present him with a medal displaying his achievement, before Kane's former Spurs team-mate Luka Modric continued the tributes by offering him another gift.

Prince William then walked on to the pitch to shake Kane's hand and present him with a framed shirt, bearing the words 'Kane 126'.

As well as holding the record for England's most capped player, the 33-year-old striker is also England's highest ever scorer with 91 goals, ahead of Wayne Rooney and Sir Bobby Charlton who netted 53 and 49 respectively during their careers.

Prince William shakes Harry Kane's hand as he celebrates the England captain's record cap

The Prince led tributes as Wembley honoured Kane ahead of England's clash with Croatia

Kane, accompanied by his four children on the pitch, held his Ballon d'Or aloft to supporters

Prince William applauded 'brilliant and remarkable' Kane on his Ballon d'Or triumph with a personal social media message after the ceremony in London.

The Prince of Wales, signing his message off with his personal 'W' initial, posted on Instagram: 'Huge congratulations to Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d'Or! What a fantastic achievement and so deserved.

'A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments.'

Kane, who has been widely regarded as a model professional and humble superstar during his career, admitted he still has an ego of sorts in an interview on the eve of his record-breaking England cap.

Asked if he has an ego, Kane replied: ‘That's a great question. I’m sure my wife will be able to say a thing or two!

'But ego is funny, because ego is many different things. I guess I have an ego to be the best, because I want to be the best. I just don't do it in a show-off way.’

On becoming England's highest appearance maker, he joked that some of his current Three Lions team-mates might catch his total by the end of their careers.

‘Jude (Bellingham) and Declan (Rice), they're on 60-odd caps already and you look at how young they are,’ he added. ‘So I'll try and give them a good number to catch! The goal record is going to be the one that's difficult to beat. I think that’s good!

He has passed Peter Shilton as England's most capped player in history - with 126 to his name

Kane receives a gift from ex-Spurs team-mate and fellow Ballon d'Or winner Luka Modric

’In football, you’ve never completed it. No matter what you’ve achieved, there is always a trophy that someone else has won or a goal record that someone else has. This is no time to rest. If anything, I've got better year on year, and the numbers have got better.

'While I'm feeling like this, why would I put any limit on myself? I'm just on the back of scoring 73 goals in one year, which is incredible, and I want to get 100 England goals as quickly as possible.

‘My biggest fear is finishing my career and thinking I could have done a bit more. I want to make sure that I cross every bridge and do everything possible so that, whenever that day comes, I can say, “I’ve done everything possible. #2697. Connor Bedard injury update is potential worst-case scenario for Blackhawks

Connor Bedard injury update is potential worst-case scenario for Blackhawks appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Chicago Blackhawks' 2026-27 season is already in serious jeopardy, and it could go completely off the rails if Connor Bedard is forced to undergo surgery for the shoulder injury he suffered on Tuesday.

The superstar forward sustained the ailment on a non-contact play during a face-off early in the third period of a 6-3 victory over the Toronto Maple Leafs at United Center.

Head coach Jeff Blashill said on Thursday that the team is consulting with the same doctor who performed Bedard's shoulder surgery this summer.

Bedard will miss at least the next four games and could face a longer absence, with the team still weighing rehab against surgery.

"Collectively as a group, I would say we're still gathering information," Blashill told reporters, including NHL.com's Tracey Myers. "Weighing the different decision process between rehab and surgery. Once those decisions are made, then I'd have more for you after that.

"He definitely won't play tonight and definitely won't play on the road trip."

The 21-year-old leads the Blackhawks with 18 points (seven goals, 11 assists) in 15 games. He scored Tuesday against Toronto before exiting the contest.

It's probably not hyperbole to say Chicago's season rests on the health of Bedard, who is far and away the most important player on the roster.

This is his third shoulder injury in less than a calendar year. The most recent came during offseason training in Vancouver in early July, leading to surgery that cost him the first six games of the 2026-27 campaign.

"His first right-shoulder injury occurred much like this one, as he was setting up for a last-second face-off against the St. Louis Blues on Dec. 12, 2025," Myers wrote. "He came back from that injury against the Washington Capitals on Jan. 9, but he didn't take face-offs in a game until Feb. 26 against the Nashville Predators, when he went 8-for-16."

With Chicago 6-13-2 and already a full 11 points back of the final wild-card berth in the Western Conference, another extended absence would be a significant blow. But for Bedard and the Blackhawks, the decision carries implications well beyond this season.

The Hawks host the Columbus Blue Jackets on Thursday night before embarking on a three-game road trip through Calgary on Saturday, Vancouver on Sunday and Seattle on Wednesday.

Bedard has amassed 221 points in 233 career NHL games. The No. 1 pick in the 2023 NHL Draft signed a five-year, $75 million contract extension prior to this season.

#2696. Brock Purdy has golden opportunity to shake up MVP race vs. Vikings

The San Francisco 49ers are facing off against the Minnesota Vikings in an NFC heavyweight battle on Sunday night in Mexico, with the No. 1 seed in the NFC on the line.

The 49ers have shown several different versions of themselves this year. We've seen dominant offensive performances throughout the year, as well as some strong defensive performances, like against the Denver Broncos.

Last week, it was the offense that led the way, as Brock Purdy threw for 389 yards and three touchdowns en route to the 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys. Normally, those numbers could be game-changing in the MVP race, especially considering how consistent Purdy has been this year.

But Cincinnati Bengals star Joe Burrow has also played exceptionally well to date and is now the runaway favorite for MVP. He's thrown for 2,795 yards (second in NFL), 27 touchdowns (first in NFL), and six interceptions, while completing an astounding 74.7 percent of his passes.

With Cincinnati sitting at 7-2, it makes sense that Burrow is the favorite for MVP, but that doesn't mean other quarterbacks like Josh Allen and Purdy still don't have a chance at the award. We saw how close the race between Drake Maye and Matthew Stafford ended up last year, and there is still a ton of regular-season football to play.

So far, Purdy has thrown for 2,369 yards, 20 touchdowns, and five interceptions, while his QBR is second in the NFL to Burrow. The biggest advantage for Purdy is that he's been the primary reason for the success of an 8-1 team. And this weekend, he'll take on the league's toughest coordinator and defense with the Minnesota Vikings, who just stifled the Green Bay Packers 30-10 on the road.

If there's any game the rest of the way that could really boost Purdy's odds for MVP, it would be this one: a primetime showdown between two top NFC teams with a ton of eyeballs on the game.

The Vikings have been excellent at throwing quarterbacks off their game defensively this season, with Brian Flores using a blitz-heavy approach to thwart quarterbacks and keep them off their game. Purdy, however, has been excellent against the blitz this season, ranking first in the NFL in passer rating against the blitz.

On Wednesday, Kyle Shanahan attributed a big part of the 49ers success amid all the moving parts to Purdy's poise.

"I just feel Brock plays the right way. Like, he just truly plays the position," Shanahan said. "He's not ever like, 'Hey, this guy's better than that guy, so I'm just going to force the ball to that guy.' Or, 'That guy didn't make the play last time, so I'm going to ignore him and go somewhere else.' Brock keeps a clear mind and just plays each play one at a time and does what he's supposed to do. If nothing's there or he can't see something or something doesn't work, then he tries to compete and make a play on his own.

"So, I don't think much changes. It's not like, 'Hey, I know you've been going to this guy all day, but he's not there so you've got to change something on you.' Brock, to me, it's the same for him, his same plan every week, regardless of who's in there. It can make it harder when some people aren't in there, but the plan never changes for him."

General manager John Lynch shared a similar sentiment this week, while believing in Purdy's preparation for the tough matchup ahead.

"I just can't say enough about Brock. Brock can play on time and rhythm, and he can also create and make things happen, as we saw the other day. You saw all of it on full display," Lynch said. "He's playing at an incredibly high level, and it's just really what we've come to expect. He's having an unbelievable season, and he knows the challenge he'll have this week against Minnesota, but I know that he'll be up for it."

This is the perfect game for Purdy to jump back into consideration for the MVP race alongside Joe Burrow, and the 49ers offense could potentially get Mike Evans back, although resting him for Week 12 against the Seattle Seahawks makes sense.

A lot will be on Purdy's shoulders, as well as Kyle Shanahan's, to devise a game plan against a defense that not many have had answers for, and it could be instrumental for the 49ers the rest of the season with the NFC race.

#2694. Fernando Mendoza’s Raiders bromance is still going strong, as postgame phone call shows

The Raiders traded Kirk Cousins to Minnesota. Nobody told Fernando Mendoza he had to lose his number.

So after Mendoza made his first NFL start Sunday against the Seahawks, he did what you might expect a young quarterback to do after spending the better part of eight months learning the job alongside an older one. He talked to Kirk.

Turns out the kid wanted to talk about how the old guy did, too.

Fernando Mendoza #15 and Cody White #82 of the Las Vegas Raiders warm up before a game at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, Nevada, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

"Yeah, we talked after both of the Raiders and the Vikings games on Sunday, and really proud of him and what he accomplished," Mendoza said.

That last part is worth a second read. Mendoza had just experienced a day he'd imagined for most of his life. He scored a touchdown of his own on his opening drive. He got sacked six times. There was enough material in his afternoon alone to keep two quarterbacks on the phone until somebody in Minnesota had to get up and shovel the driveway.

And what did Mendoza want people in Las Vegas to know about the conversation? He was proud of Cousins.

For most of their time together, you could pretty well guess which way that sentiment traveled. Cousins was the veteran starter. Mendoza was the first overall pick who would eventually take his job. Every small victory for the rookie, even something as simple as recognizing a coverage in practice that had fooled him the day before, was the kind of thing an older brother could take some pride in.

Kirk Cousins #8 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks to pass against the San Francisco 49ers in Santa Clara, Calif., Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Getty Images

Somewhere along the way, the younger brother started taking some pride in him, too.

"It's great. He's awesome. He's been a great mentor of mine, and evidently he's in a different building," Mendoza said. "And I still lean on him, and still lean on all the great mentors that I have in this building with the coaching staff and other players and leaders on our team."

Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins calls a play during an NFL game against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, in Green Bay, Wis. Tannen Maury/UPI/Shutterstock

There's something to be said for what Cousins gave Mendoza while they shared a quarterback room in Las Vegas. The rookie could watch how he worked, ask him a question, then come back the next morning with three more.

There's something even sweeter about what Cousins can give him now. His time is entirely his to offer, and Mendoza trusts him enough to keep asking for it.

The Raiders have a game to prepare for in Denver. The Vikings have their own business to attend to up in the frozen north. For the first time in months, these two can go an entire workweek without either one having much idea how the other guy is doing.

Which gives them one more reason to catch up on Sunday.

#2688. Appreciating Oso today doesn’t mean sacrificing Maluach tomorrow

There are a few things in this world I know to be true. Well done is better than well said, you should never hug a cactus, and the center position production for the Phoenix Suns has been less than stellar thus far this season. It's been a conundrum for head coach Jordan Ott to navigate since the original blueprint was disrupted in September, when Mark Williams tore his left labrum and required surgery.

The original blueprint? Start Williams, have Oso Ighodaro come off the bench, and weave opportunities for Khaman Maluach's continued development throughout the season. Perhaps those opportunities would come on the second night of a back-to-back, on nights when Williams needed rest, or in the likely scenario that Williams would miss a week or two due to injury. Instead, the significant injury to Williams derailed the entire plan, leaving Ott to navigate 48 minutes of basketball each night with some combination of Ighodaro, Maluach, and dreaded small-ball lineups.

There's a particular contingent of the Suns' fan base that seemingly despises what Oso brings to the basketball court. Whenever he has a particularly bad game, the drums begin rhythmically beating louder, like the inhabitants of Skull Island awaiting the arrival of Kong.

Guess what? When you go up against Nikola Jokic and the Denver Nuggets, chances are whoever is occupying the starting center position is in for a long night. Jokic is a three-time MVP who went for 28 points and 15 rebounds in the Suns' victory on Monday night. Yet the anti-Oso crowd will inevitably use that performance as another data point to justify why his presence in the rotation is unwarranted.

Don't get me wrong, I have my frustrations with Oso as well. One of the things we witnessed against both Denver and San Antonio, two teams possessing exceptional centers of All-NBA caliber, was how intelligently they exploited Ighodaro's offensive limitations. Whenever Oso received the basketball above the break, his defender sagged off considerably, essentially operating as a free safety while the other four defenders stuck to their assignments like glue. There's little reason to respect Ighodaro as a scoring threat from that distance because you know he's not going to pull up from 18 feet and bury a jumper in your face.

Why bother defending him out there? You can dedicate that defensive resource elsewhere, clog the interior, disrupt passing lanes, and make life considerably more difficult for the other four Suns on the court. It's sound defensive basketball, and until Oso gives opposing defenses a reason to alter that approach, it's a vulnerability that intelligent teams will continue to exploit.

Still, I don't entirely understand why some people are so vehemently opposed to Oso Ighodaro. Is it simply because he doesn't possess a jump shot? Is the allure of Khaman Maluach the answer because he can shoot a three-pointer, even though he doesn't make them with much regularity? Is there an infatuation with the modern stretch five archetype, much akin to the love affair some fans have with the traditional point guard archetype? Are we perhaps more enamored with the idea of what a player could provide than what he's actually providing?

I'm not sitting here suggesting that Oso is a complete basketball player. He has his limitations, and they're well documented. But he's a quality facilitator, as he's third on the team in assist points created (behind Booker and Gillespie). He's an excellent screener, leading the team in screen assists. He's a stellar rim runner and an average rebounder*. There is value in those attributes, even if they don't fit the archetype some envision for the center position.

*he gets pulled out to the perimeter on so many switches, it's hard to grab the defensive rebound when you're 24 feet from the rim

Ultimately, I think this requires an acknowledgment that the Suns aren't in a particularly great spot at center right now. We can't go around pissing and moaning every time one of our players gets owned by a future Hall of Famer. Nor should we be in the business of pitting our two young centers against each other, as though advocating for the development of one requires diminishing the value of the other.

The Suns are navigating a difficult situation due to an injury, and we're witnessing Khaman Maluach's development in real time. We're only 14 games into his second NBA season, and at this point, I don't believe he's equipped to handle the full responsibilities of being a starting center.

That's the operative word here. I believe he will be one day, and the developmental path the Suns currently have him on can lead him there. It's a process, one that is rushed far too often in professional sports because our desire for immediate results supersedes our appreciation for long-term development.

So if you're someone who falls into the anti-Oso camp, consider that his presence is helping set the table for the future. By absorbing responsibilities that Maluach isn't necessarily ready to handle, Ighodaro affords his younger teammate the opportunity to develop at a more reasonable pace. You can be excited about what Khaman Maluach might become while still appreciating what Oso Ighodaro provides today. There's room for both.

Denny Carter takes a close look at players who might be due for positive or negative regression headed into Week 11.

I know this sounds crazy, but Josh Downs legitimately makes the Chiefs Super Bowl contenders again. The offense opens up when he's on the field. Patrick Mahomes can actually play real quarterback and throw to real routes because there's a real receiver doing real receiver things downfield. Downs' 6.63 yards per route run last week were the second-highest among NFL wide receivers with at least four catches. Downs ran all eight of his snaps from the slot, an area of the field where he's lined up for nearly 80 percent of his career. It was remarkable to see Downs get targeted on five of his eight routes run. For context, those four receptions and 53 yards are the most Downs has had since Week 3, and this was just an early sample. We've seen a massive fantasy ceiling for receivers with Mahomes. Now, I'm not suggesting that Downs will immediately become the top target on the team and turn into Tyreek Hill or something, but we could see Downs turn into a must-start WR2 with touchdown upside every week. Looking forward, the Chiefs receivers have the fourth-easiest remaining fantasy schedule with no bye weeks and a Week 17 fantasy championship matchup against the Chargers, who are allowing the sixth-most fantasy points to receivers. This will probably be the last opportunity to buy Josh Downs, let alone buy at some sort of discount.

McBride is coming off his lowest output of the season due in large part to a tough opponent and a rookie quarterback making his debut. The McBride manager is likely a little bit nervous after last week's game and what the future may hold for this offense. That makes this week essentially the only time you can make an advantageous deal for the top tight end in fantasy. With fantasy managers fighting for the playoffs, every week becomes a must-win scenario. Over the next two weeks, McBride and the Cardinals will face the Chiefs and Commanders, who allow the seventh-most and second-most fantasy points to tight ends, respectively. The Week 14 bye for Arizona is frustrating, but that's a problem for future-you. Then, once you're in the playoffs, the Cardinals face the Jets, Saints, and Raiders, who are all in the top 12 in fantasy points allowed to tight ends. With no real target competition and a young quarterback just looking to win games, McBride becomes an easy buy-low target at a position that is perennially frustrating for fantasy football.

Over the last few weeks, Taylor's workload has decreased. In Weeks 1–6, Taylor averaged an 82 percent snap share and a 74 percent rush share. Since Week 7, those numbers have dropped to a 67 percent snap share and a 49 percent rush share.

At first, we all had the same thought: "the Colts are just protecting Taylor to trade him." Well, now the NFL trade deadline has passed, and Taylor is still with the Colts. So what gives? What we're likely seeing is a team that knows its season is over and is seeing what it has in some younger guys while keeping Taylor healthy for next year. Even in a competitive game against Miami in Week 10, rookie backup running back Seth McGowan handled 12 carries on 17 snaps compared to Taylor's 16 carries on 40 snaps. My worry here is that the Colts not only want to preserve Taylor for the future, but that the rest of the season could get ugly fast, leaving Taylor with a limited role because of game script. At first glance, it would appear that the Colts are the underdogs in each of the next two games against the Texans and Giants, with a bye week coming in Week 13. Taylor managers can expect crowded boxes along the defensive front and entire defensive game plans devised around stopping Taylor. We also have to ask the question: at what point would the Colts shut down Taylor for the season? Maybe that doesn't happen, but it's a risk I'd rather not carry on my team given the minimal upside Taylor has displayed over recent weeks.

This is a sell-low move where you hope you can get anything for him. Stevenson couldn't do much of anything against the Lions in Week 10, totaling seven touches for five yards. He's playing through a knee injury that was obviously a big factor for him. Injuries have become the identity for the Patriots at this point in the season, but at least with Stevenson, he's technically active and could have perceived RB2/flex value to one of your leaguemates. The truth is that the value simply isn't there. In fact, we may see the bottom fall out for the Patriots very soon. Drake Maye's ankle injury could spell disaster for the offense with a switch to Tommy DeVito and potentially bringing in Jimmy Garoppolo off the street. On top of the Maye injury, A.J. Brown returned only to have his appearance cut short with a hamstring issue. What's even more worrisome is that Stevenson is now in a three-headed backfield, with Corey Kiner and Lan Larison handling more than 56 percent of the snaps in the Week 10 loss. At this point in the season, I'm sure Stevenson knows that the Patriots would save more than $6 million in cap space by cutting the 29-year-old running back in the offseason. Would Stevenson consider benching himself? I know that's a wild concept, but we've seen players preserve their health for their next contract. Even if he plays, the schedule isn't very favorable, the offense is a mess, and the injury issues create a perfect storm of "I do not want this player on my fantasy team."

Burks is a really fun player. He's got speed for days and has an outside chance at being the Colts WR1 for the rest of the season in a lot of pass-heavy game scripts. In Week 10, Burks jumped from a 27 percent snap share to a 58 percent snap share. Now, there are obvious concerns. The Colts offense is not good, Daniel Jones has not been able to lead a fantasy-friendly passing attack, and Burks is a relative unknown. But looking forward in the season, the Colts receivers have the easiest remaining fantasy schedule in the NFL, and the circumstances leave an opening for someone to catch passes in this offense.

#2686. ‘Do you think Messi won because of referees?’ – Barcelona defended over Negreira case

Barcelona have been defended over the Negreira Case by a former Real Madrid striker and an ex-referee in the latest update on the saga.

Ex-Real Madrid striker Jorge López Marco 'Tote' is in no doubt at all that Barcelona did not win any games because of referees.

"It didn't influence the outcome. There was something, obviously, because the paperwork is there, but I think the right person kept all the money and cheated Barça," he told Marca.

"I've played against Barcelona my whole life. If you take Xavi, Iniesta … I could name 50 players, and tell them they won because of the referees, they'll laugh their heads off.

"Do you think Messi won because of the referees? I think Barça was cheated, they were robbed of everything, and it was divided up among a few people."

Former referee Pablo González Fuertes also spoke about Negreira and feels there is nothing to the accusations being hurled at Barca.

"I lived with Negreira. I lived through that era. Negreira was a guy who didn't even know your name. I got promoted to the First Division, and Negreira and the vice presidents back then would tell you how you were doing once a year during the season," he explained.

"You'd go to a room and they'd tell you how you were doing. I got promoted to the First Division, I walked into that room, and Negreira asked me who I was. From then on, the whole argument fell apart."

The investigation into the Negreira Case is now closed, with a verdict expected in early 2027.
