#2685. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

Here's the latest before visiting the Wolves in still-not-overly-cold Minnesota.

On Rick Brunson's decision to bring Jose Alvarado into the game against Toronto:

"Just a great call. Rick Brunson made the call of throwing Jose in to see if he can give us a spark. So, just a heckuva call by Rick Brunson and just a fantastic job by Jose producing on both sides of the ball when his name was called."

On Karl-Anthony Towns improving his passing decisions and avoiding risks:

"It's a fine balance because he's capable of making some beautiful passes in tight windows so you want to let him be him. But I thought earlier in the year — and we talked to him about it, and said it a couple times — he was trying to make the home-run pass a little too much.

"And he's gotten to a point where he's mixing it up now. We're going to trust him because he's obviously done it for many years now with good results. We'll lean on him quite a bit in that regard but if we turn the ball over too much, we'll let him know."

On Towns' basketball intelligence and ability to read the game:

"KAT's got tremendous feel. He's a smart, smart dude when it comes to a lot of things, but especially when it comes to the game of basketball."

On Towns' coachability and the impact of assistant coaches Brendan O'Connor and Darren Erman:

"It's easy to see where he is, because everything we've asked him to do, he's tried to do. So, you're extremely coachable. You got a great feel. And you got two guys in (assistant coaches) Brendan O'Connor and Darren Erman that are teaching you the game defensively at a really high level, and you're starting to see the results of it."

On the Knicks' execution and contributions throughout the roster against Toronto:

"Our execution was at an extremely high level. We had a lot of guys contribute in a lot of ways tonight."

On why the NBA must continue penalizing dangerous closeouts and landing-space violations after Brunson's injury scare:

"They got to keep track of it because it's going to happen. Everybody wants to try to block [Brunson's] shot and every other guy's shot. Some guys go forward too much and, if they do, there's got to be a heavy penalty. Because if there's no heavy penalty, then guys won't be conscious of it. They'll just keep sliding underneath guys."

On why his shooting technique sometimes exposes him to dangerous situations:

"I fade a little bit. Taller guys are usually guarding me, so I got to be able to fade a little bit. Sometimes they're not jumping straight up. They're jumping towards me. It happens."

On prioritizing getting buckets over worrying about landing on a defender's foot:

"I'm not worried about falling on his foot. I'm more worried about if he's close enough to block it. If he is too close, I probably won't shoot it. If he's not, ball is going up."

On the Knicks rediscovering their preferred style of play against Toronto:

"We just played to the best of our abilities. I know the early season hasn't looked like it, but that's how we're most comfortable."

On the disappointment of not winning a championship during his nine seasons in Minnesota:

"I wanted to win one there. I didn't accomplish that. But it was great to have those moments, to bring Minnesota back to the playoffs and be able to do a lot of things."

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

"It's going to be bittersweet. I'm just happy that I have such amazing fans and had such an amazing time in Minnesota. I love it to death. I love that place so it's going to be cool to go back."

On becoming a minority owner of Napoli's basketball team:

"Napoli is a great underdog story and reminds me of what we have built with the Knicks in many ways. It is a project built around hard work, big dreams and the incredible passion Napoli fans have for their team. I've been coming to Naples and the Amalfi Coast for years, and I know what a fan base like this can mean to a team. Seeing this club already making noise in the EuroCup tells you where it's headed.

"Matt Rizzetta and the team at Underdog Global Partners have high ambitions with a real plan for where this club is going. The Napoli journey is still very much in the first quarter, so I am excited to be a part of building this into something truly special in the years ahead."

On Instagram after being demoted from starting center to the second unit:

"Nobody gone save me, gotta save my damn self."

#2680. Record-breaking Harry Kane belongs in the company of greats that he keeps. There is only one gap in his record now and he remains as central to ending 60 years of hurt than he has ever been, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:54 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 20:17 EST, 12 November 2026

Only giants have trodden the path that Harry Kane walked at Wembley on Thursday when he strode out on to the pitch on a bitterly cold winter night, his four young children by his side, and beheld the array of trophies, honours, adulation and respect that awaited him.

It is just 16 days since Kane held his hands to his face, climbed up to the stage at the London Palladium and said 'wow' when Ronaldo 'Il Fenomeno' presented him with the Ballon d'Or trophy that anointed him the best player in the world.

Now, it sat before him on a plinth and Kane broke away from the England line-up and walked forward to hoist it aloft. He showed it to all the corners of the stadium and for a moment, it was framed against the giant tifo bearing his image and the words 'England's Finest' that towered over one end of the ground.

But the Ballon d’Or is old news in the flood of honours that is coming Kane’s way in this golden summer of a great career. Kane had become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or for a quarter of a century and on Thursday night he was to break the 37-year-old record held by Peter Shilton for the most England caps. He scored the winner, too. Of course, he did.

The occasion of England-Croatia in the Nations League was Kane's 126th appearance in an England shirt and Shilton stepped forward to hand him a small case containing a crest to mark the achievement. Finally, the Prince of Wales showed his appreciation to the England captain by presenting him with a commemorative shirt with 'Kane 126' emblazoned on it.

It was a night to feel the weight of football's history and the ghosts of greatness that people England's heritage. Kane belongs in the company he now keeps. He belongs in the pantheon of the game because he is one of the deadliest strikers in history. He belongs in the pantheon because of the humility he has shown and the dedication he devotes to improvement.

Harry Kane celebrated his record-breaking England appearance with a finely struck penalty

Before kick-off, Kane's history-making was celebrated with a commemorative shirt by the Prince of Wales

England (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Alexander-Arnold 6 (White 78, 6), Quansah 4, Burn 6, Hall 7; Rice 5 (Garner 78, 5), Anderson 6; Rogers 8, Bellingham 6, Gordon 5 (Ngumoha 78, 5); Kane 7

Croatia (4-2-3-1): Livakovic 5; Smolcic 6 (Marco Pasalic 76 5), Stanisic 6, Vuskovic 6, Gvardiol 5; Misic 5 (Modric 76, 6), Kovacic 6; Sucic 7 (Mario Pasalic 70, 5), Baturina 6, Vlasic 5; Matanovic 5 (Budimir 70, 5)

He belongs with Billy Wright, the first England player to 100 caps, and the man who set the England appearance record at 105 when he played for his country for the last time in 1959. He belongs with Bobby Charlton, who made it to 106 before the heartbreak of the 1970 World Cup quarter-final defeat to West Germany brought his international career to an end.

Kane belongs with Bobby Moore, Charlton's rival as the greatest England player of all time, who reached the new mark of 108 caps in November 1973. That was one of the great numbers in English sport until Peter Shilton finally surpassed it. He reached 125 caps by the time he played his last game for England in the third-place play-off at the 1990 World Cup.

It is quite some lineage. And now it is Kane who holds the prize. And if this was hardly a momentous match, it was a momentous occasion. If you are tired of glorying in a player like Kane, a relentless striker, a wonderful passer, the sweetest striker of the ball you will ever see, a player of vision, a man who exudes the beauty of simplicity and the wonder of modesty, then you are tired of football.

The honours are rushing at him in a giddy, babbling flood. It may be that he reaches close to 200 caps before he retires and even if it already seems likely that that record will be broken by Jude Bellingham, who has 61 caps at the age of 23, Kane's England goals tally, which stands at 92 after another goal against Croatia, will not be under threat for a generation or longer.

The gap, of course, is a tournament victory. That is what still separates Moore and Charlton from him. Kane is a dream of a player but he has not won the World Cup or the European Championship. What remains is the hope that he will put that right in the years that he has left in the game.

Winning the Nations League would not be quite the same but it would be a start and this victory over Croatia took England a small step closer to that goal. A convincing win over Spain in Madrid on Sunday would take them closer to their aim of finishing top of this group and getting a favourable draw in the quarter-finals in the spring.

Kane made his England debut in March 2015 when he was 21 and England's future looks brighter now than it did when he broke through. More than an hour before the game, the men who will follow Kane and perhaps even chase his caps record, chatted animatedly on the pitch. Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Gibbs-White are the new breed.

Morgan Rogers opened the scoring inside the opening half-an-hour and celebrated with his trademark cold celebration

England had found themselves pegged back by Croatia after slopping defending drew the visitors level

Referee Morten Krogh was summoned to the monitor to review the penalty shout on Thursday

Kane returned to Wembley triumphant for the first time since his historic Ballon d'Or win

After the Kane festivities, the first half was an anti-climax. Twenty-four minutes of relative drudgery ensued before Kane exhibited the breadth of his talent once again to help put England ahead. He got the ball 30 yards out, looked up and drifted a beautiful diagonal pass out to the right and into the path of Bellingham. Bellingham volleyed it across goal and Rogers forced it over the line.

The second half began slowly, too, but 15 minutes into it, Croatia equalised. England failed to clear a corner, Jarell Quansah tried to head the ball back to Jordan Pickford and, as Kane watched on, Petar Sucic stole in and hooked the ball past the England goalkeeper into the roof of the net.

Quansah made some kind of amends three minutes later when he was dragged down in the box and Danish referee Morten Krogh awarded a penalty. It was Kane-time again. Kane took the kick and lifted it gently and with a touch of curl down the centre of the goal. Dominic Livakovic dived to his left and the ball sailed softly over his trailing leg and into the net.

Croatia had chances to draw level but could not take them. England made changes and young Rio Ngumoha, a winger of rare talent, another with a rich future ahead of him, another who will help to fill the void when the day comes for Kane to bid farewell to England, came on as a late substitute for Gordon.

And so Kane's night of history began to draw to a close. In a 2-1 victory, he had made one and scored one. He remains as central to England's hopes of ending more than 60 years without a trophy as he ever has been. In a career that has festooned him with garlands and left no one in doubt of his greatness, it is the only gap that remains.

Harry Kane has set his sights firmly on rapidly reaching a century of international goals after becoming England’s most-capped player of all time.

The England skipper marked his 126th appearance for the Three Lions with the winner against Croatia in the Nations League – his first goal since picking up the Ballon d’Or last month.

Kane was afforded an emotional presentation pre-match at Wembley to mark both achievements and is already thinking of creating more history after moving within eight goals of a ton.

‘It’s achievable,’ Kane said. ‘I’m getting closer. Breaking the appearance record is a massive thing in the history of our game, seeing the tifo at the stadium and having my kids with me was beyond dreams.

‘It’s important to recognise our great players. It’s maybe something we haven’t done so well over the years with some of our other greats.

‘It's been a crazy few weeks. I don’t know if I’ve fully taken it all in. The reception has been overwhelming.

‘Maybe during the winter break I’ll be on a beach reflecting on everything I’ve achieved, having a drink with my wife.’

Croatia legend Luka Modric, 41, was part of the presentations ahead of kick off and Kane did not rule out attempting to prolong his career in a similar vein to the AC Milan midfielder.

‘He’s an inspiration for a lot of us,’ Kane added. ‘An incredible player and a great person, he’s looked after himself and still to be playing at this level is inspiring for me to push the limits. To see where your body and mentality takes you.

‘As long as I feel I can help, I’ll be here for as long as I can. If that’s until I’m 40, we’ll wait and see.’

Now qualified for the quarter-finals, England need to beat Spain in Madrid on Sunday to top their group and Thomas Tuchel believes they can topple the world champions.

‘It’s a completely different scenario, completely different setup,’ Tuchel said. ‘But I'm very positive that we will get what we want.’

#2678. After record-breaking contract, Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey is having his worst season

In April, the Cowboys signed kicker Brandon Aubrey to a four-year, $28 million contract, making him the highest-paid kicker in NFL history. That decision has not aged well.

Aubrey, who missed an extra point in Sunday's loss to the 49ers, is having the worst season of his NFL career this year.

Aubrey has made just 79.2 percent of his field goals this season, the worst mark of his career. And he's made just 92.6 percent of his extra points this season, also the worst mark of his career.

Those numbers aren't just bad for the highest-paid kicker in the league, they're bad for an average kicker. The league average field goal success rate this season is 84.5 percent, and the league average extra point success rate this season is 95.2 percent. Aubrey ranks 21st in the NFL in field goal percentage and 24th in extra point percentage.

Aubrey does still have a strong leg, as evidenced by the 60-yarder he hit against the Ravens. But in today's NFL, plenty of kickers have strong legs, and many of them are kicking long field goals more accurately than Aubrey is: On field goals from 50 yards and longer, Aubrey is 5-for-10 this year. There's nothing special about making 50 percent of your kicks from 50 yards out; there are 25 kickers in the NFL who have made more than 50 percent of their field goal attempts from beyond 50 yards this season.

Ups and downs for kickers aren't unusual, but this is by far the lowest "down" of Aubrey's career. And it's happening after the Cowboys made him the highest-paid kicker in NFL history.

#2677. The Sixers’ performance in crunch-time games is Good, Actually

At first, the Sixers appeared to be headed toward a blowout loss against the Orlando Magic on Wednesday. They were without all three of Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown and Dean Wade (along with Dominick Barlow and Adem Bona), and they fell into a 27-12 hole less than eight minutes into the game. Instead, the Sixers proceeded to outscore the Magic by 20 points over the remaining 40 minutes, sneaking out of Orlando with a 121-116 win.

That was their 11th clutch win of the season, which the NBA defines as a game that gets within a five-point margin with no more than five minutes remaining in regulation. The Sixers are now 11-0 in such games this season, which is by far the best record in the league. In fact, that record in clutch games puts them in rarefied air, as Mike Lynch of Sports Reference shared after Wednesday's win.

Granted, that clearly unsustainable crunch-time record is also fuel for skepticism about how good the Sixers actually are. It's safe to say that their net rating of plus-46.1 in those situations probably won't hold up for an entire season, particularly given that their overall net rating is only plus-2.7.

None of this is breaking news or hard-hitting journalism. It's stating the obvious. The Sixers are running unsustainably hot in clutch situations and will eventually lose one of these games. However, anyone who's using that record to downplay what they've done thus far this season is missing two crucial points.

The new-look Sixers are still developing chemistry with one another. They're figuring out how best to optimize their schemes both offensively and defensively. That very much remains a work in progress over a full 48-minute game, but the fact that they've been able to lock in at the end of games bodes well. That speaks to an attention to detail that Sixers teams in the past have lacked.

Granted, it helps when you have LeBron James orchestrating your late-game offense. But that's also the point. The "who takes the last shot?" questions from the offseason haven't proved to be a concern at all yet. The answer, unsurprisingly, is that the Sixers don't have a designated last-shot taker. All five guys in their starting lineups are legitimate offensive threats, so they've been adept at hunting mismatches and attacking their opponents' weak spots. That is playoff basketball in a nutshell.

Would it be ideal if the Sixers started blowing teams out so they weren't so reliant on crunch time? Of course. Buying their starters extra rest throughout the grind of the 82-game season would be a godsend. However, there's also value in getting this much crunch-time experience in the regular season, particularly for a team that's working to incorporate so many new pieces on the fly.

"You've gotta go through shit," LeBron said in the season premiere of his Mind the Game podcast this offseason. "… Those are some of the moments that we have to be able to go through some real, live battle moments, in the fight, in order to know really who we are and what we want to become. We've gotta peel the onion. We have to."

Being in these close-and-late situations will help the Sixers develop muscle memory that they can tap into later in the season and in the playoffs. They can see which plays worked and didn't work in those gotta-have-it moments. The best teams use the regular season as a lab to experiment so they have as many answers to the test as possible before the playoffs begin.

There's also a psychological component to their crunch-time performance that could pay dividends down the line. The more close wins they rack up, the more belief they'll have in one another no matter the circumstances. They'll begin to believe that no lead is insurmountable and that they can overcome any obstacle thrown in their way.

In last year's playoffs, the New York Knicks overcame double-digit deficits in every Finals game. They were 6-2 in playoff games where they went down by 10 or more points, which was the best playoff record for any team in the 30 years of play-by-play data, according to NBA.com's John Schuhmann. That didn't just suddenly begin in the playoffs, though.

"What you have to respect about the Knicks, you have to put them away every single possession," Miami Heat head coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters after the Knicks overcame a double-digit deficit in the first half of a game last December. "You can't leave anything to effing chance with that team ever. That's what they do. What they have is a will to win, all right."

LeBron and the Sixers have spent all season discussing the need for them to develop championship habits. Their early-season level of crunch-time performance might not be sustainable, but the way that they're playing in those moments matters just as much. Valuing every possession on offense and locking in defensively are non-negotiables for them to accomplish their goal of winning a championship this year.

The added bonus is that by getting off to such a hot start, they've reduced the temperature under Nick Nurse's seat for the time being. Had they stumbled out of the gate like most early-LeBron teams tend to do, Stephen A. Smith and Kendrick Perkins would likely be all over ESPN's airwaves calling for his head.

The Sixers are by no means a finished product. They'd be the first ones to admit that. But learning to win in crunch time despite that bodes well for their long-term outlook, even if it means their actual record is misaligned with their expected record for the time being. (Don't worry, Cleveland, you can still be the reigning NBA Analytics Champions.)

#2676. Anthony Gordon at Barcelona: A promising beginning, but the best is yet to come

Anthony Gordon signed for Barcelona from Newcastle United in the summer and took barely four minutes to make the Spotify Camp Nou fall in love with him.

Coming off the bench against Elche, the Englishman registered two assists in quick succession, setting the tone for what fans could expect from him.

The second assist was what really caught everyone's attention. Gordon could have scored himself but unselfishly laid it off for Fermin Lopez, who was in a better position.

Nearly three months later, his desire to work for his team has been the biggest talking point surrounding his arrival.

Gordon arrived from the English club in a deal worth around €70 million plus potential bonuses. He was expected to bring Premier League experience to Barça.

His relentless energy and genuine pace made him the perfect fit for Hansi Flick's system, and his initial impact was remarkable.

The 25-year-old attacker quickly established himself as an important creative outlet, providing much-needed impetus down the left flank with Raphinha moving centrally.

Off to a bright start. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

However, goals have proved hard to come by. It took him until October to open his account against Getafe.

He then scored against Galatasaray in the Champions League and Deportivo Alaves in the league.

By the November international break, he had registered three goals across 15 appearances, but expectations of him were much higher.

Gordon himself said as much, admitting that while he had settled in and started well, he could offer much more to the Catalan giants.

It is very evident that Hansi Flick has immense trust in Gordon and his footballing abilities.

Despite strong competition from Karim Adeyemi, the German manager has started the England international in Barcelona's three big fixtures against PSG, Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid.

However, his performances in these big games have left a lot to be desired, and this is an area he needs to work on.

Gordon may not possess the explosiveness of Adeyemi, but his intelligence and hard-working nature make him an invaluable member of this system.

Still a long way to go. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

His relationship with Fermin in particular has been interesting in these early weeks and is one to keep an eye on.

The next step for Gordon is to turn these promising performances into match-defining ones and add goals to his game.

While his unselfishness might have endeared him to the Blaugrana fans, he might have to start being more selfish on certain occasions.

Barcelona do not need Gordon to be another Raphinha or Lamine Yamal, but they need him to be the best version of himself.

They need him to be more decisive when the moments present themselves, especially in the big Champions League games.

He knows how to get into dangerous positions, play smart passes to his team-mates and link up with them. If he can sharpen his finishing, Gordon's ceiling is frighteningly high.

Flick must also manage his workload carefully, with the former Evertonian having accumulated substantial minutes in these early weeks.

The foundations have been encouraging, and the hope is that Gordon evolves from a hard-working winger into a reliable one in the coming months.

#2674. Brock Bowers returns to practice ahead of Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 11 matchup against Denver Broncos

The Las Vegas Raiders received good news ahead of their Week 11 matchup against the Denver Broncos. ESPN's Ryan McFadden posted a video of tight end Brock Bowers in full pads and participating in warmups ahead of Thursday's practice, noting that Bowers is returning to the field.

The Raiders' leading receiver exited last week's game against the Seattle Seahawks at halftime and missed Wednesday's session with ankle and quadricep injuries. While his exact status (limited or full participant) won't be known until the injury report comes out, this appears to be a step in the right direction for Bowers being able availabe on Sunday against the Broncos. And Las Vegas' offense really needs its top target.

The 'tight end' has racked up 50 catches for 676 yards and six touchdowns in eight games this season, leading the Silver and Black in all three categories despite missing the first two contests with a knee injury. According to Sumer Sports, the team's passing game averages 0.105 EPA per pass and has a 49.0 percent success rate with Bowers on the field this year. #2672. What Carlos Alcaraz has done at the ATP Finals which hasn’t been seen since 2018

Carlos Alcaraz has been dominant at the ATP Finals so far.

The second seed won his first two matches in straight sets, dropping just 10 total games against Frances Tiafoe and Daniil Medvedev. After beating Tiafoe 6-2, 6-2, Alcaraz defeated Medvedev 6-2, 6-4.

No player has conceded fewer games in their opening two matches at the ATP Finals in eight years. But who was the last player to lose 10 or fewer games, and did he go all the way and win the tournament?

South Africa's Kevin Anderson was the last man to have dominated their first two matches at the ATP Finals to the same degree as Alcaraz in 2026. Anderson arrived in London eight years ago full of confidence, having won the Vienna Open on indoor hard courts just a few weeks before.

That confidence shone through in his opening two matches at the O2 Arena. Anderson beat Dominic Thiem 6-3, 7-6 (Lost nine games) before taking down Kei Nishikori 6-0, 6-1 (Lost one game).

Unfortunately for Anderson, the wins stopped there… He returned to play Roger Federer in his final group-stage match, which he lost in straight sets, 4-6, 3-6. Despite losing to the Swiss star, Anderson advanced to the semi-finals, where he met another legend, Novak Djokovic.

He won only four games in the semis, losing to Djokovic 2-6, 2-6. Anderson made such a positive start at the 2018 ATP Finals, but couldn't keep it up, exiting the tournament with two wins and two defeats. The South African never returned to the year-end finals after 2018.

Alcaraz will look to do what Anderson couldn't and win the ATP Finals after winning his first two matches, losing 10 or fewer games. However, Alcaraz's injury could hurt his title chances.

After receiving treatment during his win over Medvedev, Alcaraz underwent an MRI on Thursday. The results cleared him to play his next match against Flavio Cobolli, but his long-term fitness remains a concern.

Alcaraz will play Cobolli on Friday, November 20, before returning a day later for his semi-final match. The Spaniard could meet Alexander Zverev, Ben Shelton, or Arthur Fils in the last four.

The world number three has never won the ATP Finals, but with rival and two-time defending champion Jannik Sinner missing this year, he will surely fancy his chances of winning the year-end championships. Only time will tell if his latest injury prevents him from going all the way and taking the title in Turin.

#2667. Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

Published: 05:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:21 EST, 13 November 2026

Pat Cummins is either the greatest actor in world sport – or the claim that the whole Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago is a figment of Usman Khawaja’s imagination.

After Cummins’s remarkable press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, in which he called Khawaja’s various assertions ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship, it was hard to discern any common ground, much less spot a middle way.

According to the blue corner, everyone was in on the scam, sandpaper was used not just at Cape Town but in the previous Test at Port Elizabeth, and there was a team meeting to discuss the question of collective responsibility.

According to the red, those who knew about the plan did not include the bowlers, nothing untoward happened at Port Elizabeth, and there was no meeting.

The only thing that can be said for certain after another tumultuous 24 hours for Australian cricket was that the two corners are now polar opposites, each eyeing the other with suspicion and incredulity. Barring an improbable climbdown, the twain can never meet.

Cummins, it must be said, eased into his work after an emotional start behind a lectern at the Cricket Central venue in Sydney’s Olympic Park. He began by stating his basic position, then invited questions, which for the next hour and a bit he handled with aplomb and a degree of statesmanship.

Pat Cummins held a remarkable press conference in Sydney to address the sandpaper claims

Speaking for more than an hour, Cummins dismissed Khawaja’s various assertions as ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship

This will not please those who still find it impossible to believe that Cummins and his fellow seamers on that trip, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, knew nothing of the scheme that led to bans for three batsmen – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

After all, as any bowler will tell you, the idea that the condition of their most prized possession might be altered without their noticing is as absurd as trying to persuade a batsman to walk out without his favourite willow.

And yet. Cummins stuck to his guns, in contrast to Khawaja’s appearance on the ABC on Wednesday evening, when he repeatedly declined to name Cummins as one of the guilty party. And while Khawaja reacted to his TV grilling by cancelling media engagements, Cummins made it clear he would be answering every question that came his way.

Whichever side you believe, and whatever the doubts that remain, his press conference grabbed the momentum from Team Khawaja.

It also made the previous day’s appearance by Mitchell Marsh, Australia’s white-ball captain for the next three weeks against England, all the more bizarre. By refusing to engage with any of the questions raised by Khawaja’s autobiography, Marsh – himself a veteran of South Africa 2018 – did little to dispel the suspicion that Khawaja had a point.

And that in turn encouraged the view that Cummins, who called his own press conference without the knowledge of Cricket Australia, might be about to come clean.

Instead, he doubled down on the denial he and his bowling colleagues had issued in 2021, but now went further, taking a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Khawaja’s integrity.

‘Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,’ said Cummins. ‘He’s dealt with the way he’s presented his story in a very casual manner and it affects a lot of people. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment, because I don’t think that’s OK. It’s not what friends do.’

Cummins plainly intended this to be his final word on the matter, but the problem facing Australian cricket is that the sore may never properly heal.

David Warner then hit back at Cummins and accused him of 'throwing Khawaja under the bus'

Only a couple of hours after Cummins finished, Warner – at Perth’s Optus Stadium as a TV pundit for the first ODI between Australia and England – was being asked for his view, and he didn’t hold back, repeating his belief that Khawaja’s version of events was ‘the truth’.

He added: ‘I really, really support him. I actually feel for him at the moment. I feel that the captain today threw Uzzy under the bus and I’m very, very disappointed about that.’

Disappointment. It’s mutual, and it’s everywhere. Cummins provided a brief distraction, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is a civil war with no obvious resolution.

Offered the chance to kick Australian cricket while it was down, England made humiliating contact with fresh air on the opening day of their eight-match white-ball trip.

Only hours after Pat Cummins had added a twist to the sandpaper saga by dismissing Usman Khawaja’s claims that the whole squad knew about the ball-tampering plans in South Africa eight years ago as ‘complete and utter nonsense’, Harry Brook’s side were blown away for 131 in the first ODI – having at one stage been 65 for eight.

Australia then romped home by seven wickets with more than 26 overs in hand to take a 1–0 lead into the second game of this three-match series in Adelaide on Sunday. For England, anyway, complete and utter nonsense felt about right.

It is not quite a year since they began their Ashes campaign here at the Optus Stadium by being bowled out in 32.5 overs in their first innings and 34.4 in their second – before stumbling to a 4–1 defeat.

Now, they obligingly split the difference, dismissed in 33.4 as Mahli Beardman, a 21-year-old fast bowler from Dunsborough, a couple of hours drive down the coast from Perth, picked up six for 34 – the best figures for Australia by an ODI debutant.

His first victim was Joe Root, caught behind for a painful 17 off 36 balls, and his second Brook, who had made only a single when he fidgeted fatally outside off stump.

That might have been enough to satisfy most newcomers, but Beardman had barely started. Jordan Cox made two before edging a poke, and Sam Curran top-edged a pull to fine leg for a duck.

When Liam Dawson, yet to score, squeezed a drive to backward point, Beardman had five wickets in 28 balls – not bad for a player whose only previous taste of international cricket had come in a T20 in Pakistan in January.

He then ended a lively last-wicket stand of 29 by removing Jofra Archer, who had just driven him down the ground for four. It was the only authentic boundary England managed off his bowling: the other, a streaky inside edge from Root, summed up the problems posed by his pace, bounce and accuracy. As bids for a place on next summer’s Ashes tour go, this was hard to ignore.

‘Laying in bed last night, that’s not what I had planned,’ said Beardman, who was taken under his wing by Australian fast-bowling legend Dennis Lillee after a mutual friend spotted him as a young teenager bowling at a bin down the side of a house. ‘It was an incredible game and it all happened so fast.’

If England had learned lessons from their collapses in the last year’s Test here, they showed little sign of being able to implement them. Players drove on the up, as they had so heedlessly a year earlier, and failed to cope with the Perth bounce.

England head coach Brendon McCullum was critical of his side's failure to adapt to the pitch, and called on them to learn from their mistakes going forward.

'It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline,' said McCullum. 'There are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away. We probably knew we were in for a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.

'We're disappointed but there are some good lessons for us. If you look towards the World Cup in South Africa there’s going to be some pitches there that will test us from a bounce point of view.'

And all this after they had played a warm-up game at the WACA – a grievous omission before the Ashes – and trained with such intensity that white-ball mentor Kevin Pietersen had declared it the best practice session he had seen from an England team.

In the event, their top-scorer was Gus Atkinson, who hit an unbeaten 29 from No 10, including England’s only six.

Mitchell Marsh, stroke-less in the previous day’s press conference, put that into perspective by clearing the ropes four times during a 29-ball half-century, while Cooper Connolly – dropped by Tom Banton at midwicket on five – hit two sixes himself.

England’s only consolation had come at the start of Australia’s reply, when Atkinson bowled Travis Head first ball off the inside edge. Head it was who had taken care of Australia’s fourth-innings chase here a year ago, thrashing a 69-ball century that knocked the stuffing out of Ben Stokes’s attack.

Instead, it was Marsh who went for his shots, stopped only when he flicked Jamie Overton to Ben Duckett at deep midwicket, by which time Australia were already halfway there. For a few hours, at least, no one was talking about sandpaper.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2665. Julius Randle on Nets' 'embarrassing' blowout loss to Bulls: 'One of the worst games I've ever been a part of'

The Brooklyn Nets wore red, white and blue alternate uniforms on Wednesday night, throwing it back to the franchise's ABA heyday when they welcomed the Chicago Bulls to Barclays Center. The evening featured an appearance by 10 members of the teams that won ABA championships in 1974 and 1976 — including the legendary "Dr. J," Julius Erving.

"I fully anticipated the Nets to be so fired up having us here, they would blow Chicago out," the Hall of Famer said during an appearance on the YES Network broadcast midway through the second quarter. "But I'm looking at 62-39, so … I was wrong."

The Nets scored Wednesday's first basket, with young guard Nolan Traoré getting a runout dunk after Egor Dëmin picked off a Josh Giddey pass. A minute later, Bulls guard Norman Powell knocked down a 3-pointer to put Chicago on top … and, well, that was all she wrote for Brooklyn.

The Nets never again led, or even tied, the visitors, trailing by as many as 37 points in a truly dismal performance that settled as a 137-107 blowout loss. At home. At the hands of what had been a three-win team, with the NBA's fifth-worst offense and absolute worst defense … and without exciting lottery pick Caleb Wilson.

It was a wretched outing — one that saw the Nets commit 20 turnovers leading to 27 Chicago points, and allow 15 first-half 3-pointers and 76 first-half points, the third straight game in which they conceded 70-plus before intermission. Brooklyn gave up 62 total points in the paint, and sat idly by as eight different Bulls scored in double figures.

In the midst of the depressing showing, courtside cameras caught Brooklyn forward Julius Randle lighting into his teammates on the Nets bench:

After finishing the night with 17 points, four assists and no rebounds in 27 minutes of work in the lopsided loss, Randle — who's soldiered through a 17-win season with the Lakers, the post-Anthony Davis doldrums in New Orleans, and the 21-win end of the David Fizdale era in New York — sounded a similarly dour note about the state of affairs for the 3-11 Nets in his postgame press conference.

"That was embarrassing," Randle said, according to Brian Lewis of the New York Post. "Been in the league for 13 years, and that's one of the worst games I've ever been a part of. And not because of the score … but it's how we did it. That wasn't cool. Nothing about it was cool. We've got to find a way to figure out the root of it or whatever, but that's just unacceptable. It's just a pride, an effort, the competitive spirit — all of that, it was nonexistent."

The Nets entered Wednesday intending to celebrate the high-water mark in franchise history, but wound up closer to a historic nadir. According to Erik Slater of Clutch Points, the last two losses "mark the first time they've given up 135 points in back-to-back games since April 1 [and] 2, 1969."

That's a far cry from where the Nets hoped to be after trading this summer for Randle, a three-time All-Star and two-time All-NBA selection who'd starred for the cross-town New York Knicks before helping the Minnesota Timberwolves make a pair of playoff runs, to pair with incumbent sweet-shooting forward Michael Porter Jr. in the frontcourt, in hopes of restoring a franchise that had the third-worst record in the NBA over the preceding three seasons to respectability.

But despite the presence of the 20-point-scoring veteran forwards and some exciting flashes from young guards Traoré, Dëmin and rookie Mikel Brown Jr., Brooklyn has remained mired in the muck, ranking among the league's worst teams on both ends of the court and looking like a team without much of a sense of who it wants to be, how it wants to play, and what its path to success might look like.

"Very disappointed, just starting with effort," head coach Jordi Fernández said after the game, according to C.J. Holmes of the New York Daily News. "We were not a competitive group. We were not a connected group. We were not a selfless group. I saw selfishness. I saw pointing fingers, and I saw guys that didn't always play hard."

That's not the brand of ball that Fernández has preached since arriving in Brooklyn in 2024. The team's desultory effort, though, suggests that maybe what he's preaching isn't quite getting across.

"I can try to say it in Spanish, because in English, they don't understand," Fernández quipped after the game. "So I'll keep trying and find whatever language works. But yeah, our effort was not good."

Julius Randle didn't mince words when describing the state of affairs for his 3-11 Nets. (Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

If the coach's message is falling on deaf ears, then it's up to the players to stem the tide and turn things around. Randle appeared to be searching for a way to do so with his impassioned entreaty on the bench; with another game coming against the Orlando Magic on Friday, he says he and his teammates have to look within for the answers they're seeking.

"I think when you win, you find ways to win. When you lose, you find excuses. Seems like a lot of excuses," Randle said, according to Collin Helwig of NetsDaily. "So, you know, for me, I've got to go back into work. I've got to go back into the film. I've got to figure out — I've got to look myself in the mirror tonight, too, like everybody else, and figure out what I can do better. Not point the finger or anything. Like, I got to figure out as a man [...] that has played this game since a kid and love it, and has given a lot to me, I got to figure out how I can help the team and be better for the team. So, you know, I put it on me."

#2663. Burnt Hills-Ballston Lake star Jahmal Owens chasing down a state football championship

BURNT HILLS - This season, Burnt Hills-Ballston Lake football's Jahmal Owens has recorded two sacks.

The number that more accurately reflects the 5-foot-11, 220-pound senior defensive end's impact for the Spartans, though, is 19, which is how many quarterback hurries Owens has recorded this year as one of the area's best pass rushers.

"He has a lot of hurries and he absolutely gets mauled out there," BH-BL head coach Kevin DeBonis said. "He is really disruptive and just runs a lot of stuff down."

"I think he makes up for his (lack of) size with his speed," said BH-BL senior linebacker Logan Tomlinson, a four-year varsity player. "He has the speed. He really is a fast guy and can run down some running backs. It is probably pretty scary for a running back knowing that if you don't outrun this guy, it is going to be embarrassing not outrunning a D-end."

Owens, who also starts on offense at left tackle, has been a vital component for the Spartans, who won the Section 2 Class A championship last week. BH-BL, ranked No. 8 in the state, returns to action Friday night at Colonie High School for a state quarterfinal contest against Section 9 champion Cornwall (8-3). Game time is 6 p.m.

Owens, who has posted 45 tackles (10 for loss), plays on a three-man defensive line along with senior end Michael Turgeon and senior nose guard Elijah Rosendo. The trio averages just 219 pounds, yet the unit has caused plenty of havoc by disrupting plays, occupying blocks and helping the team's four starting linebackers gain access to register tackles.

"They do a good job of holding their own and letting someone else rally to the ball. With those ends, we ask a ton from them because they are giving up so much size," DeBonis said. "Honestly, (Owens) doesn't care about stats. He is just the most humble kid. All he wants to do is win. The kids love him because he plays so hard."

"Everything I do, I do for the team," Owens said. "I try to open up a gap so my linebackers can come in."

Owens is truly relentless on defense and has been able to maintain his impact on that side of the ball while also helping to fuel the Spartans' ground game and protect junior quarterback Tristan West's blind side from his tackle position.

"He has never loved offense, but this year, he has embraced it. We only have a few guys going both ways. That dude needs to go both ways," DeBonis said.

"I try to enjoy the sport as much as possible and keep working hard," Owens said.

Owens hopes to continue playing football in college. His older brother, Jahi Owens, also played defensive line at BH-BL at a similar size. He graduated high school in 2010 and then played four years at Buffalo State.

"I wanted to be like him. My brother inspired me," Jahmal Owens said. "I feel like I have done pretty good, but I need to do better. We are now playing better competition and I still do not think I have reached my potential yet."

"Jahmal is just so tough. What he brings for us are just so many intangibles," DeBonis said. "He plays with joy, but there is a fire in there."

In his first season as a starter in 2025, Owens and his teammates experienced a 4-6 campaign that included a sectional quarterfinal loss against Troy - the same opponent the Spartans edged 23-21 in the Class A Super Bowl last week.

"I've had so much fun this season, more than I've had in all the years I have been playing football," Owens said. "Our biggest priority right now is to make it to the state title game."

The Raiders got an encouraging sign Thursday regarding Brock Bowers' availability for Sunday's game against the Denver Broncos.

The star tight end was on the practice field during the portion of Thursday's workout open to the media, a potentially significant development after he sat out Wednesday's practice with an ankle injury.

Bowers' official practice designation won't be revealed until later Thursday afternoon, so it remains unclear how much work he was able to do or whether he will be available Sunday.

Brock Bowers of the Las Vegas Raiders leaves the field after an injury against the Seattle Seahawks in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

Nevertheless, his presence on the field represented a step in the right direction for the Raiders and rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza, who could certainly use his most dangerous offensive weapon against one of the NFL's premier defenses.

Bowers injured his ankle on the Raiders' opening possession against the Seattle Seahawks last Sunday. Although he initially attempted to return after being evaluated on the sideline, he quickly retreated to the bench and was eventually ruled out for the remainder of the game.

His absence was a significant blow to Mendoza, who was making his first NFL start against a Seattle defense that presented a series of difficult challenges.

Without Bowers, Mendoza was deprived of his most reliable receiving option and one of the NFL's most dynamic tight ends.

The Seahawks eventually overwhelmed the Raiders' offense, sacking Mendoza six times and making life increasingly difficult for the rookie as the game progressed.

Fernando Mendoza (15) of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before a game at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. The Seahawks defeated the Raiders 21-13. Getty Images

The Broncos feature an aggressive defense coordinated by Vance Joseph, whose pressure packages and talented pass rush present another daunting assignment for Mendoza in his second career start.

Having Bowers available would provide Mendoza with a dependable target capable of creating separation, making contested catches and turning short completions into significant gains.

Las Vegas Raiders' Michael Mayer avoids a tackle from Seattle Seahawks' Josh Jobe during a game in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

It would also give Raiders coach Klint Kubiak considerably more flexibility in designing an offensive game plan intended to better protect his young quarterback.

That is especially important given the Raiders' continued struggles running the football and protecting the passer.

For now, Thursday's development offers reason for optimism.

Whether that translates into Bowers being available Sunday remains to be seen, but his return to the practice field was an encouraging first step.

If he can't play, Mendoza will likely lean on Michael Mayer, who combines with Bowers to form one of the best tight end tandems in the NFL.

#2660. Jayson Tatum owns late technical that sealed Boston's loss to Denver

To be clear: Jayson Tatum's technical foul with 6.4 seconds left in regulation wasn't the reason Boston lost to Denver on Wednesday night. The Nuggets dominated the second half, and when they doubled Tatum, the Celtics' offense struggled to be efficient, especially when their 3-point shooting went cold.

But after a Jamal Murray bucket that put the Nuggets up 104-101 with 6.4 seconds left, Tatum was hit with a controversial technical for throwing the ball toward the official John Goble, who wasn't looking at him, rather than handing it to baseline official, Eric Dalen, who was near him. Tatum and the Celtics were frustrated about a no-call on a screen to get Murray open for the shot and Dalen saw Tatum's toss as throwing the ball at an official in frustration. Tatum said postgame that was not the case.

"I told [Dalen], I wasn't mad. Wasn't a foul on me, we just called a timeout," Tatum said. "John Goble called a timeout and pointed at our bench. Thought he was looking this way, but yeah, he called a tech. For me, just find the female ref that was there, or the other ref, and whoever was probably closest, I should have just gave them the ball."

Murray sank the technical free throw, making it a four point game, and that was essentially the ballgame. The Heat could not just tie it in one possession.

After the game, coach Joe Mazzulla said Tatum has to be better as the team leader.

"We can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret it a certain type of way," Mazzulla said from the podium. "Gotta be better."

Tatum dropped 20 on the Nuggets in the first half. However, Denver focused more on doubling him in the second half, and he scored just four points on 2-of-6 shooting with five turnovers. Mazzulla said Tatum needs to be better under pressure than he was in the second half. Boston also needs to find a way to score more efficiently when defenses focus on him, because that is what will happen in the playoffs. There is a long time to go between now and the start of the postseason, but this is when coaches and teams need to build the good habits and patterns they will need in the NBA's second season.

You can't make the playoffs in 10 games, but you can definitely give yourself some breathing room when the inevitable ebbs and flows of the season strike. That's exactly what the Boston Bruins have done as they've stood out for the right reasons in a deep Atlantic Division.

Boston currently leads the division with 15 points, and while the Tampa Bay Lightning's record is technically better, the Bruins' plus-14 goal differential is tied for second in the NHL.

The biggest reason for this fast start has been the play of Jeremy Swayman in goal. He's allowed one or fewer goals in half of his starts, and Swayman's 8.02 goals saved above average ranks second to old Beantown running mate Linus Ullmark, per Natural Stat Trick.

We have a long way to go before we start discussing Vezina Trophy candidates seriously, but Swayman certainly has the potential to carry Boston to the postseason.

It helps that David Pastrnak is an elite playmaker, and the Bruins have been getting contributions from young forwards Fraser Minten and James Hagens. Morgan Geekie has also gone from goal-scoring machine to distributor with seven assists in 10 games.
